As detailed above, the GDPR requires that, in the case of a breach, the controller shall notify the breach without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it. This may raise the question of when a controller can be considered to have become “aware” of a breach. The EDPB considers that a controller should be regarded as having become “aware” when that controller has a reasonable degree of certainty that a security incident has occurred that has led to personal data being compromised. 32. However, as indicated earlier, the GDPR requires the controller to implement all appropriate technical protection and organisational measures to establish immediately whether a breach has taken place and to inform promptly the supervisory authority and the data subjects. It also states that the fact that the notification was made without undue delay should be established taking into account in particular the nature and gravity of the breach and its consequences and adverse effects for the data subject24. This puts an obligation on the controller to ensure that they will be “aware” of any breaches in a timely manner so that they can take appropriate action. 33. When, exactly, a controller can be considered to be “aware” of a particular breach will depend on the circumstances of the specific breach. In some cases, it will be relatively clear from the outset that there has been a breach, whereas in others, it may take some time to establish if personal data have been compromised. However, the emphasis should be on prompt action to investigate an incident to determine whether personal data have indeed been breached, and if so, to take remedial action and notify if required. Examples 1. In the case of a loss of a USB key with unencrypted personal data it is often not possible to ascertain whether unauthorised persons gained access to that data. Nevertheless, even though the controller may not be able to establish if a confidentiality breach has taken place, such a case has to be notified as there is a reasonable degree of certainty that an availability breach has occurred; the controller would become “aware” when it realised the USB key had been lost. 2. A third party informs a controller that they have accidentally received the personal data of one of its customers and provides evidence of the unauthorised disclosure. As the controller has been presented with clear evidence of a confidentiality breach then there can be no doubt that it has become “aware”. 3. A controller detects that there has been a possible intrusion into its network. The controller checks its systems to establish whether personal data held on that system has been compromised and confirms this is the case. Once again, as the controller now has clear evidence of a breach there can be no doubt that it has become “aware”. 24 See Recital 87 GDPR. Adopted 12 4. A cybercriminal contacts the controller after having hacked its system in order to ask for a ransom. In that case, after checking its system to confirm it has been attacked the controller has clear evidence that a breach has occurred and there is no doubt that it has become aware. 34. After first being informed of a potential breach by an individual, a media organisation, or another source, or when it has itself detected a security incident, the controller may undertake a short period of investigation in order to establish whether or not a breach has in fact occurred. During this period of investigation the controller may not be regarded as being “aware”. However, it is expected that the initial investigation should begin as soon as possible and establish with a reasonable degree of certainty whether a breach has taken place; a more detailed investigation can then follow. 35. Once the controller has become aware, a notifiable breach must be notified without undue delay, and where feasible, not later than 72 hours. During this period, the controller should assess the likely risk to individuals in order to determine whether the requirement for notification has been triggered, as well as the action(s) needed to address the breach. Such settings are also called “presets” or “factory presets”, especially for electronic devices. 41. Hence, the term “by default” when processing personal data, refers to making choices regarding configuration values or processing options that are set or prescribed in a processing system, such as a software application, service or device, or a manual processing procedure that affect the amount of personal data collected, the extent of their processing, the period of their storage and their accessibility. 42. This means that by default, the controller shall not collect more data than is necessary, they shall not process the data collected more than is necessary for their purposes, nor shall they store the data for longer than necessary. If the data used in an automated decision-making or profiling process is inaccurate, any resultant decision or profile will be flawed. Decisions may be made on the basis of outdated data or the incorrect interpretation of external data. Inaccuracies may lead to inappropriate predictions or statements about, for example, someone’s health, credit or insurance risk. Even if raw data is recorded accurately, the dataset may not be fully representative or the analytics may contain hidden bias. Controllers need to introduce robust measures to verify and ensure on an ongoing basis that data re- used or obtained indirectly is accurate and up to date. This reinforces the importance of providing clear information about the personal data being processed, so that the data subject can correct any inaccuracies and improve the quality of the data. 5. Article 5(1) (e) Storage limitation Machine-learning algorithms are designed to process large volumes of information and build correlations that allow organisations to build up very comprehensive, intimate profiles of individuals. Whilst there can be advantages to retaining data in the case of profiling, since there will be more data for the algorithm to learn from, controllers must comply with the data minimisation principle when they collect personal data and ensure that they retain those personal data for no longer than is necessary for and proportionate to the purposes for which the personal data are processed The controller’s retention policy should take into account the individuals’ rights and freedoms in line with the requirements of Article 5(1)(e). The controller should also make sure that the data remains updated throughout the retention period to reduce the risk of inaccuracies.11 B. Lawful bases for processing Automated decision-making defined in Article 22(1) is only permitted if one of the exceptions described in Chapter IV (sections C and D) applies. The following lawful bases for processing are relevant for all other automated individual decision-making and profiling. 1. Article 6(1) (a) consent Consent as a basis for processing generally is addressed in the WP29 Guidelines on consent.12 Explicit consent is one of the exceptions from the prohibition on automated decision-making and profiling defined in Article 22(1). 11 Norwegian Data Protection Authority. Controllers seeking to rely upon consent as a basis for profiling will need to show that data subjects understand exactly what they are consenting to, and remember that consent is not always an appropriate basis for the processing.13 In all cases, data subjects should have enough relevant information about the envisaged use and consequences of the processing to ensure that any consent they provide represents an informed choice. 2. Article 6(1) (b) – necessary for the performance of a contract Controllers may wish to use profiling and automated decision-making processes because they:  potentially allow for greater consistency or fairness in the decision making process (e.g. by reducing the potential for human error, discrimination and abuse of power);  reduce the risk of customers failing to meet payments for goods or services (for example by using credit referencing); or  enable them to deliver decisions within a shorter time frame and improve efficiency . Regardless of the above, these considerations alone are not sufficient to show that this type of processing is necessary under Article 6(1)(b) for the performance of a contract. As described in the WP29 Opinion on legitimate interest14, necessity should be interpreted narrowly. The following is an example of profiling that would not meet the Article 6(1)(b) basis for processing. Example A user buys some items from an on-line retailer. In order to fulfil the contract, the retailer must process the user’s credit card information for payment purposes and the user’s address to deliver the goods. Completion of the contract is not dependent upon building a profile of the user’s tastes and lifestyle choices based on his or her visits to the website. Even if profiling is specifically mentioned in the small print of the contract, this fact alone does not make it ‘necessary’ for the performance of the contract. 3. result.reason: The task 'Check whether invoice amount has been received' processes personal data because it involves verifying payment status linked to a specific customer. The invoice and payment information are personal data as they relate to an identified individual's financial transactions.

The send task 'Notify legal department' transmits personal data (customer invoice and payment details) from the After Sales department to the Legal department. This disclosure of personal data for legal proceedings constitutes processing.

The task 'Verification of the invoice amount' processes personal data by examining the customer's invoice and payment details received from After Sales. This involves consulting financial data relating to an identified individual.

The task 'SCHUFA check' involves querying a credit rating agency (SCHUFA) for information about an individual's creditworthiness. This is a clear processing of personal data, specifically financial and credit history data, which is sensitive and relates to an identifiable natural person.

The task 'Review of payment arrears' processes personal data by analyzing the customer's payment history and outstanding debts. This financial information is personal data as it relates to an identified individual's economic behavior.

The task 'File police report' involves submitting a formal report to law enforcement authorities that includes personal data about the customer (name, address, invoice details, alleged non-payment). This constitutes disclosure of personal data to an official authority.

The task 'Issue summary proceedings' involves initiating legal proceedings against the customer. This requires processing and disclosing personal data (name, address, financial details) to courts or legal authorities, which constitutes processing of personal data for legal claims.

The task 'Create customer letter regarding blocking' involves generating a communication to the customer about account blocking or legal actions. This uses the customer's personal contact details and references their specific financial situation, constituting processing of personal data.

The task 'Determination of further procedure' (in the Customer pool) processes personal data because the customer is making decisions based on personal information received from the Legal Department about their own account status, blocking, or legal proceedings. This involves processing data concerning themselves.

[content] Revised Draft Decision — A Revised Draft Decision is a formal, updated version of an initial draft decision, presented as a distinct legal instrument. The LSA (Legislation and Standards Authority) is obligated to submit a Revised Draft Decision if it intends to incorporate a relevant and reasoned objection, or if it has modified its initial decision based on informal exchanges or other considerations. This document is designed to reflect revisions made after considering objections and feedback, aiming to find consensus on previously disputed issues. This revised version is subject to a shorter assessment period compared to the initial draft. If no further objections are raised against it, the Revised Draft Decision can become legally binding. The LSA utilizes this instrument to address objections or revised reasoned objections, ultimately working towards achieving a consensus.

Under GDPR, Controller The controller wishes to market products and services through direct marketing.<SEP>Direct marketing purposes may be regarded as a legitimate interest of the controller. Direct Marketing.

Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Supervisory Authority is established primarily by data protection regulations, such as the GDPR, and focuses on compliance, breach management, and accountability. A central obligation of the Controller is to notify the Supervisory Authority of personal data breaches, typically within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach, especially if it poses a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, as per Article 33(1) and Article 27(5) GDPR. The Controller is responsible for determining if a breach is notifiable and must ensure the relevant Supervisory Authority is informed, potentially proactively notifying them of infringements or seeking advice. They must also inform the Supervisory Authority about data transfers, documenting assessments and safeguards. Controllers without an EU establishment are required to engage with local supervisory authorities in every Member State where they operate. Furthermore, the Controller must consult the Supervisory Authority if a high risk identified in a Data Protection Impact Assessment cannot be mitigated by reasonable means before processing. Controllers are also obligated to cooperate with and make records available to the Supervisory Authority upon request, demonstrating accountability and compliance. The Supervisory Authority plays a significant role in overseeing the Controller's data protection practices. It can advise Controllers on how to inform individuals about breaches and may even order them to do so, particularly for high-risk breaches. The Supervisory Authority verifies the Controller's compliance, handles complaints, and seeks amicable settlements regarding possible infringements. It possesses powers to require the Controller to provide information, carry out investigations, notify infringements, and obtain access to data and premises. The Supervisory Authority can issue warnings and reprimands, order compliance, and impose sanctions, including administrative fines under Article 83 GDPR, especially in cases of unjustified breaches. The level of the Controller's cooperation is considered by the Supervisory Authority when assessing mitigation efforts. The Supervisory Authority also promotes awareness among Controllers regarding their obligations under pertinent regulations and informs Controllers when a received complaint is dismissed or rejected. Supervisory Authority.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation between a Controller and a Data Protection Officer (DPO) is characterized by advisory support and assigned responsibility for data protection compliance, particularly under regulations such as the GDPR. The Controller is responsible for designating a DPO to help ensure adherence to these regulations. The DPO's role encompasses providing advice and information to the Controller on various data protection matters, including breach management, data protection methodologies, and audits. This includes actively participating in Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), which the Controller undertakes with the DPO's guidance. Controllers are mandated to seek the DPO's advice when conducting a DPIA, and they must ensure the DPO's timely involvement in all data protection issues, providing necessary resources and access to facilitate their tasks. Guidelines may be developed by the Controller to specify when the DPO must be consulted. While the DPO offers crucial guidance and assists in monitoring internal compliance with regulations, the ultimate responsibility for data protection compliance remains with the Controller. The DPO may be an employee of the Controller or an external party, but they must perform their duties independently. The Controller is obligated to record the name and contact details of the DPO, and these details must be included in the record of processing activities. Furthermore, in the event of a data breach, the Controller must communicate the DPO's name and contact details as a contact point for breach information as part of the notification process. Data Protection Officer.

It should be noted that Article 5(3) ePrivacy Directive also requires consent for the use of tracking techniques, such as storing cookies or gaining access to information in the terminal equipment of the user.139 Therefore, when these techniques are used in the context of direct marketing activities, such consent requirements under Article 5(3) ePrivacy Directive must be respected. Any processing operations of personal data following the aforementioned processing operations, including processing personal data obtained by accessing information in the terminal equipment, must have a legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR in order to be lawful. Therefore, consent will likely constitute the appropriate legal basis both for storing and gaining access to information already stored on the user’s device and for the subsequent processing of personal data,140 thus normally precluding reliance on Article 6(1)(f) in this context. 116. However, the ePrivacy Directive provides for exceptions to the consent requirements it imposes. For instance, an exception to the requirement of consent is permitted under Article 13(2) ePrivacy Directive when the electronic contact details are lawfully obtained – i.e., are obtained in accordance with the GDPR – from one’s own customers in the context of the sale of a product or a service. An invoice typically contains personal data such as the customer's name, address, email address, and details of the service provided (e.g., internet service). The activity 'Suspend internet' is a direct action taken against a specific customer's account. To perform this action, the ISP must process personal data (e.g., customer account identifier, service details) to identify the correct account and execute the suspension. This is a use of personal data to make a decision affecting the individual.

The activity 'Close account' involves terminating a customer's account. This requires processing personal data (e.g., customer identification, account history, contact details) to locate the account, verify identity, and perform the closure, which is a use of personal data.

The activity 'Send payment' involves the customer transmitting payment to the bank. A payment inherently contains personal financial data, such as the payer's bank account details, name, and potentially the transaction reference linking it to the customer's invoice. Sending this information constitutes processing of personal data.

The activity 'Send payment' (second instance) involves the customer transmitting a late payment. This action processes personal financial data (bank account details, payer identification) to complete the transaction, which is processing of personal data.

The activity 'Debit money' involves the bank initiating a debit transaction from a customer's account. To do this, the bank must process personal data, specifically the customer's bank account number and associated identification details, to execute the financial transaction. This is processing of personal financial data.

The activity 'Debit money' (second instance) involves the bank attempting to debit a customer's account after a previous failure. This again processes the customer's personal financial data (account details) to execute the transaction.

The activity 'Charge late fee' involves the bank applying an additional charge to a customer's account. This requires processing personal data (customer account identifier, transaction history) to identify the account and calculate/apply the fee, which is a use of personal data.

The activity 'Receive payment' involves the bank receiving a payment from a customer. Receiving a payment entails processing the incoming transaction data, which includes personal financial data (payer's account details, name, amount) to credit the correct account. This is processing of personal data.
The activity 'Receive payment' (second instance) involves the bank receiving a late payment from a customer. This again processes personal financial data contained within the payment transaction.

The activity 'Check payment' involves the bank verifying if a payment is complete. To perform this check, the bank must access and process personal data, such as the customer's account records and transaction details, to determine the payment status. This is a retrieval and consultation of personal data.

The activity 'Check payment' (second instance) is another verification step by the bank. It similarly requires accessing and processing customer account and transaction data (personal data) to assess payment completion.

ragPromptContext: [organization] Alternative Service Providers — These providers can request interoperability from gatekeepers for number-independent interpersonal communications services.

[service] Information Society Service — An Information Society Service is broadly defined as a service typically provided for remuneration, at a distance, and by electronic means, in response to an individual request from a service recipient. This category encompasses various online services, including contracts concluded or transmitted electronically. A key characteristic of an Information Society Service is that storing or accessing information in a user's terminal equipment must be strictly necessary for the provision of the service itself. This necessity can lead to certain exemptions under Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive. Specifically, for an Information Society Service, consent may not be required for gaining access to information already stored in a device (such as a vehicle) if such access is explicitly requested by the subscriber. This exemption simplifies data access under specific, user-initiated circumstances. Furthermore, an Information Society Service is defined more formally in point (b) of Article 1(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/1535. When an Information Society Service is explicitly requested by a subscriber or user, certain processing exemptions may apply. For services of this nature that are often offered online, special considerations regarding children's consent might also be applicable, as detailed in specific regulatory sections like Section 7.1.1.
[organization] Independent Body — An entity entrusted with the appointment of supervisory authority members under Member State law.

[service] Payment Service — A service that processes payments, which may cross-use identification details without consent if functionally interconnected.
A payment service is a service provided by a gatekeeper where an end user's personal data collected in a CPS can be cross-used to process a payment, relying on Article 6(1)(b) GDPR.
[method] Fraud Monitoring and Prevention — Techniques and activities aimed at detecting and preventing fraudulent activities, which can be a basis for automated processing.

[person] Client — A client is an entity represented by a law firm, in this case, Company ABC, which provides a mandate to the law firm.
A client is an individual whose personal data may be transferred by a travel agent for the purpose of organizing their travel.
The client is an organization for which an external DPO team works, and for whom a lead contact and "person in charge" is designated.
The client is the entity for whom an external DPO team works, under the responsibility of a designated lead contact.
A client is a data subject who has a relevant and appropriate relationship with a controller, often forming the basis for legitimate interest in data processing.

[concept] Data Transfers — Data transfers involve the movement of data from one location or entity to another.
Data Transfers refer to the movement of data to third countries or international organizations, which can be based on appropriate safeguards and legal remedies for data subjects.
Data transfers involve the movement of personal data, and possible risks due to absence of adequacy decisions or safeguards (Article 46) must be informed.
Data Transfers involve the movement of personal data from one entity or location to another, especially across borders.

[concept] Administrative Fines — Administrative Fines are financial or monetary penalties that supervisory authorities impose in response to infringements of legal requirements, particularly those set forth in data protection regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). These fines, detailed in Article 83 of the GDPR, are designed to be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive. The imposition of Administrative Fines intensified under the GDPR, reflecting an increased level of penalty for such infringements. The criteria for setting these fines are based on the nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement, and their calculation begins from a harmonized point, varying according to the specific circumstances of each case, guided by particular principles and guidelines under the GDPR. Certification can also be a factor in determining these penalties. For undertakings, Administrative Fines can potentially reach up to 20,000,000 EUR or 4% of their total worldwide annual turnover, with the upper limit determined by their combined turnover. While imposed by supervisory authorities, their assessment may be subject to review by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB). These fines represent a type of legal effect that can be imposed as a measure for non-compliance with the Regulation.
[concept] Compensation — Compensation is the right for any person who has suffered damage due to an infringement of the Regulation to receive payment from the controller or processor.

[organization] Gatekeeper — A Gatekeeper is an entity designated under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically pursuant to Article 3(4) or Article 3(9), indicating its provision of Core Platform Services (CPSs). Prominent examples of such organizations include Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta. These Gatekeepers control access to specific digital services and are subject to extensive legal obligations under the DMA, and in many cases, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Their role is central to the regulatory framework designed to ensure fair and contestable digital markets. Gatekeepers process the personal data of end users, often acting as controllers or processors, and are responsible for ensuring that consent obtained for data processing, particularly for online advertising and data combination, complies with both GDPR and DMA requirements. This includes the meticulous recording of consent refusals or withdrawals. They are obligated to enable continuous and real-time access to data, prevent data accumulation, and ensure robust data security. Their responsibilities extend to providing data upon request by business users or authorized third parties, free of charge, and establishing appropriate authentication and authorization procedures for such access. They must also implement security measures for personal data, comply with portability requests under DMA Article 6(9), and provide comprehensive information to data subjects. Furthermore, Gatekeepers are tasked with selecting and implementing anonymization methods for end-user data shared under Article 6(11) DMA and must implement measures to maintain service integrity and security. They also have duties concerning interoperability, including exchanging message content and personal data with other providers while ensuring security for their end users. This includes protecting metadata, verifying communication authenticity, and ensuring compliance with geographical limitations and data protection regulations for Number-Independent Interpersonal Communication Services (NIICS). Gatekeepers must design online interfaces that do not undermine user autonomy, provide reminders, and ensure fair access to datasets by altering data to mitigate identification risks and imposing contractual measures on third-party undertakings for data access and compliance monitoring. Their conduct is subject to examination for compliance with both the DMA and GDPR, and they may have a "main establishment" under the GDPR. They are also separate controllers under GDPR for their own data processing and have obligations under Article 6(4) and Article 8(1) of the DMA.

Finally, as leading practice for “receiving” data controllers, the WP29 recommends that data subjects are provided with complete information about the nature of personal data which are relevant for the performance of their services. In addition to underpinning fair processing, this allows users to limit the risks for third parties, and also any other unnecessary duplication of personal data even where no other data subjects are involved. - How can the data controller identify the data subject before answering his request? There are no prescriptive requirements to be found in the GDPR on how to authenticate the data subject. Nevertheless, Article 12(2) of the GDPR states that the data controller shall not refuse to act on request of a data subject for exercising his or her rights (including the right to data portability) unless it is processing personal data for a purpose that does not require the identification of a data subject and it can demonstrate that it is not able to identify the data subject. However, as per Article 11(2), in such circumstances the data subject can provide more information to enable his or her identification. Additionally, Article 12(6) provides that where a data controller has reasonable doubts about the identity of a data subject, it can request further information to confirm the data subject’s identity. Where a data subject provides additional information enabling his or her identification, the data controller shall not refuse to act on the request. Where information and data collected online is linked to pseudonyms or unique identifiers, data controllers can implement appropriate procedures 24 Article 12 requires that data controllers provide “any communications […] in a concise, transparent, intelligible, and easily assessable form, using clear and plain language, in particular for any information addressed specifically to a child.” 14 enabling an individual to make a data portability request and receive the data relating to him or her. In any case, data controllers must implement an authentication procedure in order to strongly ascertain the identity of the data subject requesting his or her personal data or more generally exercising the rights granted by the GDPR. These procedures often already exist. The data subjects are often already authenticated by the data controller before entering into a contract or collecting his or her consent to the processing. As a consequence, the personal data used to register the individual concerned by the processing can also be used as evidence to authenticate the data subject for portability purposes25. While in these cases, the data subjects’ prior identification may require a request for proof of their legal identity, such verification may not be relevant to assess the link between the data and the individual concerned, since such a link is not related with the official or legal identity. In essence, the ability for the data controller to request additional information to assess one’s identity cannot lead to excessive demands and to the collection of personal data which are not relevant or necessary to strengthen the link between the individual and the personal data requested. In many cases, such authentication procedures are already in place. For example, usernames and passwords are often used to allow individuals to access their data in their email accounts, social networking accounts, and accounts used for various other services, some of which individuals chose to use without revealing their full name and identity. If the size of data requested by the data subject makes transmission via the internet problematic, rather than potentially allowing for an extended time period of a maximum of three months to comply with the request26, the data controller may also need to consider alternative means of providing the data such as using streaming or saving to a CD, DVD or other physical media or allowing for the personal data to be transmitted directly to another data controller (as per Article 20(2) of the GDPR where technically feasible). - What is the time limit imposed to answer a portability request? Article 12(3) requires that the data controller provides “information on action taken” to the data subject “without undue delay” and in any event “within one month of receipt of the request”. This one month period can be extended to a maximum of three months for complex cases, provided that the data subject has been informed about the reasons for such delay within one month of the original request. Data controllers operating information society services are likely to be better equipped to be able to comply with requests within a very short time period. To meet user expectations, it is a good practice to define the timeframe in which a data portability request can typically be answered and communicate this to data subjects. Data controllers who refuse to answer a portability request shall, pursuant to Article 12(4), inform the data subject “the reasons for not taking action and on the possibility of lodging a 25 For example, when the data processing is linked to a user account, providing the relevant login and password might be sufficient to identify the data subject. 26 Article 12(3): “The controller shall provide information on action taken on a request”. 15 complaint with a supervisory authority and seeking a judicial remedy”, no later than one month after receiving the request. [method] Processing Operations — Processing Operations refer to any activities or a set of operations performed on data, particularly personal data, by institutions or data brokers. These operations encompass a vast array of actions, including the collection, storage, use, disclosure, further processing, the management of data subject rights, and the handling and manipulation of data. They can also involve linking data, forming different conducts, combining data, or cross-using data. Per Article 4(2) of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), these operations are defined as any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or on sets of personal data. These operations are composed of various components, such as data, systems, and processes, all of which should adhere to specific criteria. Activities often include the selection of targeting criteria and the display of advertisements to a specific target audience. Processing operations are a primary object of certification under the GDPR, potentially encompassing governance processes and leading to the creation of a product or service. Both data controllers and processors are obligated to demonstrate compliance when executing these operations. Actions performed on personal data should be limited to what is necessary, contributing to a defined processing purpose, and designed to process only the minimum amount of necessary data. Processing operations are actions carried out by a data controller using collected data, requiring specific information provisions and legal bases. They may also benefit from special regimes under GDPR. Examples include the collection, storage, use, or deletion of data. Some operations may involve the use of CCTV and are subject to the applicability of the household exemption. Records must be maintained for these data handling activities. Furthermore, processing operations that involve personal data may require a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) under GDPR if they pose a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. When a DPIA is required, these activities necessitate a systematic description, an assessment of necessity, proportionality, and risks, and the implementation of measures to address those risks.
Processing Operations refer to any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction.
Processing Operations involve any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, storage, etc.
Actions or sets of actions performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, storage, or disclosure.
Actions or sets of actions performed upon personal data, which supervisory authorities are generally competent to oversee, except for courts acting in judicial capacity.
Processing operations refer to any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, as defined in Article 4(2) GDPR.
Processing operations refer to activities involving personal data, such as combining or cross-using data.
[artifact] Hardware — The physical components of a device that gatekeepers may take measures to protect the integrity of when allowing third-party apps.

[organization] Producers — Producers are entities that develop processing solutions (hardware, software, services, systems). They should demonstrate Data Protection by Design and Default (DPbDD) in their development life-cycle and facilitate controllers' needs.
Producers are key enablers for DPbDD, providing solutions to controllers that embed data protection.
Producers are responsible for developing, designing, selecting, and using applications, services, and products with regard to data protection.
[data] Performance Data — Performance data, such as crash data, can be relevant to business users for providing customer support.
[concept] General and Incident Reporting — Measures specified by the implementing act for regular reporting and reporting specific incidents related to data.
[concept] Processing Operations Security — Processing Operations Security refers to the measures taken to ensure the protection and integrity of data processing activities.

[concept] Processor — A Processor, as defined by Article 4(8) of the GDPR, is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that processes personal data on behalf of a controller. This entity's primary function is to handle personal data strictly according to the controller's documented instructions, without independently determining the purposes or means of the processing activity, and thus, processors do not pursue independent objectives for data processing. A website hosting company is an example of a Processor. Processors are responsible for protecting personal data and are involved in the processing of personal data, with specific legal obligations under the GDPR, including adherence to its principles, ensuring confidentiality, and implementing robust security measures. They must provide sufficient guarantees, such as compliance with codes of conduct or certification mechanisms, and are required to operate under a binding contract or legal act with the controller. This contract typically details their responsibilities, including assisting with Data Protection by Design and by Default (DPbDD), implementing technical and organizational measures, conducting data protection impact assessments (DPIA), and providing compliance information. The processor assists the controller in carrying out a DPIA, and its roles and responsibilities in a DPIA must be contractually defined. Processors are also obligated to notify the controller of any data breach without undue delay, inform the controller of any infringing instructions, and are subject to audits. Upon termination of processing activities, they must delete or return personal data. They have specific obligations regarding personal data breaches, as mentioned in Article 33 requirements, particularly Article 33(2). Processors can also act as exporters or importers of personal data, transferring data to third countries or international organizations under specific conditions, always on behalf of the controller and must implement appropriate safeguards for data transfers. While their name may not be explicitly included in consent forms, they are listed as recipients of data. They are held liable to the controller for the performance of their sub-processors' obligations, necessitating that sub-processors also provide sufficient guarantees. Processors' activities and processing operations are assessed for GDPR compliance, and they can be the direct cause of a data breach. They may be the subject of infringement claims, addressed by the final decision of a competent supervisory authority, and can be directly and individually concerned by an EDPB binding decision, against which they may bring an action for annulment. For Processors located in the EU, they must identify an applicable ground for transfer before responding to requests from third-country authorities, as stipulated under Article 48. The designation of a representative does not affect their liability under GDPR, and they may be subject to legal actions for damages if they infringe the regulation or act outside of controller instructions. A data subject can seek judicial remedies against a processor. A Processor may be required to designate a Data Protection Officer (DPO), especially if their core activities involve key operations to achieve their goals, or if their core activities require such a designation under GDPR. When a DPO is designated, the processor is required to publish and communicate the DPO's contact details according to Article 37(7) of the GDPR. The DPO advises the processor on GDPR obligations and assists in monitoring internal compliance with the GDPR. The processor may assign the task of maintaining records of processing operations to the DPO, and the processor supports and involves the Data Protection Officer. For the cooperation procedure to apply, a Processor involved in cross-border processing must have a main or single establishment in an EU Member State. This main establishment oversees such cross-border processing. The main establishment is where its central administration is located in the Union, or where its main processing activities take place if no central administration exists in the Union. Processors are subject to the authority of a Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) or Concerned Supervisory Authority (CSA), and LSAs may interact with Processors to gather relevant information, such as investigation findings, reports, and meeting records. Processors involved in cross-border processing are subject to procedures and potential enforcement action and may be directly targeted by decisions from the LSA. As parties targeted by a draft decision, their right to be heard must comply with national law, and their rights may be affected by changes in a revised draft decision. A Processor's actions can lead to complaints and prompt action by an LSA. Processors have obligations under Article 60(10), are informed of decisions by the LSA, and are obliged to notify the LSA of any measures adopted to comply with a decision entailing corrective measures. A processor can benefit from the one-stop-shop system if established in multiple Member States, and its establishment in multiple Member States can trigger the lead authority mechanism. Guidance can be provided on their implementation of appropriate measures and demonstration of compliance.
A processor is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that processes personal data on behalf of the controller.
A processor processes personal data on behalf of a controller. An authorized third party may act as a processor for an end user if the end user is a controller.

[data] On-Device Data — On-Device Data is data exclusively processed on a device, falls within the scope of Article 6(9) DMA, and gatekeepers must enable its portability at the request of end users or authorized third parties.
Data exclusively processed and stored on an end user's device, to which gatekeepers must enable effective and continuous access under Article 6(10) DMA.

[organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

[organization] Hospital — A Hospital is a healthcare institution responsible for collecting and managing significant quantities of sensitive patient data, often utilizing an electronic health record system. This organization has been noted for experiencing a personal data breach where staff members could view unauthorized patient health files due to issues with authorization monitoring, specifically concerning staff retaining access to patient files after transferring departments; an internal investigation was conducted to address this. The sensitive nature of the data processed means that data breaches at a Hospital are highly impactful, and the unavailability of critical medical data can pose a substantial risk to individuals' rights and freedoms. Furthermore, a Hospital can also be an organization involved in scientific research, as exemplified by "Project X," which necessitates the use of real patient dental records. The Hospital has also been identified as a victim of ransomware attacks (e.g., Case No. 03), where its information systems were compromised, leading to data encryption and subsequent delays in patient care. Consequently, a Hospital is an organization legally obliged to notify relevant authorities and affected individuals in cases of cyber-attacks impacting medical records.
A hospital's core activity is providing healthcare, which inextricably involves processing health data like patient health records.
An example of an organization whose core activities involve processing health data, thus requiring the designation of a DPO.
A hospital is an organization that processes patient data in the regular course of business.
An example context where unavailability of critical medical data can pose a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms.
A hospital is an organization that holds medical records and is obliged to notify in case of a data breach, especially if it poses a high risk to patients.
An institution that can be a source of data regarding a data subject's physiological or biomedical state.
[person] Health Professional — An individual, such as a physician, who provides information related to a data subject's physiological or biomedical state.

[data] Medical Records — Medical records are highly sensitive personal data.
Medical records contain sensitive patient information held by a hospital.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[concept] Processing — Processing, in the context of data management and privacy, encompasses any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or sets of personal data. For operations involving personal data, it is crucial to determine specific purposes and means, often requiring consent from the data subject. A fundamental principle dictates that processing should be carried out in a fair and transparent manner. Processing activities can be performed by entities such as a controller or processor. Infringements related to operations involving personal data can lead to liability, damage, and potential legal proceedings.

result.reason: The activity 'An Terminal ein- und ausstempeln' (Clock in and out at a terminal) processes personal data. It involves an employee using a terminal to record their work attendance. This constitutes processing of employee personal data (specifically, timekeeping and location/attendance data) for the purposes of management, planning, and organisation of work, which is a recognized context for processing under the GDPR.

The activity 'An Web-Terminal ein- und ausstempeln' (Clock in and out at a web terminal) processes personal data. It involves an employee manually logging their work time via a web terminal. This activity processes employee personal data (timekeeping and attendance records) and involves the employee's terminal equipment (a web browser/device). The processing is for employment management purposes.

The activity 'Arbeitszeit in der Zeiterfassungsübersicht erfassen' (Record working hours in the time tracking overview) processes personal data. It involves an employee manually entering their working hours for the current day into a time tracking system. This is a direct processing of employee personal data (working time records) which is necessary for payroll, performance of the employment contract, and work organisation.

ragPromptContext: [concept] Monitoring Systems at the Work Place — Monitoring systems at the work place are methods used to observe employees, subject to safeguards for human dignity and fundamental rights.

[person] Employee — An Employee is defined as an individual who is employed by an organization or person, belonging to the legal entity of a data controller or processor. These individuals are typically authorized to process personal data, acting under the authority of the controller. Their access to personal data should be restricted based on their specific duties and role within the company. Employees may interact with personal data in various ways, such as manually deleting personal data after its retention period in accordance with internal procedures. They can also be subjects whose personal data, such as their name, is processed by services (e.g., a taxi service in an illustrative example). Employee actions can also lead to incidents, such as when an employee of a controller makes a mistake resulting in a data breach, or when an employee of a service provider has their electronic notebook stolen, as depicted in CASE No. 11. While employees generally operate under established authority, there can be exceptional cases where they unlawfully exceed this authority. Furthermore, employees may face pressure concerning consent for data processing.
Employees are individuals within an organization who may have concerns or complaints.
An employee is a data subject who has a relevant and appropriate relationship with a controller, often forming the basis for legitimate interest in data processing within a group of undertakings.

[artifact] Website User's Terminal Equipment — This refers to any device used by a website user, such as a computer or smartphone, where information might be stored or accessed.
This refers to any device used by a website user, such as a computer or smartphone, where information might be stored or accessed.

[person] End Users — End Users are defined as natural or legal persons who engage with core platform services (CPS), distinct from business users. They are also considered "data subjects" under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), signifying that their personal data is processed, often by gatekeepers and other providers of numerically independent interpersonal communication services (NIICS). These individuals benefit from fair market conditions promoted by regulatory frameworks like the Digital Markets Act (DMA). The autonomy and decision-making of End Users are protected, requiring gatekeepers to seek their consent for data access, including the processing of personal data for online advertising services or combining personal data. They should be able to freely choose to opt-in to data processing and sign-in practices, with alternative services potentially being offered. Their reasonable expectations regarding personal data processing must be considered, and they have the right to set third-party apps or app stores as their default. End Users' consent is also required for certain processing operations and for the storage of information on their terminal equipment. End Users interact with online interfaces, generating various forms of data such as ranking, query, click, and view data through their use of gatekeepers' services. When their data is shared under Article 6(11) DMA, anonymization is required to protect their identity. They are presented with choices and consent requests from gatekeepers, and their rights are safeguarded by various regulations, ultimately encouraging increased choice and includes the right to data portability under Article 6(9) DMA. End Users use services provided by gatekeepers and other NIICS providers, with their personal data managed for interoperability and security.
[data] Employees' Personal Data — Employees' personal data refers to information about employees that is subject to specific rules and safeguards regarding its processing in the employment context.
[person] Auditor — An auditor, who can be mandated by the controller, conducts inspections/audits to verify compliance.
[UNKNOWN] Information — Terminal equipment stores information and allows access to it.

[person] Employees — Employees are individuals who work for a company and are expected to comply with a code of conduct. Their personal data may be processed by employers, but consent for this processing is often not freely given due to an inherent imbalance of power between employer and employee. This group includes individuals authorized to process personal data, who require access to such data to perform their job tasks for which the processor was hired. Employees are considered a category of data subjects that can be affected by a data breach, a classification suggested by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB). This group also includes individuals from a U.S. company whose personal data is processed for human resources purposes during business trips. In some cases, employees are staff members whose actions might be monitored by employers, for example, through the use of company cars. Employees are also individuals who need training on recognizing and preventing IT attacks and reporting them, and they were among those affected by "The Breach."
Employees can be considered vulnerable data subjects due to a potential imbalance in the relationship with their employer.
Individuals who carry out processing and are advised by the DPO on their GDPR obligations.
Employees of a Controller or Processor who should be informed about existing breach procedures and how to react to breaches to ensure compliance with GDPR.
Employees are individuals whose salary details are obtained by a tax authority from their employers.
Individuals who carry out personal data processing and are to be informed and advised by the Data Protection Officer regarding their obligations.

[equipment] Terminal Equipment — Terminal equipment broadly refers to a user's device from which digital information can be accessed, processed, sent, or received. This category includes a wide range of devices such as computers, smartphones, smart TVs, and connected vehicles, often encompassing telematics devices. According to Directive 2008/63/CE, terminal equipment is specifically defined as any device directly or indirectly connected to a public telecommunications network interface for the purpose of transmitting, processing, or receiving information. This equipment serves as the point where individuals access data, potentially leading to the processing of personal data. These devices are generally owned by end-users and serve as the location where information, including sensitive data like location data, can be collected and stored. For example, collected information from contact tracing applications typically resides on the user's terminal equipment. The storage and access of information on terminal equipment are subject to stringent security measures and user-centric conditions to protect privacy and data integrity.

[method] Management, Planning, and Organisation of Work — Management, Planning, and Organisation of Work are purposes in the employment context for which specific rules for processing employees' personal data may be provided.

To assess whether consent is freely given, Article 7(4) GDPR plays an important role.22 26. Article 7(4) GDPR indicates that, inter alia, the situation of “bundling” consent with acceptance of terms or conditions, or “tying” the provision of a contract or a service to a request for consent to process personal data that are not necessary for the performance of that contract or service, is considered highly undesirable. If consent is given in this situation, it is presumed to be not freely given (recital 43). Article 7(4) seeks to ensure that the purpose of personal data processing is not disguised nor bundled with the provision of a contract of a service for which these personal data are not necessary. In doing so, the GDPR ensures that the processing of personal data for which consent is sought cannot become directly or indirectly the counter-performance of a contract. As data protection law is aiming at the protection of fundamental rights, an individual’s control over their personal data is essential and there is a strong presumption that consent to the processing of personal data that is unnecessary, cannot be seen as a mandatory consideration in exchange for the performance of a contract or the provision of a service. 28. [organization] Producers — Producers are entities that develop processing solutions (hardware, software, services, systems). They should demonstrate Data Protection by Design and Default (DPbDD) in their development life-cycle and facilitate controllers' needs.
Producers are key enablers for DPbDD, providing solutions to controllers that embed data protection.
