[method] Ad-delivery Techniques — Methods used to deliver advertisements to end users.

[data] Customer Data — Customer data refers to personal data of customers, processed by ABC Ltd. on behalf of XYZ.
Customer Data refers to personal data about customers, including purchase history, name, address, email address, and telephone number.
Information related to customers, including contact data and insurance details, which was inadvertently exposed.
Customer data is processed by insurance companies or banks, mentioned as an example of large-scale processing.
Customer data refers to information processed by insurance companies, banks, or fast-food chains.
Customer data is data actively provided by business users that has been lawfully obtained, covered by Article 6(10) DMA.

[method] Further Processing — Further processing, under Article 6(4) GDPR, involves processing personal data for a purpose other than that for which it was initially collected.
Further processing is an aspect of data handling that occurs after initial collection, such as for advertising profiles.
Further processing, also referred to as secondary use of health data, involves research on personal (health) data that was initially collected for another purpose.
Refers to processing operations that occur after the initial, primary processing of data, also known as secondary usage of health data.
The subsequent use of personal data beyond its original collection purpose.
Any processing of personal data beyond its initial purpose, requiring prior notification to data subjects.
Further Processing refers to the use of personal data for a purpose other than that for which it was initially collected.

[organization] Third-Party Undertaking Requesting Access — A third-party undertaking requesting access is an entity, often providing an online search engine, that requests access to anonymised data from a gatekeeper.
A third-party undertaking requesting access is an entity, often providing an online search engine, that requests access to anonymised data from a gatekeeper.

[method] Profiling — Profiling is a sophisticated and automated form of processing personal data specifically designed to evaluate, analyze, or predict various personal aspects of a natural person. This includes their performance at work, economic situation, health, personal preferences or interests, reliability or behavior, location, or movements. It is considered a specific type of processing operation, with the definition often referencing Article 4(4) of the GDPR, and its implications necessitate particular attention in certification criteria due to potential serious consequences for individuals. This process distinguishes itself by continuously collecting, analyzing, building, and applying data to create a profile for an individual. It can even infer special categories of data from non-special category data when combined with other information, thereby generating derived or inferred data about individuals. Such created data is frequently invisible to the data subject and is utilized in decision-making processes. Consequently, profiling is subject to specific transparency requirements, especially when integrated into automated decision-making. Data controllers have clear transparency obligations, and data subjects possess a right to information regarding profiling activities. Profiling is widely employed across numerous sectors, notably in targeted advertising, where companies leverage these profiles to deliver personalized content, sometimes based on sensitive data. Social media platforms, for instance, extensively use profiling within their targeting mechanisms. While profiling can offer benefits like increased efficiencies and resource savings, it also presents significant risks to individuals' rights and freedoms, particularly concerning children. It can lead to the creation of consumer profiles that may be unfair or discriminatory. Furthermore, profiling carries potential risks if it falls under Article 22 of the GDPR and is subject to specific data protection rights and Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) requirements. Its applications are diverse, encompassing fraud prevention, marketing, and disease prediction.
The processing of personal data to evaluate certain personal aspects relating to a natural person, particularly for advertising based on special categories of data.
Profiling is defined as any automated processing of personal data used to evaluate certain personal aspects of a natural person, such as performance at work, economic situation, health, preferences, interests, reliability, behavior, location, or movements.

[concept] Core Platform Services (CPSs) — Core Platform Services are services to which the Digital Markets Act (DMA) applies, provided by undertakings designated as gatekeepers, and include categories such as online intermediation services, online search engines, and cloud computing services.
Core Platform Services (CPSs) are services provided by gatekeepers where vast amounts of personal data are collected.
Core Platform Services are relevant services for which data is provided or generated, falling under the data access obligation of gatekeepers.

[concept] Core Platform Services — Core Platform Services (CPSs) are defined as digital services utilized by end users. Gatekeepers are designated for these services under Article 3(9) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA), which also mandates that the right to data portability applies to them under DMA Article 6(9). Furthermore, gatekeepers providing Core Platform Services are required to implement user-friendly consent mechanisms and may apply consumer profiling techniques across these digital services.

[organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Supervisory Authority is established primarily by data protection regulations, such as the GDPR, and focuses on compliance, breach management, and accountability. A central obligation of the Controller is to notify the Supervisory Authority of personal data breaches, typically within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach, especially if it poses a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, as per Article 33(1) and Article 27(5) GDPR. The Controller is responsible for determining if a breach is notifiable and must ensure the relevant Supervisory Authority is informed, potentially proactively notifying them of infringements or seeking advice. They must also inform the Supervisory Authority about data transfers, documenting assessments and safeguards. Controllers without an EU establishment are required to engage with local supervisory authorities in every Member State where they operate. Furthermore, the Controller must consult the Supervisory Authority if a high risk identified in a Data Protection Impact Assessment cannot be mitigated by reasonable means before processing. Controllers are also obligated to cooperate with and make records available to the Supervisory Authority upon request, demonstrating accountability and compliance. The Supervisory Authority plays a significant role in overseeing the Controller's data protection practices. It can advise Controllers on how to inform individuals about breaches and may even order them to do so, particularly for high-risk breaches. The Supervisory Authority verifies the Controller's compliance, handles complaints, and seeks amicable settlements regarding possible infringements. It possesses powers to require the Controller to provide information, carry out investigations, notify infringements, and obtain access to data and premises. The Supervisory Authority can issue warnings and reprimands, order compliance, and impose sanctions, including administrative fines under Article 83 GDPR, especially in cases of unjustified breaches. The level of the Controller's cooperation is considered by the Supervisory Authority when assessing mitigation efforts. The Supervisory Authority also promotes awareness among Controllers regarding their obligations under pertinent regulations and informs Controllers when a received complaint is dismissed or rejected. Only personal data that is adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purpose shall be processed.36 As a result, the controller has to predetermine which features and parameters of processing systems and their supporting functions are permissible. Data minimisation substantiates and operationalises the principle of necessity. In the further processing, the controller should periodically consider whether processed personal data is still adequate, relevant and necessary, or if the data shall be deleted or anonymized. 74. Controllers should first of all determine whether they even need to process personal data for their relevant purposes. The controller should verify whether the relevant purposes can be achieved by processing less personal data, or having less detailed or aggregated personal data or without having to process personal data at all37. Such verification should take place before any processing takes place, but could also be carried out at any point during the processing lifecycle. This is also consistent with Article 11. 75. Minimising can also refer to the degree of identification. If the purpose of the processing does not require the final set of data to refer to an identified or identifiable individual (such as in statistics), but the initial processing does (e.g. before data aggregation), then the controller shall delete or anonymize personal data as soon as identification is no longer needed. Or, if continued identification is needed for other processing activities, personal data should be pseudonymized to mitigate risks for the data subjects’ rights. 76. Key design and default data minimisation elements may include:  Data avoidance – Avoid processing personal data altogether when this is possible for the relevant purpose.  Limitation – Limit the amount of personal data collected to what is necessary for the purpose  Access limitation – Shape the data processing in a way that a minimal number of people need access to personal data to perform their duties, and limit access accordingly.  Relevance – Personal data should be relevant to the processing in question, and the controller should be able to demonstrate this relevance.  Necessity – Each personal data category shall be necessary for the specified purposes and should only be processed if it is not possible to fulfil the purpose by other means.  Aggregation – Use aggregated data when possible.  Pseudonymization – Pseudonymize personal data as soon as it is no longer necessary to have directly identifiable personal data, and store identification keys separately.  Anonymization and deletion – Where personal data is not, or no longer necessary for the purpose, personal data shall be anonymized or deleted.  Data flow – The data flow should be made efficient enough to not create more copies than necessary.  “State of the art” – The controller should apply up to date and appropriate technologies for data avoidance and minimisation. 36 Art. 5(1)(c) GDPR. 37 Recital 39 GDPR so states: “...Personal data should be processed only if the purpose of the processing could not reasonably be fulfilled by other means.” Adopted 22 Example 1 A bookshop wants to add to their revenue by selling their books online. The bookshop owner wants to set up a standardised form for the ordering process. To ensure customers fill out all the wanted information the bookshop owner makes all of the fields in the form mandatory (if you don’t fill out all the fields the customer can’t place the order). The webshop owner initially uses a standard contact form, which asks information including the customer’s date of birth, phone number and home address. However, not all the fields in the form are necessary for the purpose of buying and delivering the books. In this particular case, if the data subject pays for the product up front, the data subject’s date of birth and phone number are not necessary for the purchase of the product. [Source: EDPB_guidelines_202007_controllerprocessor_final_en] "that several different entities may act as controllers for the same processing, with each of them then being subject to the applicable data protection provisions. Correspondingly, an organisation can still be a controller even if it does not make all the decisions as to purposes and means. The criteria for joint controllership and the extent to which two or more actors jointly exercise control may take different forms, as clarified later on.13 2.1.4 “Purposes and means” 32. The fourth building block of the controller definition refers to the object of the controller’s influence, namely the “purposes and means” of the processing. It represents the substantive part of the controller concept: what a party should determine in order to qualify as controller. 33. Dictionaries define “purpose” as “an anticipated outcome that is intended or that guides your planned actions” and “means” as “how a result is obtained or an end is achieved”. 34. The GDPR establishes that data must be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a way incompatible with those purposes. Determination of the "purposes" of the processing and the "means" to achieve them is therefore particularly important. 35. Determining the purposes and the means amounts to deciding respectively the "why" and the "how" of the processing:14 given a particular processing operation, the controller is the actor who has determined why the processing is taking place (i.e., “to what end”; or “what for”) and how this objective shall be reached (i.e. which means shall be employed to attain the objective). A natural or legal person who exerts such influence over the processing of personal data, thereby participates in the determination of the purposes and means of that processing in accordance with the definition in Article 4(7) GDPR.15 36. The controller must decide on both purpose and means of the processing as described below. As a result, the controller cannot settle with only determining the purpose. It must also make decisions about the means of the processing. Conversely, the party acting as processor can never determine the purpose of the processing. 37. In practice, if a controller engages a processor to carry out the processing on its behalf, it often means that the processor shall be able to make certain decisions of its own on how to carry out the processing. The EDPB recognizes that some margin of manoeuvre may exist for the processor also to be able to make some decisions in relation to the processing. In this perspective, there is a need to provide guidance about which level of influence on the "why" and the "how" should entail the qualification of an entity as a controller and to what extent a processor may make decisions of its own. 38. When one entity clearly determines purposes and means, entrusting another entity with processing activities that amount to the execution of its detailed instructions, the situation is straightforward, and there is no doubt that the second entity should be regarded as a processor, whereas the first entity is the controller. 13 See Part I, Section 3 (“Definition of joint controllers”). 14 See also the Opinion of Advocate General Bot in Wirtschaftsakademie, C‑210/16, ECLI:EU:C:2017:796, paragraph 46. 15 Judgment in Jehovah’s witnesses, C-25/17, ECLI:EU:C:2018:551, paragraph 68. While non- essential means can also be determined by the processor, essential means are to be determined by the controller. “Essential means” are means that are closely linked to the purpose and the scope of the processing, such as the type of personal data which are processed (“which data shall be processed?”), the duration of the processing (“for how long shall they be processed?”), the categories of recipients (“who shall have access to them?”) and the categories of data subjects (“whose personal data are being processed?”). Together with the purpose of processing, the essential means are also closely linked to the question of whether the processing is lawful, necessary and proportionate. “Non-essential means” concern more practical aspects of implementation, such as the choice for a particular type of hard- or software or the detailed security measures which may be left to the processor to decide on. result.reason: The activity 'Auftragsstart' (Order Start) initiates a customer order. This inherently involves processing customer-related personal data such as name, contact details, and order specifics to create a record for the transaction.
The activity 'Batchstart' (Batch Start) begins a production batch for a specific order. This operation processes order data, which is linked to a customer and therefore constitutes personal data.

The activity 'Freigabe / Validieren' (Release / Validate) involves checking and authorizing a production batch. This validation step processes order and potentially operator data, which relates to identifiable individuals.
The activity 'Produzieren' (Produce) executes the manufacturing of goods for a customer order. This activity processes production data linked to a specific customer order, which is personal data.
The activity 'Produktionsabschluss' (Production Completion) finalizes the production process. This involves updating records related to the completed customer order, which contains personal data.

ragPromptContext: [person] Auditor — An auditor, who can be mandated by the controller, conducts inspections/audits to verify compliance.
[concept] Processor (Data) — The Processor (Data) is an entity that handles data, subject to the decisions of the lead supervisory authority and the Regulation.

[organization] Producers — Producers are entities that develop processing solutions (hardware, software, services, systems). They should demonstrate Data Protection by Design and Default (DPbDD) in their development life-cycle and facilitate controllers' needs.
Producers are key enablers for DPbDD, providing solutions to controllers that embed data protection.
Producers are responsible for developing, designing, selecting, and using applications, services, and products with regard to data protection.

[organization] Online Social Network Operator — An online social network operator processes personal data, and such processing is subject to Article 9(1) and 9(2) GDPR.
An online social network operator processes personal data, and such processing is subject to Article 9(1) and 9(2) GDPR.

[person] Business User — A business user is an individual or organization, natural or legal, operating in a commercial or professional capacity, identified as a beneficiary of the right to data access under Article 6(10) DMA.
A business user is a commercial entity or individual that utilizes gatekeeper products or services and may request access to end-user data.
An entity that requests access to end-user data from a gatekeeper under Article 6(10) DMA, with obligations under GDPR regarding data minimisation.
A Business User is a party that requests access to data, including historic and real-time data, and is subject to monitoring by data protection supervisory authorities.

[method] Approved Certification Mechanism — An approved certification mechanism is a mechanism that a processor's adherence to can be used to demonstrate the controller's compliance with obligations.
An Approved Certification Mechanism is a process or system, approved by a supervisory authority, used to demonstrate compliance with data protection requirements.
An approved certification mechanism, pursuant to Article 42, can provide appropriate safeguards for data transfers when combined with binding commitments.

[location] Denmark — Denmark is a country where supervisory authorities are authorized to issue administrative fines.
Denmark is a Member State where administrative fines can be imposed by competent national courts as a criminal penalty.

[concept] Codes of Conduct — Codes of Conduct are a crucial mechanism established under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), as outlined in Articles 40 and 41. They function as voluntary measures and guidelines that enable both data controllers and processors to ensure and demonstrate their adherence to GDPR provisions. These codes offer a practical and cost-effective approach to achieving greater consistency in data protection rights. They can also incorporate sector-specific guidance on Data Protection by Design and by Default (DPbDD), considering the particular processing characteristics and needs of enterprises. Beyond facilitating compliance, Codes of Conduct carry substantial weight in assessments of infringements; according to Article 83 of the GDPR, adherence can act as either a mitigating or aggravating factor. They are furthermore recognized as a primary type of transfer instrument listed in Article 46, offering safeguards that can be adopted by entities not directly subject to the GDPR's jurisdiction. Approved codes, therefore, serve as frameworks showcasing GDPR compliance, influencing how supervisory authorities evaluate processing activities. Some codes specifically incorporate safeguards for the processing of children's data. While primarily associated with GDPR compliance, the term "codes of conduct" also extends to guidelines for auditing processes, particularly those involving machine learning, to ensure ethical and compliant operations. These guidelines are drawn up by associations and require approval from the Supervisory Authority, with implementing acts expected for their realization.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[person] End User — An "End User" refers to an individual customer or consumer who interacts with various services, specifically Core Platform Services (CPS), and can include any natural or legal person utilizing these services, even those traditionally considered business users, with the explicit exclusion of business users in certain contexts. They are the individuals who use the products or services offered by gatekeepers or business users through a relevant CPS. A primary characteristic of an End User is that their personal data is frequently subject to processing, combination, and cross-use by gatekeepers. Their consent and preferences regarding this data processing are recorded and honored, particularly under regulations such as GDPR or the ePrivacy Directive. While their personal data may be cross-used with or without explicit consent depending on the specific legal basis, they generally have choices concerning data access. End Users are individuals whose data is collected and exchanged during interoperability, and whose data, location, and communication privacy are regulated, especially when using specific services like NIICS, where they have the ability to send or block messages. Their data is also subject to re-identification attempts by gatekeepers. A crucial aspect of the End User's rights is data portability, as outlined in DMA Article 6(9) and GDPR Article 20. End Users are individuals who request data portability, authorize third parties to port data, and interact with gatekeeper interfaces to initiate these requests. Explicit and specific consent is required from the End User for personal data transfers to third countries that do not have an adequacy decision. Furthermore, the End User's consent is essential for sharing their personal data when business users request access to it in the context of a Core Platform Service.

Under GDPR, Controller In the context of the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), a Controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This role is fundamental to the GDPR framework, outlining significant obligations and responsibilities for any party involved in deciding how personal data is processed. Controllers are accountable for ensuring compliance with all GDPR provisions, particularly as detailed in Article 3. The Controller has legal obligations to ensure compliance with the GDPR and is responsible and liable under its provisions, with these obligations often referred to as "GDPR controller obligations." The responsibilities of a Controller include applying GDPR rules to data processing, adhering to foundational principles like lawfulness and fairness (Article 5(1)), and fulfilling transparency obligations. Specific duties extend to maintaining records of processing activities (Article 30), ensuring the security of processing (Article 32), conducting data protection impact assessments (Article 35), and engaging in prior consultation (Article 36) for managing risks. Controllers must also comply with regulations regarding data storage periods, implement appropriate technical and organizational measures, and adhere to specific legal bases, such as legitimate interest, for processing data. The GDPR places a significant burden of proof on the Controller, requiring them to demonstrate "compelling legitimate grounds for the processing" when applicable. They must ensure consent mechanisms meet GDPR standards and act upon withdrawal requests. Compliance with obligations related to accountability, engaging processors, and maintaining data security is paramount. Regarding data breaches, the GDPR mandates that controllers implement appropriate security measures, ensure compliance with processing principles, and adhere to relevant provisions for breach notification, as specified in Article 60(10). Unless a breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, the Controller is required to notify the competent supervisory authority and, in certain cases, the affected individuals. The GDPR further defines notification and communication requirements for Controllers regarding breaches, and they must retain documentation in accordance with Article 33(5) of the GDPR. The GDPR also places the burden of proof regarding objections on the Controller. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to take enforcement action, including imposing fines, for any infringement of GDPR provisions resulting from a Controller's actions. The ability for data controllers to obtain GDPR certifications further underscores their pivotal role and accountability within the regulatory framework, though some Controllers currently face broad and systemic issues in compliance with the GDPR. The GDPR recognizes that Controllers may not have all information immediately and allows for phased notification.<SEP>Controllers must comply with the provisions of the GDPR, including those related to information provision.<SEP>The controller must comply with GDPR requirements, including those related to transparency and notification.<SEP>A controller's responsibilities are defined under the GDPR. GDPR.

Under GDPR, Controller The (Controller, Processor) relationship describes an arrangement, primarily defined by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), where a Processor handles personal data on behalf of a Controller. The Controller retains the primary and ultimate responsibility for ensuring overall compliance with data protection principles, including data protection by design and by default (DPbDD), and this accountability extends to any Processor and sub-processors involved. This relationship mandates that the Controller select Processors who offer sufficient guarantees regarding GDPR compliance. This relationship is formalized and governed by a legally binding contract or other legal act, often referred to as a processing agreement. This agreement details how GDPR requirements will be implemented, outlines specific obligations, and defines assistance duties. The Controller must provide documented instructions to the Processor on how to process personal data, and the Processor is obligated to comply. The Processor processes personal data only on these documented instructions. Even without a written agreement, the existence and definition of this relationship hold. The Processor has various duties, including assisting the Controller in fulfilling obligations related to data subject rights and Articles 32 to 36 of the GDPR, ensuring compliance with data protection obligations, and reporting to the Controller. This assistance includes deleting or returning personal data at the Controller's choice, providing compliance information, and cooperating with Controller-conducted audits. A critical obligation for the Processor is to notify the Controller "without undue delay" upon becoming aware of a personal data breach it is processing on behalf of the Controller, as mandated by Article 33(2) GDPR. Processors must also notify the Controller of any request from a third-country authority without undue delay and follow the Controller's instructions, unless prohibited by law. The Processor is liable to the Controller for fulfilling these obligations. The Controller can authorize the use of sub-processors, but the Processor must obtain prior written authorization from the Controller for engaging another processor. The Processor is liable to the Controller for the sub-processors' adherence to data protection obligations. In scenarios involving data transfers, such as a third-country company (Controller) engaging a non-EEA processor, the processor acts as a data exporter on behalf of the Controller. The Controller must provide a comprehensive list of all data recipients, including processors. The relationship demands good faith cooperation, involving contract negotiation and management of audit and instruction processes. Controllers also carry out Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) with the processors. In some cases, the lead supervisory authority of the Controller may also become the lead supervisory authority for the Processor. When an end user qualifies as a Controller, an authorized third party may act as a Processor. Processor.

Under GDPR, Consent The controller must inform data subjects about processing purposes to ensure valid consent.<SEP>Controllers must adhere to specific requirements to ensure consent is valid under the GDPR.<SEP>Controllers must obtain specific, granular, and informed consent from data subjects.<SEP>A controller must obtain and manage consent for processing personal data in accordance with GDPR.<SEP>If a controller relies on consent for processing, they must respect an individual's choice to withdraw it.<SEP>Controllers are responsible for obtaining and demonstrating valid consent.<SEP>A controller needs to demonstrate that it is possible to refuse or withdraw consent without detriment and ensure all conditions for consent are met. Controller.
Under GDPR, Business User A business user may access performance data for providing customer support. Performance Data.
Under GDPR, End User End users processing ported data for non-personal activities are bound by the GDPR.<SEP>End users' consent for data processing is required under GDPR. GDPR.
Under GDPR, Codes of Conduct Stakeholders, including data subjects, should be consulted when codes of conduct are drawn up or amended. Data Subjects.
Under GDPR, End User End users engage with products or services provided through the relevant CPS. Relevant CPS.

Under GDPR, Processing The processor performs the processing of personal data on behalf of the controller.<SEP>A processor is involved in the same processing concerning data.<SEP>A Processor is involved in Processing and can be liable for damage caused by it. Processor.
Under GDPR, Personal Data Personal data can be processed for the purposes of planning and organisation of work. Planning and Organisation of Work.
Under GDPR, Personal Data Processing activities use personal data.<SEP>Processing activities are carried out on personal data. Processing Activities.
Under GDPR, Core Platform Services (CPSs) End users engage with products or services provided by business users through CPSs, generating data. End User.
Under GDPR, Code of Conduct The Supervisory Authority provides an opinion on, approves, registers, and publishes codes of conduct. Supervisory Authority.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data)" signifies that the Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This involves significant authority and responsibility over the entire lifecycle of personal data, encompassing decisions related to its processing, protection, management, and transference. The Controller is explicitly responsible for establishing the retention period for documentation containing personal data and makes choices regarding its deletion or return. A core obligation of the Controller is to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and to uphold data subject rights, including guaranteeing data accuracy and facilitating the exercise of those rights. The Controller is always required to have an appropriate lawful ground for the processing of personal data, and while explicit consent may be obtained, it is not always the sole lawful basis, especially when processing is essential for a contract. The Controller is also responsible for the overall protection and security of personal data, which includes managing and responding to any data breaches, and applying appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard it. This responsibility extends to implementing measures to minimize the processing of personal data. In addition to determining purposes and means, the Controller collects, processes, and stores personal data. The Controller may also determine its identification requirements and, in the EU, has the capability to make personal data accessible to a third-country authority, and may specifically process data indicating criminal acts when considered within their legitimate interest. Persons under the direct authority of the Controller are authorized to process personal data. Under GDPR, GDPR The relationship between GDPR and a Processor is characterized by specific obligations, responsibilities, and liabilities directly imposed upon the Processor by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Data Subject is governed by a framework of rights, obligations, and legal considerations, particularly under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The Controller is authorized to process a Data Subject's personal data, frequently through contractual agreements, and is obligated to provide essential, timely, and clear information regarding these processing operations, as stipulated in GDPR Article 14(2)(b) and (f). This includes notifying Data Subjects of personal data breaches, especially if they pose a high risk to their rights and freedoms, as mentioned in Article 34 of the GDPR. Controllers are legally mandated to facilitate the easy and full exercise of data protection rights by Data Subjects, ensuring these rights can be exercised without undue hindrance and by providing a simple mechanism for their exercise. This also entails addressing requests for data erasure or objections to processing, and informing Data Subjects about changes and facilitating access to information. For specific activities like processing biometric data, the Controller must obtain explicit, informed, and freely given consent. Transparency from the Controller is also required concerning profiling and automated decision-making processes that impact the Data Subject. In all data processing activities, the Controller must carefully consider the Data Subject's interests, fundamental rights, and freedoms, acknowledging the direct impact of their actions. This assessment varies depending on the specific relationship (e.g., employer-employee, service provider-customer) and the Data Subject's particular situation. In situations involving potential surveillance, the Controller must consider the Data Subject's objection and can only proceed if there is a compelling legitimate interest or for legal claims, also assessing the Data Subject's intention to make data public. When applying the household exemption, key considerations include the Controller’s personal relationship with the Data Subject, the scale and frequency of surveillance, and any potential adverse impact it might have. There must be a balancing exercise between the competing interests of the Controller and the Data Subject's objection, with the burden of proof on the Controller. A significant imbalance, as noted in Recital 47 of the GDPR, can compromise the freedom of consent, and Controllers have been known to attempt to influence Data Subjects for more extensive data collection. It is paramount that the fundamental rights and freedoms of Data Subjects are not overridden by the Controller’s interests, even when a relevant and appropriate relationship exists (e.g., client or in the service of the controller). Controllers must provide clear information to Data Subjects to allow them to correct inaccuracies and select a method for providing information that is appropriate to the manner in which the Data Controller and Data Subject interact. The Controller is responsible for protecting the rights of Data Subjects and responding to their requests for exercising those rights. They are obligated to respond to such requests and make decisions about the processing of personal data for which they are responsible. This includes providing information and taking action on requests from the Data Subject, communicating personal data breaches, and communicating information about data processing and their rights. The Controller enables the Data Subject to monitor data processing and implements pre-contractual measures and data transfers at the Data Subject's request or in their interest. The Controller may offer goods or services to Data Subjects who are in the Union and should compensate any damage a Data Subject may suffer as a result of processing that infringes the Regulation. The Controller can also ask the Data Subject to provide additional information if there are reasonable doubts about their identity, as per Article 12(6) GDPR, and takes into account the reasonable expectations of Data Subjects based on their relationship with the controller when considering legitimate interests. [organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

[organization] Supervisory Authority — A Supervisory Authority (SA) is an independent public authority established by a European Union Member State, as mandated by Article 51 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Its core responsibility is to monitor and enforce the application of data protection law, primarily the GDPR, within its specific national jurisdiction. The overarching goal of an SA is to safeguard the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals regarding the processing of their personal data and to facilitate the free flow of personal data within the European Union. SAs act as competent national bodies under Articles 55 or 56 of the GDPR, endowed with a broad spectrum of powers, including investigation, corrective actions, authorization, and advisory functions. Their decisions, which carry legal effects, are subject to judicial remedies, and they are obligated to respect the right to be heard. Supervisory Authorities are responsible for handling complaints lodged by data subjects, especially when controllers fail to address their requests. They are also the competent national authority to which personal data breaches must be notified without undue delay, typically within 72 hours unless the breach is unlikely to pose a risk to individuals. For cross-border breaches, an SA can act as the lead authority, request further details, advise on informing individuals, and order controllers to do so. They also receive information about the Data Protection Officer's (DPO) name and contact details. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to determine the nature and gravity of infringements, ensure compliance, and order appropriate measures against data controllers or processors. This includes the ability to impose effective, proportionate, and dissuasive administrative fines for GDPR infringements, considering factors such as circumstances, economic viability, and proportionality. They may hold parent companies liable and impose fines for non-compliance with Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) requirements. Additionally, a supervisory authority must be consulted if a DPIA indicates a high residual risk that cannot be mitigated, and it possesses the power to prohibit such processing operations. They can also require documentation of a DPO designation analysis and request access to records of processing operations. Beyond enforcement, Supervisory Authorities play a crucial role in GDPR accreditation and certification mechanisms. This involves approving criteria, reviewing existing certifications, accrediting certification bodies, and potentially acting as a certification body themselves. They can establish additional accreditation requirements, sometimes in cooperation with a National Accreditation Body. SAs are authorized to oversee and approve administrative arrangements for data transfers under Article 46(3)(b) GDPR, adopt standard contractual clauses for data processing matters, approve safeguards, and apply consistency mechanisms. They are also responsible for publishing lists of processing operations subject to mandatory DPIAs and for conducting prior consultations if DPIA results indicate a high risk or if existing operations have been pre-checked. While typically one lead supervisory authority exists for cross-border processing, some Member States may have more than one SA, all of whom are bound by the content of a draft decision once consensus is reached. They are also responsible for verifying compliance with data protection regulations and may require a controller to communicate a personal data breach to the data subject.

[organization] Supervisory Authorities — Supervisory Authorities (SAs) are independent national public bodies primarily tasked with overseeing the application and enforcement of data protection law, particularly the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), within their respective countries. Their foundational mission involves protecting the fundamental rights and freedoms of data subjects while also facilitating the free flow of personal data within the European Union. These authorities play a crucial role in monitoring adherence to data protection principles, advising on and documenting proportionality and necessity tests, and ensuring the consistent application of data protection principles and individual rights. They evaluate data processing features and assess compliance, including with Article 25 of the GDPR. They are also responsible for establishing and publicizing lists of processing operations that require a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA). SAs are also responsible for monitoring and ensuring compliance with data protection rules, possessing equivalent powers and sanctions across the Union. Supervisory Authorities are endowed with significant enforcement powers under GDPR Article 58, allowing them to issue corrective measures and impose administrative fines for infringements. These fines are expected to be effective, dissuasive, and proportionate, adjusted based on aggravating and mitigating factors. Both data controllers and processors are directly accountable to these authorities for GDPR compliance. Past decisions based on Directive 95/46/EC remain in force until amended or repealed. Beyond enforcement, SAs handle and investigate complaints from data subjects, including those related to search engine providers' refusal to erase search results under Article 17 GDPR, and are responsible for assessing delisting requests. They also encourage the development of codes of conduct and foster certification mechanisms, potentially acting as certification bodies themselves, and approving criteria and issuing certifications, as well as receiving reasons for granting or withdrawing certification from certification bodies and making requirements and criteria for certification public. SAs have powers to obtain access to personal data and premises from data controllers or processors. Their competence does not extend to courts acting in their judicial capacity. Supervisory Authorities have a legal obligation to cooperate, exchange information, and endeavor to reach consensus, especially within the "One Stop Shop" (OSS) model and obligations under Article 60 of the GDPR. This involves coordinating through draft decisions, where other Supervisory Authorities (CSAs) receive relevant information and draft decisions from the Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) and provide feedback. They are considered fully acquainted with notified decisions and take decisions on issues handled in the consistency mechanism, which are registered by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB). Instances of conflicting views among Supervisory Authorities can lead to EDPB decisions, demonstrating their cooperative yet authoritative role in ensuring GDPR compliance and consistency across the EU. Supervisory Authorities are stakeholders with whom Data Protection Officers (DPOs) act as intermediaries, and data subjects and DPOs can contact them for data protection matters, with DPO contact details and name communicated to them. They are also involved in the exchange of information with controllers, processors, and the Board regarding binding corporate rules and mutual assistance, and cooperate to ensure the consistent application of the Regulation and communicate with the Board, promoting cooperation, information exchange, and training. They are regulatory bodies responsible for interpreting and enforcing data protection regulations, including assessing "substantial effect" on a case-by-case basis.

[interface] Dedicated Dashboard — An interface provided by gatekeepers to inform end users about specific recipients of their personal data, pursuant to Article 6(10) DMA.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[organization] Gatekeeper — A Gatekeeper is an entity designated under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically pursuant to Article 3(4) or Article 3(9), indicating its provision of Core Platform Services (CPSs). Prominent examples of such organizations include Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta. These Gatekeepers control access to specific digital services and are subject to extensive legal obligations under the DMA, and in many cases, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Their role is central to the regulatory framework designed to ensure fair and contestable digital markets. Gatekeepers process the personal data of end users, often acting as controllers or processors, and are responsible for ensuring that consent obtained for data processing, particularly for online advertising and data combination, complies with both GDPR and DMA requirements. This includes the meticulous recording of consent refusals or withdrawals. They are obligated to enable continuous and real-time access to data, prevent data accumulation, and ensure robust data security. Their responsibilities extend to providing data upon request by business users or authorized third parties, free of charge, and establishing appropriate authentication and authorization procedures for such access. They must also implement security measures for personal data, comply with portability requests under DMA Article 6(9), and provide comprehensive information to data subjects. Furthermore, Gatekeepers are tasked with selecting and implementing anonymization methods for end-user data shared under Article 6(11) DMA and must implement measures to maintain service integrity and security. They also have duties concerning interoperability, including exchanging message content and personal data with other providers while ensuring security for their end users. This includes protecting metadata, verifying communication authenticity, and ensuring compliance with geographical limitations and data protection regulations for Number-Independent Interpersonal Communication Services (NIICS). Gatekeepers must design online interfaces that do not undermine user autonomy, provide reminders, and ensure fair access to datasets by altering data to mitigate identification risks and imposing contractual measures on third-party undertakings for data access and compliance monitoring. Their conduct is subject to examination for compliance with both the DMA and GDPR, and they may have a "main establishment" under the GDPR. They are also separate controllers under GDPR for their own data processing and have obligations under Article 6(4) and Article 8(1) of the DMA.

[organization] Supervisory Authority — A Supervisory Authority (SA) is an independent public authority established by a European Union Member State, as mandated by Article 51 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Its core responsibility is to monitor and enforce the application of data protection law, primarily the GDPR, within its specific national jurisdiction. The overarching goal of an SA is to safeguard the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals regarding the processing of their personal data and to facilitate the free flow of personal data within the European Union. SAs act as competent national bodies under Articles 55 or 56 of the GDPR, endowed with a broad spectrum of powers, including investigation, corrective actions, authorization, and advisory functions. Their decisions, which carry legal effects, are subject to judicial remedies, and they are obligated to respect the right to be heard. Supervisory Authorities are responsible for handling complaints lodged by data subjects, especially when controllers fail to address their requests. They are also the competent national authority to which personal data breaches must be notified without undue delay, typically within 72 hours unless the breach is unlikely to pose a risk to individuals. For cross-border breaches, an SA can act as the lead authority, request further details, advise on informing individuals, and order controllers to do so. They also receive information about the Data Protection Officer's (DPO) name and contact details. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to determine the nature and gravity of infringements, ensure compliance, and order appropriate measures against data controllers or processors. This includes the ability to impose effective, proportionate, and dissuasive administrative fines for GDPR infringements, considering factors such as circumstances, economic viability, and proportionality. They may hold parent companies liable and impose fines for non-compliance with Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) requirements. Additionally, a supervisory authority must be consulted if a DPIA indicates a high residual risk that cannot be mitigated, and it possesses the power to prohibit such processing operations. They can also require documentation of a DPO designation analysis and request access to records of processing operations. Beyond enforcement, Supervisory Authorities play a crucial role in GDPR accreditation and certification mechanisms. This involves approving criteria, reviewing existing certifications, accrediting certification bodies, and potentially acting as a certification body themselves. They can establish additional accreditation requirements, sometimes in cooperation with a National Accreditation Body. SAs are authorized to oversee and approve administrative arrangements for data transfers under Article 46(3)(b) GDPR, adopt standard contractual clauses for data processing matters, approve safeguards, and apply consistency mechanisms. They are also responsible for publishing lists of processing operations subject to mandatory DPIAs and for conducting prior consultations if DPIA results indicate a high risk or if existing operations have been pre-checked. While typically one lead supervisory authority exists for cross-border processing, some Member States may have more than one SA, all of whom are bound by the content of a draft decision once consensus is reached. They are also responsible for verifying compliance with data protection regulations and may require a controller to communicate a personal data breach to the data subject.

[concept] Online Services — Online Services are digital platforms or applications delivered over the internet, frequently categorized as "information society services." These services are typically provided in exchange for remuneration, remotely, via electronic means, and in response to an individual recipient's request. Modern online services are integral to contemporary society, facilitated by mobile internet and interconnected devices, encompassing diverse sectors such as social media, e-commerce, and communication. A key characteristic of Online Services is their digital nature, often involving the processing of personal data. This processing is particularly relevant in the context of GDPR Article 6(1)(b), especially as these services are often provided under contracts that are not individually negotiated. This contractual model underscores the importance of principles like purpose limitation and data minimization. These digital platforms can also include features such as content personalization or advertising, and frequently collect detailed information regarding user engagement.
Online services are platforms or offerings where data subjects might interact with controllers, implying the use of online identifiers.
[concept] Delivery Service — A service that handles the delivery of goods, which may cross-use identification details without consent if functionally interconnected.

[service] Payment Service — A service that processes payments, which may cross-use identification details without consent if functionally interconnected.

[artifact] Online Interface — An online interface is a digital platform provided by the gatekeeper through which business users can obtain consent and end users can withdraw consent.

[person] End User — An "End User" refers to an individual customer or consumer who interacts with various services, specifically Core Platform Services (CPS), and can include any natural or legal person utilizing these services, even those traditionally considered business users, with the explicit exclusion of business users in certain contexts. They are the individuals who use the products or services offered by gatekeepers or business users through a relevant CPS. A primary characteristic of an End User is that their personal data is frequently subject to processing, combination, and cross-use by gatekeepers. Their consent and preferences regarding this data processing are recorded and honored, particularly under regulations such as GDPR or the ePrivacy Directive. While their personal data may be cross-used with or without explicit consent depending on the specific legal basis, they generally have choices concerning data access. End Users are individuals whose data is collected and exchanged during interoperability, and whose data, location, and communication privacy are regulated, especially when using specific services like NIICS, where they have the ability to send or block messages. Their data is also subject to re-identification attempts by gatekeepers. A crucial aspect of the End User's rights is data portability, as outlined in DMA Article 6(9) and GDPR Article 20. End Users are individuals who request data portability, authorize third parties to port data, and interact with gatekeeper interfaces to initiate these requests. Explicit and specific consent is required from the End User for personal data transfers to third countries that do not have an adequacy decision. Furthermore, the End User's consent is essential for sharing their personal data when business users request access to it in the context of a Core Platform Service.

Under GDPR, Controller The (Controller, Processor) relationship describes an arrangement, primarily defined by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), where a Processor handles personal data on behalf of a Controller. The Controller retains the primary and ultimate responsibility for ensuring overall compliance with data protection principles, including data protection by design and by default (DPbDD), and this accountability extends to any Processor and sub-processors involved. This relationship mandates that the Controller select Processors who offer sufficient guarantees regarding GDPR compliance. This relationship is formalized and governed by a legally binding contract or other legal act, often referred to as a processing agreement. This agreement details how GDPR requirements will be implemented, outlines specific obligations, and defines assistance duties. The Controller must provide documented instructions to the Processor on how to process personal data, and the Processor is obligated to comply. The Processor processes personal data only on these documented instructions. Even without a written agreement, the existence and definition of this relationship hold. The Processor has various duties, including assisting the Controller in fulfilling obligations related to data subject rights and Articles 32 to 36 of the GDPR, ensuring compliance with data protection obligations, and reporting to the Controller. This assistance includes deleting or returning personal data at the Controller's choice, providing compliance information, and cooperating with Controller-conducted audits. A critical obligation for the Processor is to notify the Controller "without undue delay" upon becoming aware of a personal data breach it is processing on behalf of the Controller, as mandated by Article 33(2) GDPR. Processors must also notify the Controller of any request from a third-country authority without undue delay and follow the Controller's instructions, unless prohibited by law. The Processor is liable to the Controller for fulfilling these obligations. The Controller can authorize the use of sub-processors, but the Processor must obtain prior written authorization from the Controller for engaging another processor. The Processor is liable to the Controller for the sub-processors' adherence to data protection obligations. In scenarios involving data transfers, such as a third-country company (Controller) engaging a non-EEA processor, the processor acts as a data exporter on behalf of the Controller. The Controller must provide a comprehensive list of all data recipients, including processors. The relationship demands good faith cooperation, involving contract negotiation and management of audit and instruction processes. Controllers also carry out Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) with the processors. In some cases, the lead supervisory authority of the Controller may also become the lead supervisory authority for the Processor. When an end user qualifies as a Controller, an authorized third party may act as a Processor. Processor.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data Processing)" describes the role and responsibilities of a controller in the context of personal data processing. A controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means by which personal data is processed. This includes the crucial task of assessing what processing of personal data is objectively necessary for specified purposes and ensuring that the processing is limited to those necessities. Controllers are held responsible for the overall processing of personal data, which also entails adhering to regulatory requirements. Notably, to lawfully engage in personal data processing, controllers must meet specific criteria, such as those outlined in Article 6(1)(f) of the GDPR. This comprehensive responsibility ensures compliance with relevant regulations governing personal data. Personal Data Processing.

Under GDPR, GDPR The relationship between GDPR and a Processor is characterized by specific obligations, responsibilities, and liabilities directly imposed upon the Processor by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). A processor is subject to the GDPR for any given processing operation, with its role and duties explicitly defined within the regulation.
