Under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), specifically Article 42(1) and Article 43, these organizations are subject to accreditation by supervisory authorities or national accreditation bodies. Their functions include determining data protection certification criteria and, in some instances, being responsible for accrediting data protection certification mechanisms and seals.

This activity often serves the public interest, scientific research, or statistical research. Under various data protection frameworks, such as GDPR Article 17.3.d, Archiving Purposes can serve as a specific ground for processing personal data. [Source: Guidelines_on_Personal_data_breach_notification_under_Regulation_2016679] "Article 34(3) states three conditions that, if met, do not require notification to individuals in the event of a breach. These are:  The controller has applied appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect personal data prior to the breach, in particular those measures that render personal data unintelligible to any person who is not authorised to access it. This could, for example, include protecting personal data with state-of-the-art encryption, or by tokenization.  Immediately following a breach, the controller has taken steps to ensure that the high risk posed to individuals’ rights and freedoms is no longer likely to materialise. For example, depending on the circumstances of the case, the controller may have immediately identified and taken action against the individual who has accessed personal data before they were able to do anything with it. Due regard still needs to be given to the possible consequences of any breach of confidentiality, again, depending on the nature of the data concerned.  It would involve disproportionate effort37 to contact individuals, perhaps where their contact details have been lost as a result of the breach or are not known in the first place. For example, the warehouse of a statistical office has flooded and the documents containing personal data were stored only in paper form. Instead, the controller must make a public communication or take a similar measure, whereby the individuals are informed in an equally effective manner. In the case of disproportionate effort, technical arrangements could also be envisaged to make information about the breach available on demand, which could prove useful to those individuals who may be affected by a breach, but the controller cannot otherwise contact. In accordance with the accountability principle controllers should be able to demonstrate to the supervisory authority that they meet one or more of these conditions 38. It should be borne in mind that while notification may initially not be required if there is no risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, this may change over time and the risk would have to be re-evaluated. If a controller decides not to communicate a breach to the individual, Article 34(4) explains that the supervisory authority can require it to do so, if it considers the breach is likely to result in a high risk to individuals. Alternatively, it may consider that the conditions in Article 34(3) have been met in which case notification to individuals is not required. If the supervisory authority determines that the decision not to notify data subjects is not well founded, it may consider employing its available powers and sanctions. IV. Assessing risk and high risk A. Risk as a trigger for notification 37 See WP29 Guidelines on transparency, which will consider the issue of disproportionate effort, available at http://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/just/document.cfm?doc_id=48850 38 See Article 5(2) 23 Although the GDPR introduces the obligation to notify a breach, it is not a requirement to do so in all circumstances:  Notification to the competent supervisory authority is required unless a breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals.  Communication of a breach to the individual is only triggered where it is likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms. This means that immediately upon becoming aware of a breach, it is vitally important that the controller should not only seek to contain the incident but it should also assess the risk that could result from it. There are two important reasons for this: firstly, knowing the likelihood and the potential severity of the impact on the individual will help the controller to take effective steps to contain and address the breach; secondly, it will help it to determine whether notification is required to the supervisory authority and, if necessary, to the individuals concerned. As explained above, notification of a breach is required unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, and the key trigger requiring communication of a breach to data subjects is where it is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. This risk exists when the breach may lead to physical, material or non-material damage for the individuals whose data have been breached. Examples of such damage are discrimination, identity theft or fraud, financial loss and damage to reputation. When the breach involves personal data that reveals racial or ethnic origin, political opinion, religion or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership, or includes genetic data, data concerning health or data concerning sex life, or criminal convictions and offences or related security measures, such damage should be considered likely to occur39. B. Factors to consider when assessing risk Recitals 75 and 76 of the GDPR suggest that generally when assessing risk, consideration should be given to both the likelihood and severity of the risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects. It further states that risk should be evaluated on the basis of an objective assessment. It should be noted that assessing the risk to people’s rights and freedoms as a result of a breach has a different focus to the risk considered in a DPIA)40. The DPIA considers both the risks of the data processing being carried out as planned, and the risks in case of a breach. When considering a potential breach, it looks in general terms at the likelihood of this occurring, and the damage to the data subject that might ensue; in other words, it is an assessment of a hypothetical event. With an actual breach, the event has already occurred, and so the focus is wholly about the resulting risk of the impact of the breach on individuals. Example A"

The principle of integrity and confidentiality includes protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures. The security of personal data requires appropriate measures designed to prevent and manage data breach incidents; to guarantee the proper execution of data processing tasks, and compliance with the other principles; and to facilitate the effective exercise of individuals’ rights. 84. Recital 78 states that one of the DPbDD measures could consist of enabling the controller to “create and improve security features”. Along with other DPbDD measures, Recital 78 suggests a responsibility on the controllers to continually assess whether it is using the appropriate means of processing at all times and to assess whether the chosen measures actually counter the existing vulnerabilities. Furthermore, controllers should conduct regular reviews of the information security measures that surround and protect personal data, and the procedure for handling data breaches. 85. Key design and default integrity and confidentiality elements may include:  Information security management system (ISMS) – Have an operative means of managing policies and procedures for information security.  Risk analysis – Assess the risks against the security of personal data by considering the impact on individuals’ rights and counter identified risks. For use in risk assessment; develop and maintain a comprehensive, systematic and realistic “threat modelling” and an attack surface analysis of the designed software to reduce attack vectors and opportunities to exploit weak points and vulnerabilities.  Security by design – Consider security requirements as early as possible in the system design and development and continuously integrate and perform relevant tests.  Maintenance – Regular review and test software, hardware, systems and services, etc. to uncover vulnerabilities of the systems supporting the processing.  Access control management – Only the authorized personnel who need to should have access to the personal data necessary for their processing tasks, and the controller should differentiate between access privileges of authorized personnel. o Access limitation (agents) – Shape the data processing in a way that a minimal number of people need access to personal data to perform their duties, and limit access accordingly. o Access limitation (content) – In the context of each processing operation, limit access to only those attributes per data set that are needed to perform that operation. Adopted 27 Moreover, limit access to data pertaining to those data subjects who are in the remit of the respective employee. o Access segregation – Shape the data processing in a way that no individual needs comprehensive access to all data collected about a data subject, much less all personal data of a particular category of data subjects.  Secure transfers – Transfers shall be secured against unauthorized and accidental access and changes.  Secure storage – Data storage shall be secure from unauthorized access and changes. There should be procedures to assess the risk of centralized or decentralized storage, and what categories of personal data this applies to. Some data may need additional security measures than others or isolation from others.  Pseudonymization – Personal data and back-ups/logs should be pseudonymized as a security measure to minimise risks of potential data breaches, for example using hashing or encryption.  Backups/logs – Keep back-ups and logs to the extent necessary for information security, use audit trails and event monitoring as a routine security control. These shall be protected from unauthorised and accidental access and change and reviewed regularly and incidents should be handled promptly.  Disaster recovery/ business continuity – Address information system disaster recovery and business continuity requirements to restore the availability of personal data following up major incidents.  Protection according to risk – All categories of personal data should be protected with measures adequate with respect to the risk of a security breach. Data presenting special risks should, when possible, be kept separated from the rest of the personal data.  Security incident response management – Have in place routines, procedures and resources to detect, contain, handle, report and learn from data breaches.  Incident management – Controller should have processes in place to handle breaches and incidents, in order to make the processing system more robust. This includes notification procedures, such as management of notification (to the supervisory authority) and information (to data subjects). Example A controller wants to extract large quantities of personal data from a medical database containing electronic (patient) health records to a dedicated database server in the company in order to process the extracted data for quality assurance purposes. They can also involve linking data, forming different conducts, combining data, or cross-using data. Per Article 4(2) of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), these operations are defined as any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or on sets of personal data. These operations are composed of various components, such as data, systems, and processes, all of which should adhere to specific criteria. Activities often include the selection of targeting criteria and the display of advertisements to a specific target audience. Processing operations are a primary object of certification under the GDPR, potentially encompassing governance processes and leading to the creation of a product or service. Both data controllers and processors are obligated to demonstrate compliance when executing these operations. Actions performed on personal data should be limited to what is necessary, contributing to a defined processing purpose, and designed to process only the minimum amount of necessary data. Processing operations are actions carried out by a data controller using collected data, requiring specific information provisions and legal bases. They may also benefit from special regimes under GDPR. Examples include the collection, storage, use, or deletion of data. Some operations may involve the use of CCTV and are subject to the applicability of the household exemption. Records must be maintained for these data handling activities. Furthermore, processing operations that involve personal data may require a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) under GDPR if they pose a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. When a DPIA is required, these activities necessitate a systematic description, an assessment of necessity, proportionality, and risks, and the implementation of measures to address those risks.
Processing Operations refer to any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction.
Processing Operations involve any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, storage, etc.
Actions or sets of actions performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, storage, or disclosure.
Actions or sets of actions performed upon personal data, which supervisory authorities are generally competent to oversee, except for courts acting in judicial capacity.
Processing operations refer to any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, as defined in Article 4(2) GDPR.
Processing operations refer to activities involving personal data, such as combining or cross-using data.
[artifact] Hardware — The physical components of a device that gatekeepers may take measures to protect the integrity of when allowing third-party apps.

[organization] Producers — Producers are entities that develop processing solutions (hardware, software, services, systems). They should demonstrate Data Protection by Design and Default (DPbDD) in their development life-cycle and facilitate controllers' needs.
Producers are key enablers for DPbDD, providing solutions to controllers that embed data protection.
Producers are responsible for developing, designing, selecting, and using applications, services, and products with regard to data protection.
[data] Performance Data — Performance data, such as crash data, can be relevant to business users for providing customer support.
[concept] General and Incident Reporting — Measures specified by the implementing act for regular reporting and reporting specific incidents related to data.
[concept] Processing Operations Security — Processing Operations Security refers to the measures taken to ensure the protection and integrity of data processing activities.

[concept] Processor — A Processor, as defined by Article 4(8) of the GDPR, is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that processes personal data on behalf of a controller. This entity's primary function is to handle personal data strictly according to the controller's documented instructions, without independently determining the purposes or means of the processing activity, and thus, processors do not pursue independent objectives for data processing. A website hosting company is an example of a Processor. Processors are responsible for protecting personal data and are involved in the processing of personal data, with specific legal obligations under the GDPR, including adherence to its principles, ensuring confidentiality, and implementing robust security measures. They must provide sufficient guarantees, such as compliance with codes of conduct or certification mechanisms, and are required to operate under a binding contract or legal act with the controller. This contract typically details their responsibilities, including assisting with Data Protection by Design and by Default (DPbDD), implementing technical and organizational measures, conducting data protection impact assessments (DPIA), and providing compliance information. The processor assists the controller in carrying out a DPIA, and its roles and responsibilities in a DPIA must be contractually defined. Processors are also obligated to notify the controller of any data breach without undue delay, inform the controller of any infringing instructions, and are subject to audits. Upon termination of processing activities, they must delete or return personal data. They have specific obligations regarding personal data breaches, as mentioned in Article 33 requirements, particularly Article 33(2). Processors can also act as exporters or importers of personal data, transferring data to third countries or international organizations under specific conditions, always on behalf of the controller and must implement appropriate safeguards for data transfers. While their name may not be explicitly included in consent forms, they are listed as recipients of data. They are held liable to the controller for the performance of their sub-processors' obligations, necessitating that sub-processors also provide sufficient guarantees. Processors' activities and processing operations are assessed for GDPR compliance, and they can be the direct cause of a data breach. They may be the subject of infringement claims, addressed by the final decision of a competent supervisory authority, and can be directly and individually concerned by an EDPB binding decision, against which they may bring an action for annulment. For Processors located in the EU, they must identify an applicable ground for transfer before responding to requests from third-country authorities, as stipulated under Article 48. The designation of a representative does not affect their liability under GDPR, and they may be subject to legal actions for damages if they infringe the regulation or act outside of controller instructions. A data subject can seek judicial remedies against a processor. A Processor may be required to designate a Data Protection Officer (DPO), especially if their core activities involve key operations to achieve their goals, or if their core activities require such a designation under GDPR. When a DPO is designated, the processor is required to publish and communicate the DPO's contact details according to Article 37(7) of the GDPR. The DPO advises the processor on GDPR obligations and assists in monitoring internal compliance with the GDPR. The processor may assign the task of maintaining records of processing operations to the DPO, and the processor supports and involves the Data Protection Officer. For the cooperation procedure to apply, a Processor involved in cross-border processing must have a main or single establishment in an EU Member State. This main establishment oversees such cross-border processing. The main establishment is where its central administration is located in the Union, or where its main processing activities take place if no central administration exists in the Union. Processors are subject to the authority of a Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) or Concerned Supervisory Authority (CSA), and LSAs may interact with Processors to gather relevant information, such as investigation findings, reports, and meeting records. Processors involved in cross-border processing are subject to procedures and potential enforcement action and may be directly targeted by decisions from the LSA. As parties targeted by a draft decision, their right to be heard must comply with national law, and their rights may be affected by changes in a revised draft decision. A Processor's actions can lead to complaints and prompt action by an LSA. Processors have obligations under Article 60(10), are informed of decisions by the LSA, and are obliged to notify the LSA of any measures adopted to comply with a decision entailing corrective measures. A processor can benefit from the one-stop-shop system if established in multiple Member States, and its establishment in multiple Member States can trigger the lead authority mechanism. Guidance can be provided on their implementation of appropriate measures and demonstration of compliance.
A processor is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that processes personal data on behalf of the controller.
A processor processes personal data on behalf of a controller. An authorized third party may act as a processor for an end user if the end user is a controller.

[data] On-Device Data — On-Device Data is data exclusively processed on a device, falls within the scope of Article 6(9) DMA, and gatekeepers must enable its portability at the request of end users or authorized third parties.
Data exclusively processed and stored on an end user's device, to which gatekeepers must enable effective and continuous access under Article 6(10) DMA.

[organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

A business user is a commercial entity or individual that utilizes gatekeeper products or services and may request access to end-user data.

A Business User is a party that requests access to data, including historic and real-time data, and is subject to monitoring by data protection supervisory authorities.

The Guidelines focus on controllers’ implementation of DPbDD based on the obligation in Article 25 of the GDPR.1 Other actors, such as processors and producers of products, services and applications (henceforth “producers”), who are not directly addressed in Article 25, may also find these Guidelines useful in creating GDPR compliant products and services that enable controllers to fulfil their data protection obligations.2 Recital 78 of the GDPR adds that DPbDD should be taken into consideration in the context of public tenders. Despite all controllers having the duty to integrate DPbDD into their processing activities, this provision fosters the adoption of the data protection principles, where public administrations should lead by example. The controller is responsible for the fulfilment of the DPbDD obligations for the processing carried out by their processors and sub-processors, they should therefore take this into account when contracting with these parties. 2. The requirement described in Article 25 is for controllers to have data protection designed into the processing of personal data and as a default setting and this applies throughout the processing lifecycle. DPbDD is also a requirement for processing systems pre-existing before the GDPR entered into force. Controllers must have the processing consistently updated in line with the GDPR. For more information on how to maintain an existing system in line with DPbDD, see subchapter 2.1.4 of these Guidelines. The core of the provision is to ensure appropriate and effective data protection both by design and by default, which means that controllers should be able to demonstrate that they have the appropriate measures and safeguards in the processing to ensure that the data protection principles and the rights and freedoms of data subjects are effective. 3. Chapter 2 of the Guidelines focuses on an interpretation of the requirements set forth by Article 25 and explores the legal obligations introduced by the provision. Examples on how to apply DPbDD in the context of specific data protection principles are provided in Chapter 3. 4. The Guidelines address the possibility to establish a certification mechanism to demonstrate compliance with Article 25 in Chapter 4, as well as how the Article may be enforced by supervisory authorities in Chapter 5. Finally, the Guidelines provide stakeholders with further recommendations on how to successfully implement DPbDD. The EDPB recognizes the challenges for small and medium enterprises (henceforth “SMEs”) to fully comply with the obligations of DPbDD, and provides additional recommendations specifically to SMEs in Chapter 6. 2 ANALYSIS OF ARTICLE 25(1) AND (2) DATA PROTECTION BY DESIGN AND BY DEFAULT 5. The aim of this Chapter is to explore and provide guidance on the requirements to data protection by design in Article 25(1) and to data protection by default in Article 25(2) respectively. Adopted 6 by design and data protection by default are complementary concepts, which mutually reinforce each other. Data subjects will benefit more from data protection by default if data protection by design is concurrently implemented – and vice versa. 6. DPbDD is a requirement for all controllers, including small businesses and multinational companies alike. That being the case, the complexity of implementing DPbDD may vary based on the individual processing operation. Regardless of the size however, in all cases, positive benefits for controller and data subject can be achieved by implementing DPbDD. 2.1 Article 25(1): Data protection by design 2.1.1 Controller’s obligation to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures and necessary safeguards into the processing 7. In line with Article 25(1) the controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures which are designed to implement the data protection principles and to integrate the necessary safeguards into the processing in order to meet the requirements and protect the rights and freedoms of data subjects. Both appropriate measures and necessary safeguards are meant to serve the same purpose of protecting the rights of data subjects and ensuring that the protection of their personal data is built into the processing. 8. Technical and organizational measures and necessary safeguards can be understood in a broad sense as any method or means that a controller may employ in the processing. Being appropriate means that the measures and necessary safeguards should be suited to achieve the intended purpose, i.e. they must implement the data protection principles effectively3. The requirement to appropriateness is thus closely related to the requirement of effectiveness. 9. A technical or organisational measure and safeguard can be anything from the use of advanced technical solutions to the basic training of personnel. Examples that may be suitable, depending on the context and risks associated with the processing in question, includes pseudonymization of personal data4; storing personal data available in a structured, commonly machine readable format; enabling data subjects to intervene in the processing; providing information about the storage of personal data; having malware detection systems; training employees about basic “cyber hygiene”;"

[organization] Hospital — A Hospital is a healthcare institution responsible for collecting and managing significant quantities of sensitive patient data, often utilizing an electronic health record system. This organization has been noted for experiencing a personal data breach where staff members could view unauthorized patient health files due to issues with authorization monitoring, specifically concerning staff retaining access to patient files after transferring departments; an internal investigation was conducted to address this. The sensitive nature of the data processed means that data breaches at a Hospital are highly impactful, and the unavailability of critical medical data can pose a substantial risk to individuals' rights and freedoms. Furthermore, a Hospital can also be an organization involved in scientific research, as exemplified by "Project X," which necessitates the use of real patient dental records. The Hospital has also been identified as a victim of ransomware attacks (e.g., Case No. 03), where its information systems were compromised, leading to data encryption and subsequent delays in patient care. Consequently, a Hospital is an organization legally obliged to notify relevant authorities and affected individuals in cases of cyber-attacks impacting medical records.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[concept] Processing — Processing, in the context of data management and privacy, encompasses any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or sets of personal data. For operations involving personal data, it is crucial to determine specific purposes and means, often requiring consent from the data subject. A fundamental principle dictates that processing should be carried out in a fair and transparent manner. Processing activities can be performed by entities such as a controller or processor. ragPromptContext: [organization] Alternative Service Providers — These providers can request interoperability from gatekeepers for number-independent interpersonal communications services.

[service] Information Society Service — An Information Society Service is broadly defined as a service typically provided for remuneration, at a distance, and by electronic means, in response to an individual request from a service recipient. This category encompasses various online services, including contracts concluded or transmitted electronically. A key characteristic of an Information Society Service is that storing or accessing information in a user's terminal equipment must be strictly necessary for the provision of the service itself. This necessity can lead to certain exemptions under Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive. Specifically, for an Information Society Service, consent may not be required for gaining access to information already stored in a device (such as a vehicle) if such access is explicitly requested by the subscriber. This exemption simplifies data access under specific, user-initiated circumstances. Furthermore, an Information Society Service is defined more formally in point (b) of Article 1(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/1535. When an Information Society Service is explicitly requested by a subscriber or user, certain processing exemptions may apply. For services of this nature that are often offered online, special considerations regarding children's consent might also be applicable, as detailed in specific regulatory sections like Section 7.1.1.
[organization] Independent Body — An entity entrusted with the appointment of supervisory authority members under Member State law.

[service] Payment Service — A service that processes payments, which may cross-use identification details without consent if functionally interconnected.
A payment service is a service provided by a gatekeeper where an end user's personal data collected in a CPS can be cross-used to process a payment, relying on Article 6(1)(b) GDPR.
[method] Fraud Monitoring and Prevention — Techniques and activities aimed at detecting and preventing fraudulent activities, which can be a basis for automated processing.

[person] Client — A client is an entity represented by a law firm, in this case, Company ABC, which provides a mandate to the law firm.

[concept] Data Transfers — Data transfers involve the movement of data from one location or entity to another.
Data Transfers refer to the movement of data to third countries or international organizations, which can be based on appropriate safeguards and legal remedies for data subjects.
Data transfers involve the movement of personal data, and possible risks due to absence of adequacy decisions or safeguards (Article 46) must be informed.
Data Transfers involve the movement of personal data from one entity or location to another, especially across borders.

[concept] Administrative Fines — Administrative Fines are financial or monetary penalties that supervisory authorities impose in response to infringements of legal requirements, particularly those set forth in data protection regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). These fines, detailed in Article 83 of the GDPR, are designed to be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive. The imposition of Administrative Fines intensified under the GDPR, reflecting an increased level of penalty for such infringements. The criteria for setting these fines are based on the nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement, and their calculation begins from a harmonized point, varying according to the specific circumstances of each case, guided by particular principles and guidelines under the GDPR. Certification can also be a factor in determining these penalties. For undertakings, Administrative Fines can potentially reach up to 20,000,000 EUR or 4% of their total worldwide annual turnover, with the upper limit determined by their combined turnover. While imposed by supervisory authorities, their assessment may be subject to review by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB). These fines represent a type of legal effect that can be imposed as a measure for non-compliance with the Regulation.
[concept] Compensation — Compensation is the right for any person who has suffered damage due to an infringement of the Regulation to receive payment from the controller or processor.

[organization] Gatekeeper — A Gatekeeper is an entity designated under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically pursuant to Article 3(4) or Article 3(9), indicating its provision of Core Platform Services (CPSs). Prominent examples of such organizations include Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta. These Gatekeepers control access to specific digital services and are subject to extensive legal obligations under the DMA, and in many cases, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Their role is central to the regulatory framework designed to ensure fair and contestable digital markets. Gatekeepers process the personal data of end users, often acting as controllers or processors, and are responsible for ensuring that consent obtained for data processing, particularly for online advertising and data combination, complies with both GDPR and DMA requirements. This includes the meticulous recording of consent refusals or withdrawals. They are obligated to enable continuous and real-time access to data, prevent data accumulation, and ensure robust data security. Their responsibilities extend to providing data upon request by business users or authorized third parties, free of charge, and establishing appropriate authentication and authorization procedures for such access. They must also implement security measures for personal data, comply with portability requests under DMA Article 6(9), and provide comprehensive information to data subjects. Furthermore, Gatekeepers are tasked with selecting and implementing anonymization methods for end-user data shared under Article 6(11) DMA and must implement measures to maintain service integrity and security. They also have duties concerning interoperability, including exchanging message content and personal data with other providers while ensuring security for their end users. This includes protecting metadata, verifying communication authenticity, and ensuring compliance with geographical limitations and data protection regulations for Number-Independent Interpersonal Communication Services (NIICS). Gatekeepers must design online interfaces that do not undermine user autonomy, provide reminders, and ensure fair access to datasets by altering data to mitigate identification risks and imposing contractual measures on third-party undertakings for data access and compliance monitoring. Their conduct is subject to examination for compliance with both the DMA and GDPR, and they may have a "main establishment" under the GDPR. They are also separate controllers under GDPR for their own data processing and have obligations under Article 6(4) and Article 8(1) of the DMA.

Finally, as leading practice for “receiving” data controllers, the WP29 recommends that data subjects are provided with complete information about the nature of personal data which are relevant for the performance of their services. In addition to underpinning fair processing, this allows users to limit the risks for third parties, and also any other unnecessary duplication of personal data even where no other data subjects are involved. - How can the data controller identify the data subject before answering his request? There are no prescriptive requirements to be found in the GDPR on how to authenticate the data subject. Nevertheless, Article 12(2) of the GDPR states that the data controller shall not refuse to act on request of a data subject for exercising his or her rights (including the right to data portability) unless it is processing personal data for a purpose that does not require the identification of a data subject and it can demonstrate that it is not able to identify the data subject. However, as per Article 11(2), in such circumstances the data subject can provide more information to enable his or her identification. Additionally, Article 12(6) provides that where a data controller has reasonable doubts about the identity of a data subject, it can request further information to confirm the data subject’s identity. Where a data subject provides additional information enabling his or her identification, the data controller shall not refuse to act on the request. Where information and data collected online is linked to pseudonyms or unique identifiers, data controllers can implement appropriate procedures 24 Article 12 requires that data controllers provide “any communications […] in a concise, transparent, intelligible, and easily assessable form, using clear and plain language, in particular for any information addressed specifically to a child.” 14 enabling an individual to make a data portability request and receive the data relating to him or her. In any case, data controllers must implement an authentication procedure in order to strongly ascertain the identity of the data subject requesting his or her personal data or more generally exercising the rights granted by the GDPR. These procedures often already exist. The data subjects are often already authenticated by the data controller before entering into a contract or collecting his or her consent to the processing. As a consequence, the personal data used to register the individual concerned by the processing can also be used as evidence to authenticate the data subject for portability purposes25. While in these cases, the data subjects’ prior identification may require a request for proof of their legal identity, such verification may not be relevant to assess the link between the data and the individual concerned, since such a link is not related with the official or legal identity. In essence, the ability for the data controller to request additional information to assess one’s identity cannot lead to excessive demands and to the collection of personal data which are not relevant or necessary to strengthen the link between the individual and the personal data requested. In many cases, such authentication procedures are already in place. For example, usernames and passwords are often used to allow individuals to access their data in their email accounts, social networking accounts, and accounts used for various other services, some of which individuals chose to use without revealing their full name and identity. If the size of data requested by the data subject makes transmission via the internet problematic, rather than potentially allowing for an extended time period of a maximum of three months to comply with the request26, the data controller may also need to consider alternative means of providing the data such as using streaming or saving to a CD, DVD or other physical media or allowing for the personal data to be transmitted directly to another data controller (as per Article 20(2) of the GDPR where technically feasible). - What is the time limit imposed to answer a portability request? Article 12(3) requires that the data controller provides “information on action taken” to the data subject “without undue delay” and in any event “within one month of receipt of the request”. This one month period can be extended to a maximum of three months for complex cases, provided that the data subject has been informed about the reasons for such delay within one month of the original request. Data controllers operating information society services are likely to be better equipped to be able to comply with requests within a very short time period. To meet user expectations, it is a good practice to define the timeframe in which a data portability request can typically be answered and communicate this to data subjects. Data controllers who refuse to answer a portability request shall, pursuant to Article 12(4), inform the data subject “the reasons for not taking action and on the possibility of lodging a 25 For example, when the data processing is linked to a user account, providing the relevant login and password might be sufficient to identify the data subject. 26 Article 12(3): “The controller shall provide information on action taken on a request”. 15 complaint with a supervisory authority and seeking a judicial remedy”, no later than one month after receiving the request. Data controllers must respect the obligation to respond within the given terms, even if it concerns a refusal. In other words, the data controller cannot remain silent when it is asked to answer a data portability request. - In which cases can a data portability request be rejected or a fee charged? Article 12 prohibits the data controller from charging a fee for the provision of the personal data, unless the data controller can demonstrate that the requests are manifestly unfounded or excessive, “in particular because of their repetitive"

[content] Revised Draft Decision — A Revised Draft Decision is a formal, updated version of an initial draft decision, presented as a distinct legal instrument. The LSA (Legislation and Standards Authority) is obligated to submit a Revised Draft Decision if it intends to incorporate a relevant and reasoned objection, or if it has modified its initial decision based on informal exchanges or other considerations. This document is designed to reflect revisions made after considering objections and feedback, aiming to find consensus on previously disputed issues. This revised version is subject to a shorter assessment period compared to the initial draft. If no further objections are raised against it, the Revised Draft Decision can become legally binding. The LSA utilizes this instrument to address objections or revised reasoned objections, ultimately working towards achieving a consensus.
A Revised Draft Decision is an updated version of a draft decision, submitted by the Lead Supervisory Authority if it intends to follow an objection, for further opinion.

Under GDPR, 72-Hour Notification Deadline The controller is generally required to notify within 72 hours, but delays are permissible with reasons. Controller.

Under GDPR, Controller The controller wishes to market products and services through direct marketing.<SEP>Direct marketing purposes may be regarded as a legitimate interest of the controller. Direct Marketing.

Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Supervisory Authority is established primarily by data protection regulations, such as the GDPR, and focuses on compliance, breach management, and accountability. A central obligation of the Controller is to notify the Supervisory Authority of personal data breaches, typically within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach, especially if it poses a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, as per Article 33(1) and Article 27(5) GDPR. The Controller is responsible for determining if a breach is notifiable and must ensure the relevant Supervisory Authority is informed, potentially proactively notifying them of infringements or seeking advice. They must also inform the Supervisory Authority about data transfers, documenting assessments and safeguards. Controllers without an EU establishment are required to engage with local supervisory authorities in every Member State where they operate. Furthermore, the Controller must consult the Supervisory Authority if a high risk identified in a Data Protection Impact Assessment cannot be mitigated by reasonable means before processing. Controllers are also obligated to cooperate with and make records available to the Supervisory Authority upon request, demonstrating accountability and compliance. The Supervisory Authority plays a significant role in overseeing the Controller's data protection practices. It can advise Controllers on how to inform individuals about breaches and may even order them to do so, particularly for high-risk breaches. The Supervisory Authority verifies the Controller's compliance, handles complaints, and seeks amicable settlements regarding possible infringements. It possesses powers to require the Controller to provide information, carry out investigations, notify infringements, and obtain access to data and premises. The Supervisory Authority can issue warnings and reprimands, order compliance, and impose sanctions, including administrative fines under Article 83 GDPR, especially in cases of unjustified breaches. The level of the Controller's cooperation is considered by the Supervisory Authority when assessing mitigation efforts. The Supervisory Authority also promotes awareness among Controllers regarding their obligations under pertinent regulations and informs Controllers when a received complaint is dismissed or rejected. Supervisory Authority.
Under GDPR, Controller A plaintiff has the choice to bring an action against a Controller before courts where the Controller has an establishment or the Data Subject resides. National Court.
Under GDPR, Controller Codes of conduct recommend out-of-court proceedings for resolving disputes between controllers and data subjects. Out-Of-Court Proceedings.

Under GDPR, Controller The controller should differentiate between access privileges of authorized personnel and limit access to data for employees.<SEP>Employees are generally not considered controllers but act under the authority of the controller.<SEP>An employee under the direct authority of the controller can process personal data. Employee.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation between a Controller and a Data Protection Officer (DPO) is characterized by advisory support and assigned responsibility for data protection compliance, particularly under regulations such as the GDPR. The Controller is responsible for designating a DPO to help ensure adherence to these regulations. The DPO's role encompasses providing advice and information to the Controller on various data protection matters, including breach management, data protection methodologies, and audits. This includes actively participating in Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), which the Controller undertakes with the DPO's guidance. Controllers are mandated to seek the DPO's advice when conducting a DPIA, and they must ensure the DPO's timely involvement in all data protection issues, providing necessary resources and access to facilitate their tasks. Guidelines may be developed by the Controller to specify when the DPO must be consulted. While the DPO offers crucial guidance and assists in monitoring internal compliance with regulations, the ultimate responsibility for data protection compliance remains with the Controller. The DPO may be an employee of the Controller or an external party, but they must perform their duties independently. The Controller is obligated to record the name and contact details of the DPO, and these details must be included in the record of processing activities. Furthermore, in the event of a data breach, the Controller must communicate the DPO's name and contact details as a contact point for breach information as part of the notification process. Data Protection Officer.
Under GDPR, Complainant The complainant makes a claim against the controller, alleging an infringement.<SEP>The controller and complainant interact regarding the cross-border processing. Controller.

Under GDPR, Controller A controller determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.<SEP>The controller decides on the purposes and means of processing personal data.<SEP>A controller is involved in the same processing concerning data.<SEP>Any Controller involved in Processing shall be liable for damage caused by Processing which infringes this Regulation. Processing.

Under GDPR, Controller The processing of personal data to fulfill a legal obligation finds its legal basis in Article 6(1)(c) GDPR.<SEP>The controller is subject to legal obligations regarding personal data processing. Legal Obligation.
Under GDPR, Draft Decision The GDPR does not define the concept of the draft decision.<SEP>The GDPR states that a draft decision is to be submitted to CSAs for their opinion. GDPR.
Under GDPR, End User End users processing ported data for non-personal activities are bound by the GDPR.<SEP>End users' consent for data processing is required under GDPR. GDPR.
Under GDPR, End User Account Settings Gatekeepers prompt end users and record their preferences via signed-in end users’ account settings. Gatekeeper.
Under GDPR, Government Infringement Reports are transmitted to the Government. Infringement Reports.
Under GDPR, Controller or Processor The supervisory authority notifies its final decision to the controller or the processor. Supervisory Authority.

Under GDPR, Legal Person A legal person cannot challenge the validity of an EDPB binding decision in national courts if they failed to bring an action for annulment before the CJEU within the prescribed period.<SEP>A National Court may not refer a question on the validity of a Board decision at the request of a Legal Person if they had the opportunity to bring an action for annulment and did not. National Court.
Under GDPR, Judicial Authorities The Supervisory Authority can bring infringements to the attention of judicial authorities and commence legal proceedings. Supervisory Authority.
Under GDPR, Data Transfers Data transfers can be necessary in relation to a legal claim, including judicial, administrative, or out-of-court procedures. Legal Claim.
Under GDPR, Controller Controllers should verify the identity of a data subject requests access, particularly in context of online services. Online Services.
Under GDPR, Data Subject Personal data, though restricted, may be required by the data subject for legal claims. Legal Claims.

Under GDPR, Adequate Level of Protection The examination procedure should be used by the Commission for the adoption of implementing acts on the adequate level of protection afforded by a third country or international organisation.<SEP>The Commission decides whether an adequate level of protection is ensured. Commission.
Under GDPR, Commission's Initiative The EDPB replied to the Commission's Initiative for a voluntary business pledge. EDPB.

Under GDPR, GDPR The Supervisory Authority determines its approach to certification to pursue the intent of GDPR, considering its tasks and powers under GDPR articles, and monitors and enforces the application of the regulation.<SEP>The supervisory authority's accreditation function is a task pursuant to GDPR Articles 57(1)(q) and 58(3)(e).<SEP>The GDPR empowers the Supervisory Authority to perform accreditation and certification functions.<SEP>Supervisory Authorities are tasked with enforcing the GDPR.<SEP>The supervisory authority oversees the application of the GDPR and receives DPIA reports under specific conditions. Supervisory Authority.
Under GDPR, Controller The controller may delay communicating a breach to data subjects based on the advice of law-enforcement authorities. Law-Enforcement Authorities.

Under GDPR, Controller The final decision of the competent supervisory authority will be addressed to the controller.<SEP>The controller has duties to ensure processing activities comply with the final decision, as per Article 60(10) GDPR.<SEP>The Controller shall take necessary measures to ensure compliance with the Final Decision. Final Decision.
Under GDPR, Controller The Controller ascertains the compatibility of Further Processing with the initial collection purpose. Further Processing.

Under GDPR, Controller A controller makes decisions on the purposes and means of processing activities.<SEP>The controller should maintain records of processing activities under its responsibility. Processing Activities.
Under GDPR, Delivery Service Identification details may be cross-used by a delivery service without consent, under Article 5(2), point (c) DMA. Personal Data.

Under GDPR, Data Protection Officer GDPR requires the designation of a data protection officer if processing involves regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects.<SEP>The GDPR specifies mandatory tasks for the Data Protection Officer.<SEP>The GDPR provides the legal framework in which Data Protection Officers operate and facilitates compliance.<SEP>The Data Protection Officer has duties defined by the GDPR, including monitoring compliance.<SEP>The DPO's role, resources, and independence are defined by the GDPR.<SEP>The Data Protection Officer's role is defined by the GDPR.<SEP>The DPO functions and requirements are governed by the GDPR. GDPR.
Under GDPR, Business User Business users authorizing third parties to process personal data must ensure compliance with GDPR, including contract requirements under Article 28 GDPR. GDPR.

[concept] Processing — Processing, in the context of data management and privacy, encompasses any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or sets of personal data. These operations can be conducted through automated means or otherwise. This broad definition includes, but is not limited to, collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure, or destruction. The concept of processing extends to any act of handling or dealing with data, directly or indirectly, that has the potential to affect the interests and fundamental rights of data subjects. For operations involving personal data, it is crucial to determine specific purposes and means, often requiring consent from the data subject. A fundamental principle dictates that processing should be carried out in a fair and transparent manner. Processing activities can be performed by entities such as a controller or processor. Infringements related to operations involving personal data can lead to liability, damage, and potential legal proceedings.

[organization] Gatekeepers — Gatekeepers are undertakings, primarily digital platforms, designated by the European Commission. These entities provide core platform services, acting as essential gateways between business users and end users, and possess significant data-driven advantages. They may also be entities offering number-independent interpersonal communications services. Gatekeepers are explicitly addressed by the Digital Markets Act (DMA) and its Guidelines, with harmonized rules applying to them to ensure contestable and fair markets. They may fall under the notion of large online platforms and function as either controllers or processors of personal data, specifically identified as controllers under the GDPR in certain scenarios. Gatekeepers face extensive obligations concerning data processing and user consent. They must enable end users to freely choose to opt-in to data processing and sign-in practices covered by Article 5(2) DMA. This requires providing a user-friendly solution for users to provide, modify, or withdraw consent, including offering granular choices regarding the combination or cross-use of personal data. When seeking consent, Gatekeepers must specify the intended purpose of personal data processing. They are also obliged to adopt technical and organizational measures to comply with the GDPR and facilitate compliance for DMA beneficiaries, while ensuring valid and user-friendly consent mechanisms that respect data protection principles. Additionally, Gatekeepers are required to offer interoperability and comply with data minimization principles. They must enable data portability under Article 6(9) DMA, maintaining an internal list of porting data categories. Data sharing obligations under Article 6(11) DMA also apply, including the requirement to ensure data anonymization. Gatekeepers must submit independently audited descriptions of their consumer profiling techniques to the European Commission within six months of their designation under DMA Article 15. While incentivized to innovate, they must not undermine other DMA obligations and have specific responsibilities regarding third-party apps and app stores.

[person] Data Subject — A Data Subject is defined as an identified or identifiable natural person to whom personal data relates and whose personal data undergoes processing, encompassing operations such as collection, holding, storing, or other manipulations, including biometric and location data. This individual can be identified, directly or indirectly, by reference to an identifier or specific factors of their identity. End users are often considered Data Subjects, and their vital interests may necessitate data processing. Even if a Data Subject's data has been anonymized such that they are no longer identifiable, they are still considered a Data Subject. Their behavior or identity may be monitored, and any personal data relating to them requires either consent or another legitimate basis for lawful processing. Data processing concerning Data Subjects is subject to regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly if goods or services are offered to them within the European Union. Under Article 6 of the GDPR, explicit consent is often required for processing, including profiling and automated decision-making. This consent must be demonstrably obtained through deliberate, informed action. Data Subjects possess fundamental rights to safeguard their human dignity and legitimate interests, including rights to access, rectification, erasure, objection to processing, and data portability. They also have the right to be informed about and challenge automated decision-making and, in some contexts, request delisting from search engines. They can monitor data processing, should be offered format choices for reusing their data, and can transmit their personal data from one controller to another, taking responsibility for securing it in their own system. Data controllers are obligated to provide Data Subjects with specific information, including the identity of their representative, and to communicate efficiently. Their views should be sought during a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) where appropriate. When biometric data is processed, an alternative solution must be offered, and Data Subjects should be consulted during the drafting of codes of conduct when feasible. A Data Subject is also an individual whose personal data may be affected by a data breach, putting their rights and freedoms at risk. In such an event, the controller must inform them, especially if there is a likely high risk of adverse effects or potential damage; communication of the breach is obligatory if their personal data has been compromised and depending on the severity of the consequences. Their vital interests, reasonable expectations (influenced by factors like age, public figure status, and professional position), and personal data require consistent protection, necessitating that their rights and freedoms be safeguarded. They may contact the Data Protection Officer, lodge complaints with supervisory authorities, and seek judicial remedy. A Data Subject has the right to compensation for material or non-material damage suffered due to an infringement of the regulation. Their identity may be scrutinized by a controller if doubts arise.

[person] Children — Children are consistently identified as a vulnerable category of data subjects and individuals who require specific and enhanced protection regarding their personal data, especially under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This heightened protection is due to their susceptibility to influence from targeted campaigns, their potential lack of awareness regarding risks and their rights concerning personal data processing, and their possible inability to knowingly and thoughtfully oppose or consent to such processing. The GDPR mandates particular consideration for Children's capacity to provide informed consent for data processing. Their personal data receives heightened protection, particularly in relation to information society services, with the age for valid consent varying between 13 and 16 years under Article 8 of the GDPR. Compliance with national laws concerning contractual capacity is also essential when engaging with Children. They also require comprehensible information about personal data processing due to their vulnerability. As individuals who may be disproportionately affected by legislative measures, Children merit specific protection, particularly concerning profiling for marketing and automated decision-making with significant effects. Article 12.1 of the GDPR specifies that clear and plain language is especially important when providing information to Children, an audience segment that benefits from child-centred language and transparency. Recital 38 GDPR additionally highlights the particular attention required for Children regarding data processing. These principles are further reinforced through codes of conduct that address their personal data protection and consent mechanisms. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child recognizes individuals under the age of 18 years as Children.
