Under GDPR, Controller In the context of the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), a Controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This role is fundamental to the GDPR framework, outlining significant obligations and responsibilities for any party involved in deciding how personal data is processed. Controllers are accountable for ensuring compliance with all GDPR provisions, particularly as detailed in Article 3. The Controller has legal obligations to ensure compliance with the GDPR and is responsible and liable under its provisions, with these obligations often referred to as "GDPR controller obligations." The responsibilities of a Controller include applying GDPR rules to data processing, adhering to foundational principles like lawfulness and fairness (Article 5(1)), and fulfilling transparency obligations. Specific duties extend to maintaining records of processing activities (Article 30), ensuring the security of processing (Article 32), conducting data protection impact assessments (Article 35), and engaging in prior consultation (Article 36) for managing risks. Controllers must also comply with regulations regarding data storage periods, implement appropriate technical and organizational measures, and adhere to specific legal bases, such as legitimate interest, for processing data. The GDPR places a significant burden of proof on the Controller, requiring them to demonstrate "compelling legitimate grounds for the processing" when applicable. They must ensure consent mechanisms meet GDPR standards and act upon withdrawal requests. Compliance with obligations related to accountability, engaging processors, and maintaining data security is paramount. Regarding data breaches, the GDPR mandates that controllers implement appropriate security measures, ensure compliance with processing principles, and adhere to relevant provisions for breach notification, as specified in Article 60(10). Unless a breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, the Controller is required to notify the competent supervisory authority and, in certain cases, the affected individuals. The GDPR further defines notification and communication requirements for Controllers regarding breaches, and they must retain documentation in accordance with Article 33(5) of the GDPR. The GDPR also places the burden of proof regarding objections on the Controller. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to take enforcement action, including imposing fines, for any infringement of GDPR provisions resulting from a Controller's actions. The ability for data controllers to obtain GDPR certifications further underscores their pivotal role and accountability within the regulatory framework, though some Controllers currently face broad and systemic issues in compliance with the GDPR. The GDPR recognizes that Controllers may not have all information immediately and allows for phased notification.<SEP>Controllers must comply with the provisions of the GDPR, including those related to information provision.<SEP>The controller must comply with GDPR requirements, including those related to transparency and notification.<SEP>A controller's responsibilities are defined under the GDPR. Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data)" signifies that the Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This involves significant authority and responsibility over the entire lifecycle of personal data, encompassing decisions related to its processing, protection, management, and transference. The Controller is explicitly responsible for establishing the retention period for documentation containing personal data and makes choices regarding its deletion or return. A core obligation of the Controller is to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and to uphold data subject rights, including guaranteeing data accuracy and facilitating the exercise of those rights. The Controller is always required to have an appropriate lawful ground for the processing of personal data, and while explicit consent may be obtained, it is not always the sole lawful basis, especially when processing is essential for a contract. The Controller is also responsible for the overall protection and security of personal data, which includes managing and responding to any data breaches, and applying appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard it. This responsibility extends to implementing measures to minimize the processing of personal data. In addition to determining purposes and means, the Controller collects, processes, and stores personal data. The Controller may also determine its identification requirements and, in the EU, has the capability to make personal data accessible to a third-country authority, and may specifically process data indicating criminal acts when considered within their legitimate interest. Persons under the direct authority of the Controller are authorized to process personal data. The Controller is ultimately responsible and liable for any processing of personal data, including its transferring. Personal Data.

ragPromptContext: [data] End User Information — This refers to data about users, including observed behavior like likes, viewed content, or session time, which gatekeepers might cross-use.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.
[organization] Requested Supervisory Authority — A requested supervisory authority is the supervisory authority that receives a request for assistance from another supervisory authority.

[data] Authorisation Proof — Proof of authorisation is documentation that gatekeepers should keep to demonstrate that third parties have obtained consent from end users, including the duration of such authorisation.

[method] Management, Planning, and Organisation of Work — Management, Planning, and Organisation of Work are purposes in the employment context for which specific rules for processing employees' personal data may be provided.

[person] Employee — An Employee is defined as an individual who is employed by an organization or person, belonging to the legal entity of a data controller or processor. These individuals are typically authorized to process personal data, acting under the authority of the controller. Their access to personal data should be restricted based on their specific duties and role within the company. Employees may interact with personal data in various ways, such as manually deleting personal data after its retention period in accordance with internal procedures. They can also be subjects whose personal data, such as their name, is processed by services (e.g., a taxi service in an illustrative example). Employee actions can also lead to incidents, such as when an employee of a controller makes a mistake resulting in a data breach, or when an employee of a service provider has their electronic notebook stolen, as depicted in CASE No. 11. While employees generally operate under established authority, there can be exceptional cases where they unlawfully exceed this authority. Furthermore, employees may face pressure concerning consent for data processing.

Example 5: Controller in the EU sends data to a processor in a third country Company X established in Austria, acting as controller, provides personal data of its employees or customers to Company Z in a third country, which processes these data as processor on behalf of Company X. In this case, data are provided from a controller, which as regards the processing in question, is subject to the GDPR, to a processor in a third country. Hence, the provision of data will be considered as a transfer of personal data to a third country and therefore Chapter V of the GDPR applies. It is also important to note that Article 44 of the GDPR clearly envisages that a transfer may not only be carried out by a controller but also by a processor. Therefore, there will be a transfer situation where a processor (either under Article 3(1) or under Article 3(2) for a given processing, as explained above) sends data to another processor or even to a controller in a third country as instructed by its controller.18 In these cases, the processor acts as a data exporter on behalf of the controller and has to ensure that the provisions of Chapter V are complied with for the transfer at stake according to the instructions of the controller, including that an appropriate transfer tool is used. Considering that the transfer is a processing activity carried out on behalf of the controller, the controller is also responsible and could be liable under Chapter V, and also has to ensure that the processor provides for sufficient guarantees under Article 28. Since XYZ is a controller in a third country, the disclosure of data from ABC to XYZ is regarded as a transfer of personal data and therefore Chapter V applies. (68) To further strengthen the control over his or her own data, where the processing of personal data is carried out by automated means, the data subject should also be allowed to receive personal data concerning him or her which he or she has provided to a controller in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable and interoperable format, and to transmit it to another controller. Data controllers should be encouraged to develop interoperable formats that enable data portability. That right should apply where the data subject provided the personal data on the basis of his or her consent or the processing is necessary for the performance of a contract. It should not apply where processing is based on a legal ground other than consent or contract. By its very nature, that right should not be exercised against controllers processing personal data in the exercise of their public duties. It should therefore not apply where the processing of the personal data is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject or for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of an official authority vested in the controller. This communication inherently processes personal data, as the customer must identify themselves (e.g., by providing a name, order number, or contact details) to discuss a missing delivery. The call itself is a form of communication using personal contact data.

The activity 'Logistikzentrum anrufen' involves the customer calling the logistics center. This is another direct communication where the customer likely provides personal identifiers (name, order details) to inquire about their delivery status, processing personal data through the call.

The activity 'Anruf beenden' (first occurrence) concludes a phone call. While ending a call is a simple action, it is part of the processing chain of a communication that involved personal data. The act of terminating the call is an operation performed in the context of processing that personal communication.

The activity 'Anruf beenden' (second occurrence) concludes another phone call. Similar to the first, it is an operation performed as part of processing a personal communication (the callback from the company), which involved the customer's personal data.

The activity 'Beschwerde anhören' (listening to a complaint) involves processing a complaint from a customer. A complaint inherently contains personal data, as it relates to a specific individual (the complainant) and their specific issue (a missing delivery). The activity is associated with a 'Beschwerde' (complaint) data object, which is defined in the knowledge base as a formal grievance lodged by a data subject, often concerning the processing of their personal data.

The activity 'Anruf weiterleiten' (forwarding a call) involves transferring a communication concerning a customer complaint. Forwarding the call transmits the context of the complaint, which includes the customer's personal data (e.g., identity, issue details) to another department (Steuer Abteilung).

The activity 'Kunden anrufen' (calling the customer) involves the company initiating contact with a specific customer. This requires using the customer's personal contact data (phone number) and likely involves discussing their personal order/delivery details, constituting processing of personal data.

The activity 'Sendung veranlasssen' (arranging shipment) involves taking action on a specific customer's delivery. To arrange a shipment, personal data such as the customer's name, address, and order details must be processed.

The activity 'Beschwerde anhören' (listening to a complaint) in the Steuer Abteilung involves processing the forwarded customer complaint. As with the first complaint listening activity, this processes personal data contained within the complaint. It is also associated with a 'Beschwerde' data object.

The activity 'Weiterleitung an Logistik empfehlen' (recommending forwarding to logistics) involves making a recommendation based on the customer's complaint. This recommendation is based on the processed personal data from the complaint and facilitates its further transmission to another department.

The activity 'Beschwerde aufnehmen' (recording a complaint) in the logistics department involves formally documenting the customer's complaint. Recording a complaint creates a record containing the customer's personal data and the details of their issue. It is associated with a 'Beschwerde' data object.

The activity 'Problemermittlung' (problem investigation) in logistics involves investigating the cause of the customer's delivery issue. This investigation operates on the personal data context of a specific customer's complaint and order.

The activity 'Problem weiterleitung' (problem forwarding) involves passing the investigated problem (which is tied to a specific customer's case) to another role (Inventarmanager). This transmits information related to the customer's personal data.

The activity 'Problemermittlung' (problem investigation) by the Inventarmanager involves further investigation into the inventory-related aspect of the customer's delivery problem. This continues to process data in the context of the specific customer's case.

The activity 'Zwischenstand weiterleiten' (forwarding interim status) involves sending an update on the investigation back to the customer. This transmits information derived from the customer's personal case, likely including identifiers or order references.

The activity 'Anruf beenden' (ending a call) by the Inventarmanager concludes the internal communication chain related to the customer's case. It is an operation performed in the context of processing that personal data.

The activity 'Formular ausfüllen' (filling out a form) involves creating or completing a form. The form is likely related to the customer's complaint or delivery issue (e.g., a loss/damage report, internal processing form). Creating such a record involves inputting or structuring personal data about the customer and their case. It is associated with a 'Formular' data object.

The activity 'Formular auswerten' (evaluating the form) involves analyzing the completed form. This analysis processes the personal data contained within the form to reach a conclusion or decision regarding the customer's case.

The activity 'Auswertung weiterleiten' (forwarding the evaluation) involves transmitting the results of the form evaluation. This disseminates information derived from the customer's personal data to initiate the next step (the customer callback).

An important aspect of BCRs is that they require approval from a supervisory authority, and in specific contexts, they may also require Board approval as defined in Article 47. Additionally, BCRs are subject to specific formats and procedures for electronic information exchange between data controllers, processors, and supervisory authorities. They are also known to include requirements such as the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing, as referenced in Articles 47(1) and 47(2)(e) of relevant regulations. These grievances are typically lodged with a supervisory authority, making it a Concerned Supervisory Authority (CSA) particularly involved in the case. A complaint serves as the basis for investigations, specifically regarding data subjects' rights and alleged GDPR infringements, and defines the scope of data processing under scrutiny for potential violations. Upon receiving a complaint, the supervisory authority can take various actions, including dismissing, rejecting, or acting upon it. The granting of a complaint can be full or partial, and any decision made regarding it by supervisory authorities is considered an envisaged action. This decision is based on a determination by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) and must be adopted by the Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) and/or the Concerned Supervisory Authority (CSA) within one month of being notified of the EDPB's decision. Medical records contain sensitive health data about identifiable patients, which qualifies as personal data under GDPR.

The activity 'Decide on further procedure of treatment' processes personal data because it involves making a medical decision based on the patient's health records (Kardex). This decision-making uses sensitive health data, which is personal data.

The activity 'Perform consultative evaluation' processes personal data because it involves conducting a medical evaluation of a patient. This evaluation generates or uses health data (diagnoses, observations) related to an identifiable individual, which is personal data.

[organization] Commission — The Commission, most often referring to the European Commission, is a central body within the European Union with extensive responsibilities and powers, particularly in relation to data protection, digital markets, and legal frameworks. It serves as a regulatory authority with the sole power to implement and enforce the Digital Markets Act (DMA). The Commission issues guidelines, such as those in accordance with Article 47 DMA, and is solely responsible for interpreting the DMA provisions covered by these guidelines. It can impose sanctions, conduct proceedings and investigations under the DMA, and is involved in the coherent enforcement of both the DMA and GDPR, cooperating with national authorities and possessing investigatory powers. Under the GDPR, the Commission plays a crucial role in developing a code of icons for standardized information and is empowered to adopt delegated acts to determine the information for these icons. It can also adopt Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) to regulate data processing between controllers and processors and lay down such clauses more broadly. A key function includes making adequacy decisions regarding the level of data protection in third countries or international organizations for international data transfers. The Commission monitors these decisions, consults with the European Data Protection Board ("the Board" or EDPB), evaluates their functioning, and reports findings. It can also adopt delegated acts specifying criteria and requirements for certification mechanisms and standardized icons, and implementing acts for specifying technical standards for data protection certification and safeguards. It cooperates with supervisory authorities in third countries to develop international cooperation mechanisms regarding personal data protection, specifying formats and procedures for information exchange relating to Binding Corporate Rules and mutual assistance. Member States must notify the Commission of adopted laws and amendments related to data protection provisions, and the Commission receives Supervisory Authority activity reports. The Commission designates gatekeepers regarding Core Platform Services (CPSs) and recognizes adequacy for data transfers. It has legal powers to regulate data sharing under Article 6(11) DMA via an implementing act pursuant to Article 8(2) DMA. It may specify the ineligibility of potential third-party recipients and consult with other bodies to ensure compliance with DMA obligations. The Commission assesses whether a third country provides an adequate level of protection for personal data and sometimes considers the display of advertisements as part of online advertising CPS and other CPS. It receives audited descriptions of profiling techniques from gatekeepers and transmits them to the EDPB. The Commission participates in the Board's activities without voting rights, can designate a representative, and can request matters to be handled within the consistency mechanism, including requesting opinions from the Board. It is informed of Board decisions and receives communications from the Board Chair. Ultimately, the Commission is granted delegated power to adopt and notify delegated acts, prepare and submit reports, examine the application and functioning of the Regulation, request information, and submit proposals for the overall effectiveness and implementation of data protection regulations, cooperating with the EDPB and supervisory authorities to assess processing operations and consider guidelines for gatekeepers regarding interoperability and geographical limitations.

[concept] Consent — Consent, as defined by Regulations 2016/679 (GDPR), particularly under Articles 4(11), 6(1)(a), and 7, is a fundamental legal basis for the processing of personal data. It signifies a freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of the data subject's or end user's wishes, demonstrated by a clear, affirmative action, agreeing to the processing of their personal data for specified purposes. This applies to various data handling scenarios, including direct information retrieval, targeted advertising, processing of location data, or the storing/accessing of information on their devices. It is also an alternative legal basis for direct marketing activities when legitimate interest is not applicable and a legal ground for processing sensitive data, such as health or biometric data, under Article 9(2)(a) GDPR. For consent to be valid, it must adhere to strict conditions: it must be given freely, without coercion, intimidation, deception, or negative consequences for withholding it. It must also be specific, informed, and granular, ensuring the data subject fully understands what data will be processed, for what purposes, and by whom. This comprehensiveness is crucial, and it grants data subjects control over their personal data processing. Consent is a reversible decision, easily withdrawable at any time. While essential for various data handling scenarios and mandated by regulations like the ePrivacy Directive and the Digital Markets Act (DMA) for certain operations, such as electronic communications or specific tracking techniques, obtaining valid consent can be particularly challenging in complex contexts, including connected vehicles. Consent also holds significance for data portability and international transfers of personal data, especially to third countries without an adequacy decision. Furthermore, it is a key condition for certain derogations under Article 49(1)(a), requiring explicit agreement for proposed transfers. It is a requirement for gatekeepers to enable data sharing but is generally not legally feasible for silent party data as per Article 6 of the GDPR. Despite its importance, obtaining valid consent does not diminish the controller's obligations under the GDPR. In broader contexts, the overarching obligation of endeavoring to reach consensus places concomitant obligations on both the LSA and other CSAs. Consent is a key requirement under DMA and GDPR, requiring an explicit, clear, and straightforward user experience, particularly for cross-use of personal data, and can be refused or withdrawn.

Therefore, the terms “data concerning health”, “processing for the purpose of scientific research” as well as “further processing” (also referred to as “primary and secondary usage of health data”) must be defined. 3.1 “Data concerning health” 7. According to Article 4 (15) GDPR, “data concerning health” means “personal data related to the physical or mental health of a natural person, including the provision of health care services, which reveal information about his or her health status”. As indicated by Recital 53, data concerning health deserves higher protection, as the use of such sensitive data may have significant adverse impacts for data subjects. In the light of this and the relevant jurisprudence of the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”),4 the term “data concerning health” must be given a wide interpretation. 8. Data concerning health can be derived from different sources, for example: 1. Information collected by a health care provider in a patient record (such as medical history and results of examinations and treatments). 2. Information that becomes health data by cross referencing with other data thus revealing the state of health or health risks (such as the assumption that a person has a higher risk of suffering heart attacks based on the high blood pressure measured over a certain period of time). 3. Information from a “self check” survey, where data subjects answer questions related to their health (such as stating symptoms). 4. Information that becomes health data because of its usage in a specific context (such as information regarding a recent trip to or presence in a region affected with COVID-19 processed by a medical professional to make a diagnosis). 3.2 “Processing for the purpose of scientific research” 9. Article 4 GDPR does not entail an explicit definition of “processing for the purpose of scientific research”. As indicated by Recital 159, “the term processing of personal data for scientific research purposes should be interpreted in a broad manner including for example technological development and demonstration, fundamental research, applied research and privately funded research. In addition, it should take into account the Union’s objective under Article 179 (1) TFEU of achieving a European Research Area. Scientific research purposes should also include studies conducted in the public interest in the area of public health.” 10. The former Article 29-Working-Party has already pointed out that the term may not be stretched beyond its common meaning though and understands that “scientific research” in this context means 4 See for example, regarding the Directive 95/46/EC, ECJ 6.11.2003, C-101/01 (Lindqvist) paragraph 50. Adopted 6 “a research project set up in accordance with relevant sector-related methodological and ethical standards, in conformity with good practice”.5 3.3 “Further processing” 11. Finally, when talking about “processing of health data for the purpose of scientific research”, there are two types of data usages: 1. Research on personal (health) data which consists in the use of data directly collected for the purpose of scientific studies (“primary use”). 2. Research on personal (health) data which consists of the further processing of data initially collected for another purpose (“secondary use”). 12. Example 1: For conducting a clinical trial on individuals suspected to be infected with SARS-CoV-2, health data are collected and questionnaires are used. This is a case of “primary use” of health data as defined above. 13. Example 2: A data subject has consulted a health care provider as a patient regarding symptoms of the SARS-CoV-2. If health data recorded by the health care provider is being used for scientific research purposes later on, this usage is classified as further processing of health data (secondary use) that has been collected for another initial purpose. 14. The distinction between scientific research based on primary or secondary usage of health data will become particularly important when talking about the legal basis for the processing, the information obligations and the purpose limitation principle pursuant to Article 5 (1) (b) GDPR as outlined below. 4 LEGAL BASIS FOR THE PROCESSING 15. All processing of personal data concerning health must comply with the principles relating to processing set out in Article 5 GDPR and with one of the legal grounds and the specific derogations listed respectively in Article 6 and Article 9 GDPR for the lawful processing of this special category of personal data.6 16. Legal bases and applicable derogations for processing health data for the purpose of scientific research are provided for respectively in Article 6 and Article 9. In the following section, the rules concerning consent and respective national legislation are addressed. It has to be noted that there is no ranking between the legal bases stipulated in the GDPR. 4.1 Consent 17. The consent of the data subject, collected pursuant to Article 6 (1) (a) and Article 9 (2) (a) GDPR, may provide a legal basis for the processing of data concerning health in the COVID-19 context. 18. However, it has to be noted that all the conditions for explicit consent, particularly those found in Article 4 (11), Article 6 (1) (a), Article 7 and Article 9 (2) (a) GDPR, must be fulfilled. [organization] Hospital — A Hospital is a healthcare institution responsible for collecting and managing significant quantities of sensitive patient data, often utilizing an electronic health record system. This organization has been noted for experiencing a personal data breach where staff members could view unauthorized patient health files due to issues with authorization monitoring, specifically concerning staff retaining access to patient files after transferring departments; an internal investigation was conducted to address this. The sensitive nature of the data processed means that data breaches at a Hospital are highly impactful, and the unavailability of critical medical data can pose a substantial risk to individuals' rights and freedoms. Furthermore, a Hospital can also be an organization involved in scientific research, as exemplified by "Project X," which necessitates the use of real patient dental records. The Hospital has also been identified as a victim of ransomware attacks (e.g., Case No. 03), where its information systems were compromised, leading to data encryption and subsequent delays in patient care. Consequently, a Hospital is an organization legally obliged to notify relevant authorities and affected individuals in cases of cyber-attacks impacting medical records.

[data] Medical Records — Medical records are highly sensitive personal data.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

This involves significant authority and responsibility over the entire lifecycle of personal data, encompassing decisions related to its processing, protection, management, and transference. The Controller is explicitly responsible for establishing the retention period for documentation containing personal data and makes choices regarding its deletion or return. A core obligation of the Controller is to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and to uphold data subject rights, including guaranteeing data accuracy and facilitating the exercise of those rights. Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Supervisory Authority is established primarily by data protection regulations, such as the GDPR, and focuses on compliance, breach management, and accountability. A central obligation of the Controller is to notify the Supervisory Authority of personal data breaches, typically within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach, especially if it poses a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, as per Article 33(1) and Article 27(5) GDPR. The Controller is responsible for determining if a breach is notifiable and must ensure the relevant Supervisory Authority is informed, potentially proactively notifying them of infringements or seeking advice. They must also inform the Supervisory Authority about data transfers, documenting assessments and safeguards. Controllers without an EU establishment are required to engage with local supervisory authorities in every Member State where they operate. Furthermore, the Controller must consult the Supervisory Authority if a high risk identified in a Data Protection Impact Assessment cannot be mitigated by reasonable means before processing. Controllers are also obligated to cooperate with and make records available to the Supervisory Authority upon request, demonstrating accountability and compliance. The Supervisory Authority plays a significant role in overseeing the Controller's data protection practices. It can advise Controllers on how to inform individuals about breaches and may even order them to do so, particularly for high-risk breaches. The Supervisory Authority verifies the Controller's compliance, handles complaints, and seeks amicable settlements regarding possible infringements. It possesses powers to require the Controller to provide information, carry out investigations, notify infringements, and obtain access to data and premises. Example 2 A public transportation company wishes to gather statistical information based on travellers’ routes. This is useful for the purposes of making proper choices on changes in public transport schedules and proper routings of the trains. The passengers have to pass their ticket through a reader every time they enter or exit a means of transport. Having carried out a risk assessment related to the rights and freedoms of passengers’ regarding the collection of passengers’ travel routes, the controller establishes that it is possible to identify the passengers in circumstances where they live or work in scarcely populated areas, based on single route identification thanks to the ticket identifier. Therefore, since it is not necessary for the purpose of optimizing the public transport schedules and routings of the trains, the controller does not store the ticket identifier. Once the trip is over, the controller only stores the individual travel routes so as to not be able to identify trips connected to a single ticket, but only retains information about separate travel routes. In cases where there can still be a risk of identifying a person solely by their public transportation travel route the controller implements statistical measures to reduce the risk, such as cutting the beginning and the end of the route. Example 3 A courier aims at assessing the effectiveness of its deliveries in terms of delivery times, workload scheduling and fuel consumption. In order to reach this goal, the courier has to process a number of personal data relating to both employees (drivers) and customers (addresses, items to be delivered, etc.). This processing operation entails risks of both monitoring employees, which requires specific legal safeguards, and tracking customers’ habits through the knowledge of the delivered items over time. These risks can be significantly reduced with appropriate pseudonymization of employees and customers. In particular if pseudonymization keys are frequently rotated and macro areas are considered instead of detailed addresses, an effective data minimisation is pursued, and the controller Adopted 23 can solely focus on the delivery process and on the purpose of resource optimization, without crossing the threshold of monitoring individuals’ (customers’ or employees’) behaviours. Example 4 A hospital is collecting data about its patients in a hospital information system (electronic health record). Hospital staff needs to access patient files to inform their decisions regarding care for and treatment of the patients, and for the documentation of all diagnostic, care and treatment actions taken. By default, access is granted to only those members of the medical staff who are assigned to the treatment of the respective patient in the speciality department she or he is assigned to. The group of people with access to a patient’s file is enlarged if other departments or diagnostic units are involved in the treatment. After the patient is discharged, and billing is completed, access is reduced to a small group of employees per speciality department who answer requests for medical information or a consultation made or asked for by other medical service providers upon authorization by the respective patient. 3.6 Accuracy 77. The requirements should be seen in relation to the risks and consequences of the concrete use of data. Inaccurate personal data could be a risk to the data subjects’ rights and freedoms, for example when leading to a faulty diagnosis or wrongful treatment of a health protocol, or an incorrect image of a person can lead to decisions being made on the wrong basis either manually, using automated decision-making, or through artificial intelligence. 79. Key design and default accuracy elements may include:  Data source – Sources of personal data should be reliable in terms of data accuracy.  Degree of accuracy – Each personal data element should be as accurate as necessary for the specified purposes.  Measurably accurate - Reduce the number of false positives/negatives, for example biases in automated decisions and artificial intelligence.  Verification – Depending on the nature of the data, in relation to how often it may change, the controller should verify the correctness of personal data with the data subject before and at different stages of the processing (e.g. to age requirements).  Erasure/rectification – The controller shall erase or rectify inaccurate data without delay. The controller shall in particular facilitate this where the data subjects are or were children and later want to remove such personal data.39  Error propagation avoidance – Controllers should mitigate the effect of an accumulated error in the processing chain. 38 Art. 5(1)(d) GDPR. 39 Cf. Recital 65. Adopted 24  Access – Data subjects should be given information about and effective access to personal data in accordance with the GDPR articles 12 to 15 in order to control accuracy and rectify as needed.  Continued accuracy – Personal data should be accurate at all stages of the processing, tests of accuracy should be carried out at critical steps.  Up to date – Personal data shall be updated if necessary for the purpose.  Data design - Use of technological and organisational design features to decrease inaccuracy, for example present concise predetermined choices instead of free text fields. Thus, for example, it must be legally possible to transfer data (including certain personal data) if the data subject, whilst outside the EU, is unconscious and in need of urgent medical care, and only a exporter (e.g. his usual doctor), established in an EU Member State, is able to supply these data. [data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[method] Data Protection Training — Appropriate training provided to personnel who have permanent or regular access to personal data to ensure their understanding and adherence to data protection principles.

[person] Business Users — Business Users are defined as natural or legal persons who operate in a commercial or professional capacity and utilize core platform services (CPSs). These users are entities that engage with services provided by gatekeepers and are central to the implementation of data protection and privacy features, adhering to principles of data protection by design and by default, as outlined in relevant guidelines. A key aspect of Business Users' rights is their entitlement to data access under Article 6(10) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA). They are considered beneficiaries of this right, enabling them to request and utilize data generated through CPSs. In exercising this right, Business Users may need to obtain explicit consent from end-users. The DMA aims to promote fair market conditions that benefit these users, fostering an environment where they are incentivized to innovate.

The principle of integrity and confidentiality includes protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures. Recital 78 states that one of the DPbDD measures could consist of enabling the controller to “create and improve security features”. Key design and default integrity and confidentiality elements may include:  Information security management system (ISMS) – Have an operative means of managing policies and procedures for information security.  Risk analysis – Assess the risks against the security of personal data by considering the impact on individuals’ rights and counter identified risks. For use in risk assessment; develop and maintain a comprehensive, systematic and realistic “threat modelling” and an attack surface analysis of the designed software to reduce attack vectors and opportunities to exploit weak points and vulnerabilities.  Security by design – Consider security requirements as early as possible in the system design and development and continuously integrate and perform relevant tests.  Maintenance – Regular review and test software, hardware, systems and services, etc. to uncover vulnerabilities of the systems supporting the processing.  Access control management – Only the authorized personnel who need to should have access to the personal data necessary for their processing tasks, and the controller should differentiate between access privileges of authorized personnel. o Access limitation (agents) – Shape the data processing in a way that a minimal number of people need access to personal data to perform their duties, and limit access accordingly. o Access limitation (content) – In the context of each processing operation, limit access to only those attributes per data set that are needed to perform that operation. Adopted 27 Moreover, limit access to data pertaining to those data subjects who are in the remit of the respective employee. o Access segregation – Shape the data processing in a way that no individual needs comprehensive access to all data collected about a data subject, much less all personal data of a particular category of data subjects.  Secure transfers – Transfers shall be secured against unauthorized and accidental access and changes.  Secure storage – Data storage shall be secure from unauthorized access and changes. There should be procedures to assess the risk of centralized or decentralized storage, and what categories of personal data this applies to. Some data may need additional security measures than others or isolation from others.  Pseudonymization – Personal data and back-ups/logs should be pseudonymized as a security measure to minimise risks of potential data breaches, for example using hashing or encryption.  Backups/logs – Keep back-ups and logs to the extent necessary for information security, use audit trails and event monitoring as a routine security control. These shall be protected from unauthorised and accidental access and change and reviewed regularly and incidents should be handled promptly.  Disaster recovery/ business continuity – Address information system disaster recovery and business continuity requirements to restore the availability of personal data following up major incidents.  Protection according to risk – All categories of personal data should be protected with measures adequate with respect to the risk of a security breach. Data presenting special risks should, when possible, be kept separated from the rest of the personal data.  Security incident response management – Have in place routines, procedures and resources to detect, contain, handle, report and learn from data breaches.  Incident management – Controller should have processes in place to handle breaches and incidents, in order to make the processing system more robust. [organization] International Organisation — An International Organisation is defined as an entity established under international law, often by a treaty or another instrument governed by international law, and possessing its own international legal personality. These organizations typically have international membership, scope, or presence, with members from multiple countries. They can be bodies set up by an agreement between two or more nations, or organizations and their subordinate bodies governed by public international law, operating across national borders. International Organisations are frequently involved in the processing and transfer of personal data, functioning as recipients or "importers" of such data. This involvement means they are subject to Chapter V of the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), requiring adherence to specific conditions and safeguards for these transfers, especially concerning EEA (European Economic Area) personal data. When receiving personal data, they are expected to provide assurances regarding individual data rights under their internal rules. These organizations participate in multilateral or regional systems, and their level of personal data protection is assessed and monitored by the Commission. The Commission also cooperates with International Organisations and supervisory authorities. The adequacy of personal data protection provided by an International Organisation is subject to assessment. In cases where data protection is deemed insufficient, a Supervisory Authority might suspend data flows to it. It is also noted that these organizations may have privileges and immunities that could impact external independent oversight. Although potentially located outside the EU, an International Organisation is an entity to which personal data may be transferred under specific conditions.

[organization] Gatekeeper — A Gatekeeper is an entity designated under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically pursuant to Article 3(4) or Article 3(9), indicating its provision of Core Platform Services (CPSs). Prominent examples of such organizations include Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta. These Gatekeepers control access to specific digital services and are subject to extensive legal obligations under the DMA, and in many cases, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Their role is central to the regulatory framework designed to ensure fair and contestable digital markets. Gatekeepers process the personal data of end users, often acting as controllers or processors, and are responsible for ensuring that consent obtained for data processing, particularly for online advertising and data combination, complies with both GDPR and DMA requirements. This includes the meticulous recording of consent refusals or withdrawals. They are obligated to enable continuous and real-time access to data, prevent data accumulation, and ensure robust data security. Their responsibilities extend to providing data upon request by business users or authorized third parties, free of charge, and establishing appropriate authentication and authorization procedures for such access. They must also implement security measures for personal data, comply with portability requests under DMA Article 6(9), and provide comprehensive information to data subjects. Furthermore, Gatekeepers are tasked with selecting and implementing anonymization methods for end-user data shared under Article 6(11) DMA and must implement measures to maintain service integrity and security. They also have duties concerning interoperability, including exchanging message content and personal data with other providers while ensuring security for their end users. This includes protecting metadata, verifying communication authenticity, and ensuring compliance with geographical limitations and data protection regulations for Number-Independent Interpersonal Communication Services (NIICS). Gatekeepers must design online interfaces that do not undermine user autonomy, provide reminders, and ensure fair access to datasets by altering data to mitigate identification risks and imposing contractual measures on third-party undertakings for data access and compliance monitoring. Their conduct is subject to examination for compliance with both the DMA and GDPR, and they may have a "main establishment" under the GDPR. They are also separate controllers under GDPR for their own data processing and have obligations under Article 6(4) and Article 8(1) of the DMA.

[method] Processing Operations — Processing Operations refer to any activities or a set of operations performed on data, particularly personal data, by institutions or data brokers. These operations encompass a vast array of actions, including the collection, storage, use, disclosure, further processing, the management of data subject rights, and the handling and manipulation of data. They can also involve linking data, forming different conducts, combining data, or cross-using data. Per Article 4(2) of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), these operations are defined as any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or on sets of personal data. These operations are composed of various components, such as data, systems, and processes, all of which should adhere to specific criteria. Activities often include the selection of targeting criteria and the display of advertisements to a specific target audience. Processing operations are a primary object of certification under the GDPR, potentially encompassing governance processes and leading to the creation of a product or service. Both data controllers and processors are obligated to demonstrate compliance when executing these operations. Actions performed on personal data should be limited to what is necessary, contributing to a defined processing purpose, and designed to process only the minimum amount of necessary data. Processing operations are actions carried out by a data controller using collected data, requiring specific information provisions and legal bases. They may also benefit from special regimes under GDPR. Examples include the collection, storage, use, or deletion of data. Some operations may involve the use of CCTV and are subject to the applicability of the household exemption. Records must be maintained for these data handling activities. Furthermore, processing operations that involve personal data may require a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) under GDPR if they pose a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. When a DPIA is required, these activities necessitate a systematic description, an assessment of necessity, proportionality, and risks, and the implementation of measures to address those risks.
Processing Operations refer to any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction.

Under GDPR, Controller The (Controller, Processor) relationship describes an arrangement, primarily defined by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), where a Processor handles personal data on behalf of a Controller. The Controller retains the primary and ultimate responsibility for ensuring overall compliance with data protection principles, including data protection by design and by default (DPbDD), and this accountability extends to any Processor and sub-processors involved. This relationship mandates that the Controller select Processors who offer sufficient guarantees regarding GDPR compliance. This relationship is formalized and governed by a legally binding contract or other legal act, often referred to as a processing agreement. This agreement details how GDPR requirements will be implemented, outlines specific obligations, and defines assistance duties. The Controller must provide documented instructions to the Processor on how to process personal data, and the Processor is obligated to comply. The Processor processes personal data only on these documented instructions. Even without a written agreement, the existence and definition of this relationship hold. The Processor has various duties, including assisting the Controller in fulfilling obligations related to data subject rights and Articles 32 to 36 of the GDPR, ensuring compliance with data protection obligations, and reporting to the Controller. This assistance includes deleting or returning personal data at the Controller's choice, providing compliance information, and cooperating with Controller-conducted audits. A critical obligation for the Processor is to notify the Controller "without undue delay" upon becoming aware of a personal data breach it is processing on behalf of the Controller, as mandated by Article 33(2) GDPR. Processors must also notify the Controller of any request from a third-country authority without undue delay and follow the Controller's instructions, unless prohibited by law. The Processor is liable to the Controller for fulfilling these obligations. The Controller can authorize the use of sub-processors, but the Processor must obtain prior written authorization from the Controller for engaging another processor. The Processor is liable to the Controller for the sub-processors' adherence to data protection obligations. In scenarios involving data transfers, such as a third-country company (Controller) engaging a non-EEA processor, the processor acts as a data exporter on behalf of the Controller. The Controller must provide a comprehensive list of all data recipients, including processors. The relationship demands good faith cooperation, involving contract negotiation and management of audit and instruction processes. Controllers also carry out Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) with the processors. In some cases, the lead supervisory authority of the Controller may also become the lead supervisory authority for the Processor. When an end user qualifies as a Controller, an authorized third party may act as a Processor. Processor.

Under GDPR, Controller The (Controller, Processor) relationship describes an arrangement, primarily defined by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), where a Processor handles personal data on behalf of a Controller. The Controller retains the primary and ultimate responsibility for ensuring overall compliance with data protection principles, including data protection by design and by default (DPbDD), and this accountability extends to any Processor and sub-processors involved. This relationship mandates that the Controller select Processors who offer sufficient guarantees regarding GDPR compliance. This relationship is formalized and governed by a legally binding contract or other legal act, often referred to as a processing agreement. This agreement details how GDPR requirements will be implemented, outlines specific obligations, and defines assistance duties. The Controller must provide documented instructions to the Processor on how to process personal data, and the Processor is obligated to comply. The Processor processes personal data only on these documented instructions. Even without a written agreement, the existence and definition of this relationship hold. The Processor has various duties, including assisting the Controller in fulfilling obligations related to data subject rights and Articles 32 to 36 of the GDPR, ensuring compliance with data protection obligations, and reporting to the Controller. This assistance includes deleting or returning personal data at the Controller's choice, providing compliance information, and cooperating with Controller-conducted audits. A critical obligation for the Processor is to notify the Controller "without undue delay" upon becoming aware of a personal data breach it is processing on behalf of the Controller, as mandated by Article 33(2) GDPR. Processors must also notify the Controller of any request from a third-country authority without undue delay and follow the Controller's instructions, unless prohibited by law. The Processor is liable to the Controller for fulfilling these obligations. The Controller can authorize the use of sub-processors, but the Processor must obtain prior written authorization from the Controller for engaging another processor. The Processor is liable to the Controller for the sub-processors' adherence to data protection obligations. In scenarios involving data transfers, such as a third-country company (Controller) engaging a non-EEA processor, the processor acts as a data exporter on behalf of the Controller. The Controller must provide a comprehensive list of all data recipients, including processors. The relationship demands good faith cooperation, involving contract negotiation and management of audit and instruction processes. Controllers also carry out Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) with the processors. In some cases, the lead supervisory authority of the Controller may also become the lead supervisory authority for the Processor. When an end user qualifies as a Controller, an authorized third party may act as a Processor. Processor.
