ragPromptContext: [person] End User — An "End User" refers to an individual customer or consumer who interacts with various services, specifically Core Platform Services (CPS), and can include any natural or legal person utilizing these services, even those traditionally considered business users, with the explicit exclusion of business users in certain contexts. They are the individuals who use the products or services offered by gatekeepers or business users through a relevant CPS. A primary characteristic of an End User is that their personal data is frequently subject to processing, combination, and cross-use by gatekeepers. Their consent and preferences regarding this data processing are recorded and honored, particularly under regulations such as GDPR or the ePrivacy Directive. While their personal data may be cross-used with or without explicit consent depending on the specific legal basis, they generally have choices concerning data access. End Users are individuals whose data is collected and exchanged during interoperability, and whose data, location, and communication privacy are regulated, especially when using specific services like NIICS, where they have the ability to send or block messages. Their data is also subject to re-identification attempts by gatekeepers. A crucial aspect of the End User's rights is data portability, as outlined in DMA Article 6(9) and GDPR Article 20. End Users are individuals who request data portability, authorize third parties to port data, and interact with gatekeeper interfaces to initiate these requests. Explicit and specific consent is required from the End User for personal data transfers to third countries that do not have an adequacy decision. Furthermore, the End User's consent is essential for sharing their personal data when business users request access to it in the context of a Core Platform Service.

[data] Customer Data — Customer data refers to personal data of customers, processed by ABC Ltd. on behalf of XYZ.
Customer Data refers to personal data about customers, including purchase history, name, address, email address, and telephone number.
Information related to customers, including contact data and insurance details, which was inadvertently exposed.
Customer data is processed by insurance companies or banks, mentioned as an example of large-scale processing.
Customer data refers to information processed by insurance companies, banks, or fast-food chains.
Customer data is data actively provided by business users that has been lawfully obtained, covered by Article 6(10) DMA.

[concept] Contract Performance — The fulfillment of obligations outlined in a contract, which may include providing a service.
A legitimate basis for processing personal data where it is necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is a party, or for taking pre-contractual steps.
[concept] Delivery Service — A service that handles the delivery of goods, which may cross-use identification details without consent if functionally interconnected.
[data] End User Payment History — Data detailing an end user's payment transactions, accessible under Article 6(10) DMA.

[concept] Online Choice Architecture — The design of user interfaces and choices impacting data portability and data access.
Online choice architecture refers to the design of consent screens and interfaces by gatekeepers, which should not undermine user autonomy or nudge users towards specific choices.
Online choice architecture refers to the design of consent screens and online interfaces by gatekeepers, which should not undermine user autonomy.

[person] Data Subject — A Data Subject is defined as an identified or identifiable natural person to whom personal data relates and whose personal data undergoes processing, encompassing operations such as collection, holding, storing, or other manipulations, including biometric and location data. This individual can be identified, directly or indirectly, by reference to an identifier or specific factors of their identity. End users are often considered Data Subjects, and their vital interests may necessitate data processing. Even if a Data Subject's data has been anonymized such that they are no longer identifiable, they are still considered a Data Subject. Their behavior or identity may be monitored, and any personal data relating to them requires either consent or another legitimate basis for lawful processing. Data processing concerning Data Subjects is subject to regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly if goods or services are offered to them within the European Union. Under Article 6 of the GDPR, explicit consent is often required for processing, including profiling and automated decision-making. This consent must be demonstrably obtained through deliberate, informed action. Data Subjects possess fundamental rights to safeguard their human dignity and legitimate interests, including rights to access, rectification, erasure, objection to processing, and data portability. They also have the right to be informed about and challenge automated decision-making and, in some contexts, request delisting from search engines. They can monitor data processing, should be offered format choices for reusing their data, and can transmit their personal data from one controller to another, taking responsibility for securing it in their own system. Data controllers are obligated to provide Data Subjects with specific information, including the identity of their representative, and to communicate efficiently. Their views should be sought during a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) where appropriate. When biometric data is processed, an alternative solution must be offered, and Data Subjects should be consulted during the drafting of codes of conduct when feasible. A Data Subject is also an individual whose personal data may be affected by a data breach, putting their rights and freedoms at risk. In such an event, the controller must inform them, especially if there is a likely high risk of adverse effects or potential damage; communication of the breach is obligatory if their personal data has been compromised and depending on the severity of the consequences. Their vital interests, reasonable expectations (influenced by factors like age, public figure status, and professional position), and personal data require consistent protection, necessitating that their rights and freedoms be safeguarded. They may contact the Data Protection Officer, lodge complaints with supervisory authorities, and seek judicial remedy. A Data Subject has the right to compensation for material or non-material damage suffered due to an infringement of the regulation. Their identity may be scrutinized by a controller if doubts arise.

[organization] Gatekeeper — A Gatekeeper is an entity designated under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically pursuant to Article 3(4) or Article 3(9), indicating its provision of Core Platform Services (CPSs). Prominent examples of such organizations include Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta. These Gatekeepers control access to specific digital services and are subject to extensive legal obligations under the DMA, and in many cases, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Their role is central to the regulatory framework designed to ensure fair and contestable digital markets. Gatekeepers process the personal data of end users, often acting as controllers or processors, and are responsible for ensuring that consent obtained for data processing, particularly for online advertising and data combination, complies with both GDPR and DMA requirements. This includes the meticulous recording of consent refusals or withdrawals. They are obligated to enable continuous and real-time access to data, prevent data accumulation, and ensure robust data security. Their responsibilities extend to providing data upon request by business users or authorized third parties, free of charge, and establishing appropriate authentication and authorization procedures for such access. They must also implement security measures for personal data, comply with portability requests under DMA Article 6(9), and provide comprehensive information to data subjects. Furthermore, Gatekeepers are tasked with selecting and implementing anonymization methods for end-user data shared under Article 6(11) DMA and must implement measures to maintain service integrity and security. They also have duties concerning interoperability, including exchanging message content and personal data with other providers while ensuring security for their end users. This includes protecting metadata, verifying communication authenticity, and ensuring compliance with geographical limitations and data protection regulations for Number-Independent Interpersonal Communication Services (NIICS). Gatekeepers must design online interfaces that do not undermine user autonomy, provide reminders, and ensure fair access to datasets by altering data to mitigate identification risks and imposing contractual measures on third-party undertakings for data access and compliance monitoring. Their conduct is subject to examination for compliance with both the DMA and GDPR, and they may have a "main establishment" under the GDPR. They are also separate controllers under GDPR for their own data processing and have obligations under Article 6(4) and Article 8(1) of the DMA.
[artifact] Complaint Submission Form — A Complaint Submission Form is a method, potentially electronic, provided by supervisory authorities to facilitate the lodging of complaints by data subjects.

[concept] Data Portability — Data Portability is a fundamental right that empowers data subjects and, in some contexts, end users or authorized third parties, to obtain their personal data from a data controller or gatekeeper. This right mandates that personal data be provided in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable, and often interoperable format. Its primary purpose is to enable individuals to reuse their personal data for their own objectives across various services. Explicitly outlined in Article 20 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and Article 6(9) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA), Data Portability also includes the ability for data subjects to transmit this personal data to another data controller without hindrance. This transfer mechanism enhances individual control over their personal information and promotes their active participation within the data ecosystem. For data controllers, fulfilling this right often necessitates additional processing to extract and filter data, ensuring interoperable systems are in place. Beyond individual rights, Data Portability is recognized as a crucial element for fostering innovation in the digital sector. It facilitates the transfer of data from one service to another, which is essential for multi-homing—using multiple services concurrently—and for switching between services. This ability to easily transfer data between different services is considered a key enabler for a more dynamic and competitive digital market.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation `(Controller, Processing of Personal Data)` describes the multifaceted role and responsibilities of a controller concerning the processing of personal data. A controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This determination is made independently, and the specified purposes and means must explicitly relate to the processing of personal data. In this context, the controller is actively involved in and carries out the processing of personal data. A core responsibility of the controller is to ensure and demonstrate compliance with the principles governing personal data processing, particularly those outlined in the GDPR. This includes ensuring that all processing activities have an appropriate legal basis. Furthermore, controllers are expected to innovate to maintain compliance with evolving legal parameters. The controller's responsibilities also extend to respecting the rights of data subjects. Specifically, if a data subject objects to the processing of their personal data, the controller shall cease processing unless compelling legitimate grounds for the processing can be demonstrated. [Source: Guidelines_on_Personal_data_breach_notification_under_Regulation_2016679] "Article 34(3) states three conditions that, if met, do not require notification to individuals in the event of a breach. These are:  The controller has applied appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect personal data prior to the breach, in particular those measures that render personal data unintelligible to any person who is not authorised to access it. This could, for example, include protecting personal data with state-of-the-art encryption, or by tokenization.  Immediately following a breach, the controller has taken steps to ensure that the high risk posed to individuals’ rights and freedoms is no longer likely to materialise. For example, depending on the circumstances of the case, the controller may have immediately identified and taken action against the individual who has accessed personal data before they were able to do anything with it. Due regard still needs to be given to the possible consequences of any breach of confidentiality, again, depending on the nature of the data concerned.  It would involve disproportionate effort37 to contact individuals, perhaps where their contact details have been lost as a result of the breach or are not known in the first place. For example, the warehouse of a statistical office has flooded and the documents containing personal data were stored only in paper form. Instead, the controller must make a public communication or take a similar measure, whereby the individuals are informed in an equally effective manner. In the case of disproportionate effort, technical arrangements could also be envisaged to make information about the breach available on demand, which could prove useful to those individuals who may be affected by a breach, but the controller cannot otherwise contact. In accordance with the accountability principle controllers should be able to demonstrate to the supervisory authority that they meet one or more of these conditions 38. It should be borne in mind that while notification may initially not be required if there is no risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, this may change over time and the risk would have to be re-evaluated. If a controller decides not to communicate a breach to the individual, Article 34(4) explains that the supervisory authority can require it to do so, if it considers the breach is likely to result in a high risk to individuals. [person] Data Protection Officer — A Data Protection Officer (DPO) is an individual, organization, or team responsible for overseeing, advising on, and monitoring an entity's data protection strategy and its implementation to ensure compliance with relevant data protection laws and regulations, particularly the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), as detailed in Articles 37 to 39. This role requires expert knowledge of data protection law and practices. The DPO's responsibilities include providing guidance on appropriate measures and demonstrating compliance regarding personal data processing, assisting the controller or processor in monitoring internal compliance with regulations, and advising on Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), including their performance, monitoring, and documenting related advice and decisions. DPOs also play a crucial role in assessing the applicability of GDPR Article 6(1)(f). They act as a key contact point for information regarding personal data breaches, cooperating with supervisory authorities, and their contact details may need to be communicated as part of GDPR information duties. They are involved in all issues related to personal data protection, supported by controllers and processors with necessary resources, and report directly to the highest management level. Appointment of a DPO may be mandatory under GDPR Article 37, especially when an organization's core activities involve processing special categories of data or regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects, though organizations can also voluntarily appoint one. Whether an employee or an external contractor, the DPO must perform duties independently, without fear of dismissal or penalization, and avoid conflicts of interest, meaning they cannot represent a controller or processor in court for data protection matters. While responsible for monitoring compliance of data processing operations, the DPO's role cannot be certified under GDPR Article 42.7. The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) encourages DPO involvement in integrating data protection by design and by default principles, highlighting their essential role in accountability and record-keeping in personal data protection.

[concept] Processing of Personal Data — Processing of Personal Data is defined as any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or on sets of personal data. This comprehensive definition encompasses a wide array of activities, including the collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure, or destruction of such data. It specifically refers to the handling or manipulation of information pertaining to an identified or identifiable natural person, whether or not by automated means, and also includes manual processing within a filing system. The processing of personal data is actively governed by various data protection rules and legal frameworks, most notably the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and PSD2 regulations. Article 5 of the GDPR outlines key principles that must be adhered to during such processing, emphasizing that operations must be lawful, fair, and transparent. The legality of these operations is established through specific legal bases, as detailed in Article 6(1)(b) of the GDPR, with consent being one of these permissible lawful bases. Operations involving personal data must be carried out lawfully, securely, and confidentially, safeguarding individuals' rights in compliance with these regulations. Furthermore, the processing of personal data is an activity for which a "controller" determines the purposes and means. It can be performed by various entities, and is central to discussions of concepts like joint controllership. This activity is also central to discussions about "core activities" and "large scale" operations under GDPR, especially when dealing with special categories of personal data, biometric data, or data on criminal convictions and offenses. The global relevance of this definition is underscored by calls for its inclusion in international agreements.

[organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

At the same time, the contract should take into account “the specific tasks and responsibilities of the processor in the context of the processing to be carried out and the risk to the rights and freedoms of the data subject”.51 Generally speaking, the contract between the parties should be drafted in light of the specific data processing activity. For instance, there is no need to impose particularly stringent protections and procedures on a processor entrusted with a processing activity from which only minor risks arise: while each processor must comply with the requirements set out by the Regulation, the measures and procedures should be tailored to the specific situation. In any event, all elements of Article 28(3) must be covered by the contract. At the same time, the contract should include some elements that may help the processor in understanding the risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects arising from the processing: because the activity is performed on behalf of the controller, often the controller has a deeper understanding of the risks that the processing entails since the controller is aware of the circumstances in which the processing is embedded. 114. While the subject matter of the processing is a broad concept, it needs to be formulated with enough specifications so that it is clear what the main object of the processing is;  the duration52 of the processing: the exact period of time, or the criteria used to determine it, should be specified; for instance, reference could be made to the duration of the processing agreement;  the nature of the processing: the type of operations performed as part of the processing (for instance: “filming”, “recording”, “archiving of images”, ...) and purpose of the processing (for instance: detecting unlawful entry). ragPromptContext: [concept] Delivery Service — A service that handles the delivery of goods, which may cross-use identification details without consent if functionally interconnected.
[artifact] Products — Products are items that process personal data or are based on its processing.

[concept] Archiving Purposes — Archiving Purposes refers to the practice of collecting, preserving, and storing records and data, typically for long-term reference, historical preservation, or administrative reasons. This activity often serves the public interest, scientific research, or statistical research. Under various data protection frameworks, such as GDPR Article 17.3.d, Archiving Purposes can serve as a specific ground for processing personal data. This designation may allow for exceptions to certain individual rights, including the right to erasure (delisting) or exemptions from specific information provision obligations for data controllers. Such exceptions are generally foreseen under certain conditions and are often subject to appropriate safeguards to protect the rights and freedoms of data subjects.
Archiving purposes in the public interest can exempt controllers from certain information provision obligations or allow for data retention.
Archiving purposes is one of the reasons for processing personal data, often in the public interest, subject to safeguards.
The storage of records and data for historical preservation or long-term reference.

[concept] Fraud Detection — An organizational and technical measure integrated to detect fraudulent activities related to biometric data.
Fraud detection is a purpose for which a gatekeeper may be legally required to combine or cross-use personal data.
Fraud detection is a purpose for which a gatekeeper may be legally required to combine or cross-use personal data.

[person] Business User — A business user is an individual or organization, natural or legal, operating in a commercial or professional capacity, identified as a beneficiary of the right to data access under Article 6(10) DMA.
A business user is a commercial entity or individual that utilizes gatekeeper products or services and may request access to end-user data.
An entity that requests access to end-user data from a gatekeeper under Article 6(10) DMA, with obligations under GDPR regarding data minimisation.
A Business User is a party that requests access to data, including historic and real-time data, and is subject to monitoring by data protection supervisory authorities.
[data] Employees' Personal Data — Employees' personal data refers to information about employees that is subject to specific rules and safeguards regarding its processing in the employment context.

[organization] Gatekeeper — A Gatekeeper is an entity designated under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically pursuant to Article 3(4) or Article 3(9), indicating its provision of Core Platform Services (CPSs). Prominent examples of such organizations include Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta. These Gatekeepers control access to specific digital services and are subject to extensive legal obligations under the DMA, and in many cases, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Their role is central to the regulatory framework designed to ensure fair and contestable digital markets. Gatekeepers process the personal data of end users, often acting as controllers or processors, and are responsible for ensuring that consent obtained for data processing, particularly for online advertising and data combination, complies with both GDPR and DMA requirements. This includes the meticulous recording of consent refusals or withdrawals. They are obligated to enable continuous and real-time access to data, prevent data accumulation, and ensure robust data security. Their responsibilities extend to providing data upon request by business users or authorized third parties, free of charge, and establishing appropriate authentication and authorization procedures for such access. They must also implement security measures for personal data, comply with portability requests under DMA Article 6(9), and provide comprehensive information to data subjects. Furthermore, Gatekeepers are tasked with selecting and implementing anonymization methods for end-user data shared under Article 6(11) DMA and must implement measures to maintain service integrity and security. They also have duties concerning interoperability, including exchanging message content and personal data with other providers while ensuring security for their end users. This includes protecting metadata, verifying communication authenticity, and ensuring compliance with geographical limitations and data protection regulations for Number-Independent Interpersonal Communication Services (NIICS). Gatekeepers must design online interfaces that do not undermine user autonomy, provide reminders, and ensure fair access to datasets by altering data to mitigate identification risks and imposing contractual measures on third-party undertakings for data access and compliance monitoring. Their conduct is subject to examination for compliance with both the DMA and GDPR, and they may have a "main establishment" under the GDPR. They are also separate controllers under GDPR for their own data processing and have obligations under Article 6(4) and Article 8(1) of the DMA.

[organization] Government — One of the bodies responsible for appointing members of supervisory authorities, through a transparent procedure.
The Government is the executive body in a Member State that supervisory authorities may advise on data protection measures.
The Government is an entity to which reports on infringements and measures taken are transmitted by supervisory authorities.

[location] Third Countries — Third Countries are defined as nations or jurisdictions situated outside the geographical and legal boundaries of the European Union (EU) and the European Economic Area (EEA). These countries operate under distinct legal systems and data protection standards compared to those within the EU/EEA. The term "Third Countries" frequently arises in discussions concerning international personal data transfers. When personal data is transferred to a Third Country, it falls under the specific provisions of Chapter V (Article 44 et seq.) of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). These regulations ensure that adequate data protection is maintained, even though these countries are outside the direct jurisdiction of the GDPR. Such transfers are contingent upon compliance with the GDPR and the existence of adequate protection levels, which may be facilitated through specific safeguards or international agreements. Data subjects should generally be informed when their data is transferred to Third Countries. Furthermore, the legal definition of "public bodies" within Third Countries is determined by their respective domestic laws. These countries can also be locations where competent authorities may cooperate with the European Commission and supervisory authorities on a basis of reciprocity for the enforcement of personal data protection.

[concept] Online Search Engines — Online search engines are services that gatekeepers are obliged to provide with access to ranking, query, click, and view data under Article 6(11) DMA.
Online search engines provide access to ranking, query, click, and view data generated by end-users.
Online search engines are services provided by gatekeepers and third-party undertakings, subject to data access obligations under Article 6(11) DMA.
Online search engines are services provided by requesting third-party undertakings that receive and reuse data shared by gatekeepers.

Under GDPR, Controller The (Controller, Processor) relationship describes an arrangement, primarily defined by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), where a Processor handles personal data on behalf of a Controller. The Controller retains the primary and ultimate responsibility for ensuring overall compliance with data protection principles, including data protection by design and by default (DPbDD), and this accountability extends to any Processor and sub-processors involved. This relationship mandates that the Controller select Processors who offer sufficient guarantees regarding GDPR compliance. This relationship is formalized and governed by a legally binding contract or other legal act, often referred to as a processing agreement. This agreement details how GDPR requirements will be implemented, outlines specific obligations, and defines assistance duties. The Controller must provide documented instructions to the Processor on how to process personal data, and the Processor is obligated to comply. The Processor processes personal data only on these documented instructions. Even without a written agreement, the existence and definition of this relationship hold. The Processor has various duties, including assisting the Controller in fulfilling obligations related to data subject rights and Articles 32 to 36 of the GDPR, ensuring compliance with data protection obligations, and reporting to the Controller. This assistance includes deleting or returning personal data at the Controller's choice, providing compliance information, and cooperating with Controller-conducted audits. A critical obligation for the Processor is to notify the Controller "without undue delay" upon becoming aware of a personal data breach it is processing on behalf of the Controller, as mandated by Article 33(2) GDPR. Processors must also notify the Controller of any request from a third-country authority without undue delay and follow the Controller's instructions, unless prohibited by law. The Processor is liable to the Controller for fulfilling these obligations. The Controller can authorize the use of sub-processors, but the Processor must obtain prior written authorization from the Controller for engaging another processor. The Processor is liable to the Controller for the sub-processors' adherence to data protection obligations. In scenarios involving data transfers, such as a third-country company (Controller) engaging a non-EEA processor, the processor acts as a data exporter on behalf of the Controller. The Controller must provide a comprehensive list of all data recipients, including processors. The relationship demands good faith cooperation, involving contract negotiation and management of audit and instruction processes. Controllers also carry out Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) with the processors. In some cases, the lead supervisory authority of the Controller may also become the lead supervisory authority for the Processor. When an end user qualifies as a Controller, an authorized third party may act as a Processor. Processor.

Under GDPR, GDPR The relationship between GDPR and a Processor is characterized by specific obligations, responsibilities, and liabilities directly imposed upon the Processor by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). A processor is subject to the GDPR for any given processing operation, with its role and duties explicitly defined within the regulation. This subjection is set forth in Article 3 of the GDPR, which establishes its territorial scope and applicability, even extending to non-EEA processors when they are engaged by third-country companies. In such cases, these processors must also comply with Article 28 and Chapter V of the GDPR. The GDPR directly imposes various obligations on processors, detailing their responsibilities concerning personal data protection. Processors must ensure compliance with these requirements, particularly by adhering to the instructions provided by controllers. Key responsibilities include compliance with Article 30 (records of processing activities), Article 32 (security of processing), Article 35 (data protection impact assessment), and Article 36 (prior consultation with a supervisory authority) regarding risks. Processors are also subject to GDPR obligations relating to their liability for sub-processors, as outlined in Article 28(4). Furthermore, the GDPR requires processors to implement appropriate security measures and outlines their obligations regarding data breaches and notifications, including the requirement to notify any breach to their controller. Supervisory Authorities (SAs) have the power to take action against a processor for infringing GDPR provisions. The regulation categorizes various infringements that can lead to fines for processors. Certifications under the GDPR are also issued to data processors, further emphasizing their direct accountability and the regulatory oversight they are subject to. These collective requirements define the responsibility and liability of the processor under the GDPR.<SEP>The GDPR, specifically Article 60(10), imposes duties on the processor.<SEP>The Processor is responsible for ensuring data processing adheres to GDPR provisions.<SEP>The Processor is responsible for compliance with the GDPR and must be able to demonstrate it.<SEP>The processing by a processor is governed by a contract or legal act that ensures compliance with GDPR articles. Processor.

Under GDPR, Personal Data The relation "(Personal Data, Processor)" defines the role and responsibilities of a Processor in handling Personal Data. A Processor is an entity that processes personal data strictly on behalf of and under the instructions of a Controller, operating as an agent in managing, extracting, handling, and transferring this data. Key duties include the implementation of robust security measures to protect the personal data entrusted to them. Processors are authorized to perform operations involving personal data, and individuals working under the direct authority of the Processor are also permitted to process such data. Upon the termination of processing activities, the Processor is generally obligated to either delete or return the personal data to the Controller, unless a legal requirement necessitates its storage. Furthermore, a Processor may transfer personal data, and within the context of the EU, they might even make personal data accessible to a third-country authority. Processor.

They are the individuals who use the products or services offered by gatekeepers or business users through a relevant CPS. A primary characteristic of an End User is that their personal data is frequently subject to processing, combination, and cross-use by gatekeepers. Their consent and preferences regarding this data processing are recorded and honored, particularly under regulations such as GDPR or the ePrivacy Directive. While their personal data may be cross-used with or without explicit consent depending on the specific legal basis, they generally have choices concerning data access. Their data is also subject to re-identification attempts by gatekeepers. A crucial aspect of the End User's rights is data portability, as outlined in DMA Article 6(9) and GDPR Article 20. End Users are individuals who request data portability, authorize third parties to port data, and interact with gatekeeper interfaces to initiate these requests. Explicit and specific consent is required from the End User for personal data transfers to third countries that do not have an adequacy decision. Furthermore, the End User's consent is essential for sharing their personal data when business users request access to it in the context of a Core Platform Service.

[person] Data Subject — A Data Subject is defined as an identified or identifiable natural person to whom personal data relates and whose personal data undergoes processing, encompassing operations such as collection, holding, storing, or other manipulations, including biometric and location data. This individual can be identified, directly or indirectly, by reference to an identifier or specific factors of their identity. End users are often considered Data Subjects, and their vital interests may necessitate data processing. Even if a Data Subject's data has been anonymized such that they are no longer identifiable, they are still considered a Data Subject. Their behavior or identity may be monitored, and any personal data relating to them requires either consent or another legitimate basis for lawful processing. Data processing concerning Data Subjects is subject to regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly if goods or services are offered to them within the European Union. Under Article 6 of the GDPR, explicit consent is often required for processing, including profiling and automated decision-making. This consent must be demonstrably obtained through deliberate, informed action. Data Subjects possess fundamental rights to safeguard their human dignity and legitimate interests, including rights to access, rectification, erasure, objection to processing, and data portability. They also have the right to be informed about and challenge automated decision-making and, in some contexts, request delisting from search engines. They can monitor data processing, should be offered format choices for reusing their data, and can transmit their personal data from one controller to another, taking responsibility for securing it in their own system. Data controllers are obligated to provide Data Subjects with specific information, including the identity of their representative, and to communicate efficiently. Their views should be sought during a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) where appropriate. When biometric data is processed, an alternative solution must be offered, and Data Subjects should be consulted during the drafting of codes of conduct when feasible. A Data Subject is also an individual whose personal data may be affected by a data breach, putting their rights and freedoms at risk. In such an event, the controller must inform them, especially if there is a likely high risk of adverse effects or potential damage; communication of the breach is obligatory if their personal data has been compromised and depending on the severity of the consequences. Their vital interests, reasonable expectations (influenced by factors like age, public figure status, and professional position), and personal data require consistent protection, necessitating that their rights and freedoms be safeguarded. They may contact the Data Protection Officer, lodge complaints with supervisory authorities, and seek judicial remedy. A Data Subject has the right to compensation for material or non-material damage suffered due to an infringement of the regulation. Their identity may be scrutinized by a controller if doubts arise.

[organization] Gatekeeper — A Gatekeeper is an entity designated under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically pursuant to Article 3(4) or Article 3(9), indicating its provision of Core Platform Services (CPSs). Prominent examples of such organizations include Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta. These Gatekeepers control access to specific digital services and are subject to extensive legal obligations under the DMA, and in many cases, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Their role is central to the regulatory framework designed to ensure fair and contestable digital markets. Gatekeepers process the personal data of end users, often acting as controllers or processors, and are responsible for ensuring that consent obtained for data processing, particularly for online advertising and data combination, complies with both GDPR and DMA requirements. This includes the meticulous recording of consent refusals or withdrawals. They are obligated to enable continuous and real-time access to data, prevent data accumulation, and ensure robust data security. Their responsibilities extend to providing data upon request by business users or authorized third parties, free of charge, and establishing appropriate authentication and authorization procedures for such access. They must also implement security measures for personal data, comply with portability requests under DMA Article 6(9), and provide comprehensive information to data subjects. Furthermore, Gatekeepers are tasked with selecting and implementing anonymization methods for end-user data shared under Article 6(11) DMA and must implement measures to maintain service integrity and security. They also have duties concerning interoperability, including exchanging message content and personal data with other providers while ensuring security for their end users. This includes protecting metadata, verifying communication authenticity, and ensuring compliance with geographical limitations and data protection regulations for Number-Independent Interpersonal Communication Services (NIICS). Gatekeepers must design online interfaces that do not undermine user autonomy, provide reminders, and ensure fair access to datasets by altering data to mitigate identification risks and imposing contractual measures on third-party undertakings for data access and compliance monitoring. Their conduct is subject to examination for compliance with both the DMA and GDPR, and they may have a "main establishment" under the GDPR. They are also separate controllers under GDPR for their own data processing and have obligations under Article 6(4) and Article 8(1) of the DMA.

Article 6(1) (a) consent Consent as a basis for processing generally is addressed in the WP29 Guidelines on consent.12 Explicit consent is one of the exceptions from the prohibition on automated decision-making and profiling defined in Article 22(1). 11 Norwegian Data Protection Authority. The Great Data Race – How commercial utilisation of personal data challenges privacy, Report, November 2015. Datatilsynet https://www.datatilsynet.no/English/Publications/The- Great-Data-Race/ Accessed 24 April 201712 Article 29 Data Protection Working Party. Guidelines on Consent under Regulation 2016/679 WP259, 28 November 2017, http://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/just/document.cfm?doc_id=48849. Accessed 18 December 2017 13 Profiling can be opaque. Often it relies upon data that is derived or inferred from other data, rather than data directly provided by the data subject. Controllers seeking to rely upon consent as a basis for profiling will need to show that data subjects understand exactly what they are consenting to, and remember that consent is not always an appropriate basis for the processing.13 In all cases, data subjects should have enough relevant information about the envisaged use and consequences of the processing to ensure that any consent they provide represents an informed choice. 2. Article 6(1) (b) – necessary for the performance of a contract Controllers may wish to use profiling and automated decision-making processes because they:  potentially allow for greater consistency or fairness in the decision making process (e.g. by reducing the potential for human error, discrimination and abuse of power);  reduce the risk of customers failing to meet payments for goods or services (for example by using credit referencing); or  enable them to deliver decisions within a shorter time frame and improve efficiency . Regardless of the above, these considerations alone are not sufficient to show that this type of processing is necessary under Article 6(1)(b) for the performance of a contract. As described in the WP29 Opinion on legitimate interest14, necessity should be interpreted narrowly. The following is an example of profiling that would not meet the Article 6(1)(b) basis for processing. Example A user buys some items from an on-line retailer. In order to fulfil the contract, the retailer must process the user’s credit card information for payment purposes and the user’s address to deliver the goods. Completion of the contract is not dependent upon building a profile of the user’s tastes and lifestyle choices based on his or her visits to the website. Even if profiling is specifically mentioned in the small print of the contract, this fact alone does not make it ‘necessary’ for the performance of the contract. 3. Article 6(1) (c) – necessary for compliance with a legal obligation There may be instances where there will be a legal obligation15 to carry out profiling – for example in connection with fraud prevention or money laundering. The WP29 Opinion on legitimate interests16 provides useful information about this basis for processing, including the safeguards to be applied. 12 Article 29 Data Protection Working Party. Guidelines on Consent under Regulation 2016/679 WP259, 28 November 2017, http://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/just/document.cfm?doc_id=48849. Accessed 18 December 2017"

[method] Processing Operations — Processing Operations refer to any activities or a set of operations performed on data, particularly personal data, by institutions or data brokers. These operations encompass a vast array of actions, including the collection, storage, use, disclosure, further processing, the management of data subject rights, and the handling and manipulation of data. They can also involve linking data, forming different conducts, combining data, or cross-using data. Per Article 4(2) of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), these operations are defined as any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or on sets of personal data. These operations are composed of various components, such as data, systems, and processes, all of which should adhere to specific criteria. Activities often include the selection of targeting criteria and the display of advertisements to a specific target audience. Processing operations are a primary object of certification under the GDPR, potentially encompassing governance processes and leading to the creation of a product or service. Both data controllers and processors are obligated to demonstrate compliance when executing these operations. Actions performed on personal data should be limited to what is necessary, contributing to a defined processing purpose, and designed to process only the minimum amount of necessary data. Processing operations are actions carried out by a data controller using collected data, requiring specific information provisions and legal bases. They may also benefit from special regimes under GDPR. Examples include the collection, storage, use, or deletion of data. Some operations may involve the use of CCTV and are subject to the applicability of the household exemption. Records must be maintained for these data handling activities. Furthermore, processing operations that involve personal data may require a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) under GDPR if they pose a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. When a DPIA is required, these activities necessitate a systematic description, an assessment of necessity, proportionality, and risks, and the implementation of measures to address those risks.
Processing Operations refer to any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction.
Processing Operations involve any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, storage, etc.
Actions or sets of actions performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, storage, or disclosure.
Actions or sets of actions performed upon personal data, which supervisory authorities are generally competent to oversee, except for courts acting in judicial capacity.
Processing operations refer to any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, as defined in Article 4(2) GDPR.
Processing operations refer to activities involving personal data, such as combining or cross-using data.
[artifact] Hardware — The physical components of a device that gatekeepers may take measures to protect the integrity of when allowing third-party apps.

[organization] Producers — Producers are entities that develop processing solutions (hardware, software, services, systems). They should demonstrate Data Protection by Design and Default (DPbDD) in their development life-cycle and facilitate controllers' needs.
Producers are key enablers for DPbDD, providing solutions to controllers that embed data protection.
Producers are responsible for developing, designing, selecting, and using applications, services, and products with regard to data protection.
[data] Performance Data — Performance data, such as crash data, can be relevant to business users for providing customer support.
[concept] General and Incident Reporting — Measures specified by the implementing act for regular reporting and reporting specific incidents related to data.
[concept] Processing Operations Security — Processing Operations Security refers to the measures taken to ensure the protection and integrity of data processing activities.

[concept] Processor — A Processor, as defined by Article 4(8) of the GDPR, is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that processes personal data on behalf of a controller. This entity's primary function is to handle personal data strictly according to the controller's documented instructions, without independently determining the purposes or means of the processing activity, and thus, processors do not pursue independent objectives for data processing. A website hosting company is an example of a Processor. Processors are responsible for protecting personal data and are involved in the processing of personal data, with specific legal obligations under the GDPR, including adherence to its principles, ensuring confidentiality, and implementing robust security measures. They must provide sufficient guarantees, such as compliance with codes of conduct or certification mechanisms, and are required to operate under a binding contract or legal act with the controller. This contract typically details their responsibilities, including assisting with Data Protection by Design and by Default (DPbDD), implementing technical and organizational measures, conducting data protection impact assessments (DPIA), and providing compliance information. The processor assists the controller in carrying out a DPIA, and its roles and responsibilities in a DPIA must be contractually defined. Processors are also obligated to notify the controller of any data breach without undue delay, inform the controller of any infringing instructions, and are subject to audits. Upon termination of processing activities, they must delete or return personal data. They have specific obligations regarding personal data breaches, as mentioned in Article 33 requirements, particularly Article 33(2). Processors can also act as exporters or importers of personal data, transferring data to third countries or international organizations under specific conditions, always on behalf of the controller and must implement appropriate safeguards for data transfers. While their name may not be explicitly included in consent forms, they are listed as recipients of data. They are held liable to the controller for the performance of their sub-processors' obligations, necessitating that sub-processors also provide sufficient guarantees. Processors' activities and processing operations are assessed for GDPR compliance, and they can be the direct cause of a data breach. They may be the subject of infringement claims, addressed by the final decision of a competent supervisory authority, and can be directly and individually concerned by an EDPB binding decision, against which they may bring an action for annulment. For Processors located in the EU, they must identify an applicable ground for transfer before responding to requests from third-country authorities, as stipulated under Article 48. The designation of a representative does not affect their liability under GDPR, and they may be subject to legal actions for damages if they infringe the regulation or act outside of controller instructions. A data subject can seek judicial remedies against a processor. A Processor may be required to designate a Data Protection Officer (DPO), especially if their core activities involve key operations to achieve their goals, or if their core activities require such a designation under GDPR. When a DPO is designated, the processor is required to publish and communicate the DPO's contact details according to Article 37(7) of the GDPR. The DPO advises the processor on GDPR obligations and assists in monitoring internal compliance with the GDPR. The processor may assign the task of maintaining records of processing operations to the DPO, and the processor supports and involves the Data Protection Officer. For the cooperation procedure to apply, a Processor involved in cross-border processing must have a main or single establishment in an EU Member State. This main establishment oversees such cross-border processing. The main establishment is where its central administration is located in the Union, or where its main processing activities take place if no central administration exists in the Union. Processors are subject to the authority of a Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) or Concerned Supervisory Authority (CSA), and LSAs may interact with Processors to gather relevant information, such as investigation findings, reports, and meeting records. Processors involved in cross-border processing are subject to procedures and potential enforcement action and may be directly targeted by decisions from the LSA. As parties targeted by a draft decision, their right to be heard must comply with national law, and their rights may be affected by changes in a revised draft decision. A Processor's actions can lead to complaints and prompt action by an LSA. Processors have obligations under Article 60(10), are informed of decisions by the LSA, and are obliged to notify the LSA of any measures adopted to comply with a decision entailing corrective measures. A processor can benefit from the one-stop-shop system if established in multiple Member States, and its establishment in multiple Member States can trigger the lead authority mechanism. Guidance can be provided on their implementation of appropriate measures and demonstration of compliance.
A processor is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that processes personal data on behalf of the controller.
A processor processes personal data on behalf of a controller. An authorized third party may act as a processor for an end user if the end user is a controller.

[data] On-Device Data — On-Device Data is data exclusively processed on a device, falls within the scope of Article 6(9) DMA, and gatekeepers must enable its portability at the request of end users or authorized third parties.
Data exclusively processed and stored on an end user's device, to which gatekeepers must enable effective and continuous access under Article 6(10) DMA.

[organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

Under GDPR, 72-Hour Notification Deadline The controller is generally required to notify within 72 hours, but delays are permissible with reasons. Controller.

Under GDPR, Controller The controller wishes to market products and services through direct marketing.<SEP>Direct marketing purposes may be regarded as a legitimate interest of the controller. Direct Marketing.

Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Supervisory Authority is established primarily by data protection regulations, such as the GDPR, and focuses on compliance, breach management, and accountability. A central obligation of the Controller is to notify the Supervisory Authority of personal data breaches, typically within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach, especially if it poses a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, as per Article 33(1) and Article 27(5) GDPR. The Controller is responsible for determining if a breach is notifiable and must ensure the relevant Supervisory Authority is informed, potentially proactively notifying them of infringements or seeking advice. They must also inform the Supervisory Authority about data transfers, documenting assessments and safeguards. Controllers without an EU establishment are required to engage with local supervisory authorities in every Member State where they operate. Furthermore, the Controller must consult the Supervisory Authority if a high risk identified in a Data Protection Impact Assessment cannot be mitigated by reasonable means before processing. Controllers are also obligated to cooperate with and make records available to the Supervisory Authority upon request, demonstrating accountability and compliance. The Supervisory Authority plays a significant role in overseeing the Controller's data protection practices. It can advise Controllers on how to inform individuals about breaches and may even order them to do so, particularly for high-risk breaches. The Supervisory Authority verifies the Controller's compliance, handles complaints, and seeks amicable settlements regarding possible infringements. It possesses powers to require the Controller to provide information, carry out investigations, notify infringements, and obtain access to data and premises. The Supervisory Authority can issue warnings and reprimands, order compliance, and impose sanctions, including administrative fines under Article 83 GDPR, especially in cases of unjustified breaches. The level of the Controller's cooperation is considered by the Supervisory Authority when assessing mitigation efforts. The Supervisory Authority also promotes awareness among Controllers regarding their obligations under pertinent regulations and informs Controllers when a received complaint is dismissed or rejected. Supervisory Authority.
Under GDPR, Controller A plaintiff has the choice to bring an action against a Controller before courts where the Controller has an establishment or the Data Subject resides. National Court.
Under GDPR, Controller Codes of conduct recommend out-of-court proceedings for resolving disputes between controllers and data subjects. Out-Of-Court Proceedings.

Under GDPR, Controller The controller should differentiate between access privileges of authorized personnel and limit access to data for employees.<SEP>Employees are generally not considered controllers but act under the authority of the controller.<SEP>An employee under the direct authority of the controller can process personal data. Employee.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation between a Controller and a Data Protection Officer (DPO) is characterized by advisory support and assigned responsibility for data protection compliance, particularly under regulations such as the GDPR. The Controller is responsible for designating a DPO to help ensure adherence to these regulations. The DPO's role encompasses providing advice and information to the Controller on various data protection matters, including breach management, data protection methodologies, and audits. This includes actively participating in Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), which the Controller undertakes with the DPO's guidance. Controllers are mandated to seek the DPO's advice when conducting a DPIA, and they must ensure the DPO's timely involvement in all data protection issues, providing necessary resources and access to facilitate their tasks. Guidelines may be developed by the Controller to specify when the DPO must be consulted. While the DPO offers crucial guidance and assists in monitoring internal compliance with regulations, the ultimate responsibility for data protection compliance remains with the Controller. The DPO may be an employee of the Controller or an external party, but they must perform their duties independently. The Controller is obligated to record the name and contact details of the DPO, and these details must be included in the record of processing activities. Furthermore, in the event of a data breach, the Controller must communicate the DPO's name and contact details as a contact point for breach information as part of the notification process. Data Protection Officer.

ragPromptContext: [organization] Alternative Service Providers — These providers can request interoperability from gatekeepers for number-independent interpersonal communications services.

[service] Information Society Service — An Information Society Service is broadly defined as a service typically provided for remuneration, at a distance, and by electronic means, in response to an individual request from a service recipient. This category encompasses various online services, including contracts concluded or transmitted electronically. A key characteristic of an Information Society Service is that storing or accessing information in a user's terminal equipment must be strictly necessary for the provision of the service itself. This necessity can lead to certain exemptions under Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive. Specifically, for an Information Society Service, consent may not be required for gaining access to information already stored in a device (such as a vehicle) if such access is explicitly requested by the subscriber. This exemption simplifies data access under specific, user-initiated circumstances. Furthermore, an Information Society Service is defined more formally in point (b) of Article 1(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/1535. When an Information Society Service is explicitly requested by a subscriber or user, certain processing exemptions may apply. For services of this nature that are often offered online, special considerations regarding children's consent might also be applicable, as detailed in specific regulatory sections like Section 7.1.1.
[organization] Independent Body — An entity entrusted with the appointment of supervisory authority members under Member State law.

[service] Payment Service — A service that processes payments, which may cross-use identification details without consent if functionally interconnected.
A payment service is a service provided by a gatekeeper where an end user's personal data collected in a CPS can be cross-used to process a payment, relying on Article 6(1)(b) GDPR.
[method] Fraud Monitoring and Prevention — Techniques and activities aimed at detecting and preventing fraudulent activities, which can be a basis for automated processing.

[person] Client — A client is an entity represented by a law firm, in this case, Company ABC, which provides a mandate to the law firm.
A client is an individual whose personal data may be transferred by a travel agent for the purpose of organizing their travel.
The client is an organization for which an external DPO team works, and for whom a lead contact and "person in charge" is designated.
The client is the entity for whom an external DPO team works, under the responsibility of a designated lead contact.
A client is a data subject who has a relevant and appropriate relationship with a controller, often forming the basis for legitimate interest in data processing.

[concept] Data Transfers — Data transfers involve the movement of data from one location or entity to another.
Data Transfers refer to the movement of data to third countries or international organizations, which can be based on appropriate safeguards and legal remedies for data subjects.
Data transfers involve the movement of personal data, and possible risks due to absence of adequacy decisions or safeguards (Article 46) must be informed.
Data Transfers involve the movement of personal data from one entity or location to another, especially across borders.

[concept] Administrative Fines — Administrative Fines are financial or monetary penalties that supervisory authorities impose in response to infringements of legal requirements, particularly those set forth in data protection regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). These fines, detailed in Article 83 of the GDPR, are designed to be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive. The imposition of Administrative Fines intensified under the GDPR, reflecting an increased level of penalty for such infringements. The criteria for setting these fines are based on the nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement, and their calculation begins from a harmonized point, varying according to the specific circumstances of each case, guided by particular principles and guidelines under the GDPR. Certification can also be a factor in determining these penalties. For undertakings, Administrative Fines can potentially reach up to 20,000,000 EUR or 4% of their total worldwide annual turnover, with the upper limit determined by their combined turnover. While imposed by supervisory authorities, their assessment may be subject to review by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB). These fines represent a type of legal effect that can be imposed as a measure for non-compliance with the Regulation.
[concept] Compensation — Compensation is the right for any person who has suffered damage due to an infringement of the Regulation to receive payment from the controller or processor.

[organization] Gatekeeper — A Gatekeeper is an entity designated under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically pursuant to Article 3(4) or Article 3(9), indicating its provision of Core Platform Services (CPSs). Prominent examples of such organizations include Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta. These Gatekeepers control access to specific digital services and are subject to extensive legal obligations under the DMA, and in many cases, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Their role is central to the regulatory framework designed to ensure fair and contestable digital markets. Gatekeepers process the personal data of end users, often acting as controllers or processors, and are responsible for ensuring that consent obtained for data processing, particularly for online advertising and data combination, complies with both GDPR and DMA requirements. This includes the meticulous recording of consent refusals or withdrawals. They are obligated to enable continuous and real-time access to data, prevent data accumulation, and ensure robust data security. Their responsibilities extend to providing data upon request by business users or authorized third parties, free of charge, and establishing appropriate authentication and authorization procedures for such access. They must also implement security measures for personal data, comply with portability requests under DMA Article 6(9), and provide comprehensive information to data subjects. Furthermore, Gatekeepers are tasked with selecting and implementing anonymization methods for end-user data shared under Article 6(11) DMA and must implement measures to maintain service integrity and security. They also have duties concerning interoperability, including exchanging message content and personal data with other providers while ensuring security for their end users. This includes protecting metadata, verifying communication authenticity, and ensuring compliance with geographical limitations and data protection regulations for Number-Independent Interpersonal Communication Services (NIICS). Gatekeepers must design online interfaces that do not undermine user autonomy, provide reminders, and ensure fair access to datasets by altering data to mitigate identification risks and imposing contractual measures on third-party undertakings for data access and compliance monitoring. Their conduct is subject to examination for compliance with both the DMA and GDPR, and they may have a "main establishment" under the GDPR. They are also separate controllers under GDPR for their own data processing and have obligations under Article 6(4) and Article 8(1) of the DMA.

Finally, as leading practice for “receiving” data controllers, the WP29 recommends that data subjects are provided with complete information about the nature of personal data which are relevant for the performance of their services. In addition to underpinning fair processing, this allows users to limit the risks for third parties, and also any other unnecessary duplication of personal data even where no other data subjects are involved. - How can the data controller identify the data subject before answering his request? There are no prescriptive requirements to be found in the GDPR on how to authenticate the data subject. Nevertheless, Article 12(2) of the GDPR states that the data controller shall not refuse to act on request of a data subject for exercising his or her rights (including the right to data portability) unless it is processing personal data for a purpose that does not require the identification of a data subject and it can demonstrate that it is not able to identify the data subject. However, as per Article 11(2), in such circumstances the data subject can provide more information to enable his or her identification. Additionally, Article 12(6) provides that where a data controller has reasonable doubts about the identity of a data subject, it can request further information to confirm the data subject’s identity. Where a data subject provides additional information enabling his or her identification, the data controller shall not refuse to act on the request. Where information and data collected online is linked to pseudonyms or unique identifiers, data controllers can implement appropriate procedures 24 Article 12 requires that data controllers provide “any communications […] in a concise, transparent, intelligible, and easily assessable form, using clear and plain language, in particular for any information addressed specifically to a child.” 14 enabling an individual to make a data portability request and receive the data relating to him or her. In any case, data controllers must implement an authentication procedure in order to strongly ascertain the identity of the data subject requesting his or her personal data or more generally exercising the rights granted by the GDPR. These procedures often already exist. The data subjects are often already authenticated by the data controller before entering into a contract or collecting his or her consent to the processing. As a consequence, the personal data used to register the individual concerned by the processing can also be used as evidence to authenticate the data subject for portability purposes25. While in these cases, the data subjects’ prior identification may require a request for proof of their legal identity, such verification may not be relevant to assess the link between the data and the individual concerned, since such a link is not related with the official or legal identity. In essence, the ability for the data controller to request additional information to assess one’s identity cannot lead to excessive demands and to the collection of personal data which are not relevant or necessary to strengthen the link between the individual and the personal data requested. In many cases, such authentication procedures are already in place. For example, usernames and passwords are often used to allow individuals to access their data in their email accounts, social networking accounts, and accounts used for various other services, some of which individuals chose to use without revealing their full name and identity. If the size of data requested by the data subject makes transmission via the internet problematic, rather than potentially allowing for an extended time period of a maximum of three months to comply with the request26, the data controller may also need to consider alternative means of providing the data such as using streaming or saving to a CD, DVD or other physical media or allowing for the personal data to be transmitted directly to another data controller (as per Article 20(2) of the GDPR where technically feasible). - What is the time limit imposed to answer a portability request? Article 12(3) requires that the data controller provides “information on action taken” to the data subject “without undue delay” and in any event “within one month of receipt of the request”. This one month period can be extended to a maximum of three months for complex cases, provided that the data subject has been informed about the reasons for such delay within one month of the original request. Data controllers operating information society services are likely to be better equipped to be able to comply with requests within a very short time period. To meet user expectations, it is a good practice to define the timeframe in which a data portability request can typically be answered and communicate this to data subjects.
