Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data)" signifies that the Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This involves significant authority and responsibility over the entire lifecycle of personal data, encompassing decisions related to its processing, protection, management, and transference. The Controller is explicitly responsible for establishing the retention period for documentation containing personal data and makes choices regarding its deletion or return. A core obligation of the Controller is to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and to uphold data subject rights, including guaranteeing data accuracy and facilitating the exercise of those rights. The Controller is always required to have an appropriate lawful ground for the processing of personal data, and while explicit consent may be obtained, it is not always the sole lawful basis, especially when processing is essential for a contract. The Controller is also responsible for the overall protection and security of personal data, which includes managing and responding to any data breaches, and applying appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard it. This responsibility extends to implementing measures to minimize the processing of personal data. In addition to determining purposes and means, the Controller collects, processes, and stores personal data. The Controller may also determine its identification requirements and, in the EU, has the capability to make personal data accessible to a third-country authority, and may specifically process data indicating criminal acts when considered within their legitimate interest. Persons under the direct authority of the Controller are authorized to process personal data. The Controller is ultimately responsible and liable for any processing of personal data, including its transferring. Personal Data.

Under GDPR, GDPR The relationship between GDPR and a Processor is characterized by specific obligations, responsibilities, and liabilities directly imposed upon the Processor by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). A processor is subject to the GDPR for any given processing operation, with its role and duties explicitly defined within the regulation. This subjection is set forth in Article 3 of the GDPR, which establishes its territorial scope and applicability, even extending to non-EEA processors when they are engaged by third-country companies. In such cases, these processors must also comply with Article 28 and Chapter V of the GDPR. The GDPR directly imposes various obligations on processors, detailing their responsibilities concerning personal data protection. Processors must ensure compliance with these requirements, particularly by adhering to the instructions provided by controllers. Key responsibilities include compliance with Article 30 (records of processing activities), Article 32 (security of processing), Article 35 (data protection impact assessment), and Article 36 (prior consultation with a supervisory authority) regarding risks. Processors are also subject to GDPR obligations relating to their liability for sub-processors, as outlined in Article 28(4). Furthermore, the GDPR requires processors to implement appropriate security measures and outlines their obligations regarding data breaches and notifications, including the requirement to notify any breach to their controller. Supervisory Authorities (SAs) have the power to take action against a processor for infringing GDPR provisions. The regulation categorizes various infringements that can lead to fines for processors. Certifications under the GDPR are also issued to data processors, further emphasizing their direct accountability and the regulatory oversight they are subject to. These collective requirements define the responsibility and liability of the processor under the GDPR.<SEP>The GDPR, specifically Article 60(10), imposes duties on the processor.<SEP>The Processor is responsible for ensuring data processing adheres to GDPR provisions.<SEP>The Processor is responsible for compliance with the GDPR and must be able to demonstrate it.<SEP>The processing by a processor is governed by a contract or legal act that ensures compliance with GDPR articles. Processor.

Under GDPR, Personal Data The relation "(Personal Data, Processor)" defines the role and responsibilities of a Processor in handling Personal Data. A Processor is an entity that processes personal data strictly on behalf of and under the instructions of a Controller, operating as an agent in managing, extracting, handling, and transferring this data. Key duties include the implementation of robust security measures to protect the personal data entrusted to them. Processors are authorized to perform operations involving personal data, and individuals working under the direct authority of the Processor are also permitted to process such data. Upon the termination of processing activities, the Processor is generally obligated to either delete or return the personal data to the Controller, unless a legal requirement necessitates its storage. Furthermore, a Processor may transfer personal data, and within the context of the EU, they might even make personal data accessible to a third-country authority. Processor.

Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Data Subject is governed by a framework of rights, obligations, and legal considerations, particularly under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The Controller is authorized to process a Data Subject's personal data, frequently through contractual agreements, and is obligated to provide essential, timely, and clear information regarding these processing operations, as stipulated in GDPR Article 14(2)(b) and (f). This includes notifying Data Subjects of personal data breaches, especially if they pose a high risk to their rights and freedoms, as mentioned in Article 34 of the GDPR. Controllers are legally mandated to facilitate the easy and full exercise of data protection rights by Data Subjects, ensuring these rights can be exercised without undue hindrance and by providing a simple mechanism for their exercise. This also entails addressing requests for data erasure or objections to processing, and informing Data Subjects about changes and facilitating access to information. For specific activities like processing biometric data, the Controller must obtain explicit, informed, and freely given consent. Transparency from the Controller is also required concerning profiling and automated decision-making processes that impact the Data Subject. In all data processing activities, the Controller must carefully consider the Data Subject's interests, fundamental rights, and freedoms, acknowledging the direct impact of their actions. This assessment varies depending on the specific relationship (e.g., employer-employee, service provider-customer) and the Data Subject's particular situation. In situations involving potential surveillance, the Controller must consider the Data Subject's objection and can only proceed if there is a compelling legitimate interest or for legal claims, also assessing the Data Subject's intention to make data public. When applying the household exemption, key considerations include the Controller’s personal relationship with the Data Subject, the scale and frequency of surveillance, and any potential adverse impact it might have. There must be a balancing exercise between the competing interests of the Controller and the Data Subject's objection, with the burden of proof on the Controller. A significant imbalance, as noted in Recital 47 of the GDPR, can compromise the freedom of consent, and Controllers have been known to attempt to influence Data Subjects for more extensive data collection. It is paramount that the fundamental rights and freedoms of Data Subjects are not overridden by the Controller’s interests, even when a relevant and appropriate relationship exists (e.g., client or in the service of the controller). Controllers must provide clear information to Data Subjects to allow them to correct inaccuracies and select a method for providing information that is appropriate to the manner in which the Data Controller and Data Subject interact. The Controller is responsible for protecting the rights of Data Subjects and responding to their requests for exercising those rights. They are obligated to respond to such requests and make decisions about the processing of personal data for which they are responsible. This includes providing information and taking action on requests from the Data Subject, communicating personal data breaches, and communicating information about data processing and their rights. The Controller enables the Data Subject to monitor data processing and implements pre-contractual measures and data transfers at the Data Subject's request or in their interest. The Controller may offer goods or services to Data Subjects who are in the Union and should compensate any damage a Data Subject may suffer as a result of processing that infringes the Regulation. The Controller can also ask the Data Subject to provide additional information if there are reasonable doubts about their identity, as per Article 12(6) GDPR, and takes into account the reasonable expectations of Data Subjects based on their relationship with the controller when considering legitimate interests. Data Subject.

Under GDPR, Automated Processing Profiling is a form of automated processing, requiring it to be automated.<SEP>Automated processing can include profiling.<SEP>Automated processing, including profiling, evaluates personal aspects.<SEP>Profiling is a form of automated processing of personal data. Profiling.

[Source: EDPB_guidelines_202007_controllerprocessor_final_en] "that several different entities may act as controllers for the same processing, with each of them then being subject to the applicable data protection provisions. Correspondingly, an organisation can still be a controller even if it does not make all the decisions as to purposes and means. The criteria for joint controllership and the extent to which two or more actors jointly exercise control may take different forms, as clarified later on.13 2.1.4 “Purposes and means” 32. The fourth building block of the controller definition refers to the object of the controller’s influence, namely the “purposes and means” of the processing. It represents the substantive part of the controller concept: what a party should determine in order to qualify as controller. 33. Dictionaries define “purpose” as “an anticipated outcome that is intended or that guides your planned actions” and “means” as “how a result is obtained or an end is achieved”. 34. The GDPR establishes that data must be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a way incompatible with those purposes. Determination of the "purposes" of the processing and the "means" to achieve them is therefore particularly important. 35. Determining the purposes and the means amounts to deciding respectively the "why" and the "how" of the processing:14 given a particular processing operation, the controller is the actor who has determined why the processing is taking place (i.e., “to what end”; or “what for”) and how this objective shall be reached (i.e. which means shall be employed to attain the objective). A natural or legal person who exerts such influence over the processing of personal data, thereby participates in the determination of the purposes and means of that processing in accordance with the definition in Article 4(7) GDPR.15 36. The controller must decide on both purpose and means of the processing as described below. As a result, the controller cannot settle with only determining the purpose. It must also make decisions about the means of the processing. Conversely, the party acting as processor can never determine the purpose of the processing. 37. In practice, if a controller engages a processor to carry out the processing on its behalf, it often means that the processor shall be able to make certain decisions of its own on how to carry out the processing. The EDPB recognizes that some margin of manoeuvre may exist for the processor also to be able to make some decisions in relation to the processing. In this perspective, there is a need to provide guidance about which level of influence on the "why" and the "how" should entail the qualification of an entity as a controller and to what extent a processor may make decisions of its own. 38. When one entity clearly determines purposes and means, entrusting another entity with processing activities that amount to the execution of its detailed instructions, the situation is straightforward, and there is no doubt that the second entity should be regarded as a processor, whereas the first entity is the controller. 13 See Part I, Section 3 (“Definition of joint controllers”). 14 See also the Opinion of Advocate General Bot in Wirtschaftsakademie, C‑210/16, ECLI:EU:C:2017:796, paragraph 46. 15 Judgment in Jehovah’s witnesses, C-25/17, ECLI:EU:C:2018:551, paragraph 68. Adopted - After public consultation 15 Essential vs. non-essential means 39. The question is where to draw the line between decisions that are reserved to the controller and decisions that can be left to the discretion of the processor. Decisions on the purpose of the processing are clearly always for the controller to make. 40. As regards the determination of means, a distinction can be made between essential and non-essential means. “Essential means” are traditionally and inherently reserved to the controller. While non- essential means can also be determined by the processor, essential means are to be determined by the controller. “Essential means” are means that are closely linked to the purpose and the scope of the processing, such as the type of personal data which are processed (“which data shall be processed?”), the duration of the processing (“for how long shall they be processed?”), the categories of recipients (“who shall have access to them?”) and the categories of data subjects (“whose personal data are being processed?”). Together with the purpose of processing, the essential means are also closely linked to the question of whether the processing is lawful, necessary and proportionate. “Non-essential means” concern more practical aspects of implementation, such as the choice for a particular type of hard- or software or the detailed security measures which may be left to the processor to decide on. Example: Payroll administration Employer A hires another company to administer the payment of salaries to its employees. Employer A gives clear instructions on who to pay, what amounts, by what date, by which bank, how long the data shall be stored, what data should be disclosed to the tax authority etc. In this case, the processing of data is carried out for Company A’s purpose to pay salaries to its employees and the payroll administrator may not use the data for any purpose of its own. The way in which the payroll administrator should carry out the processing is in essence clearly and tightly defined. Nevertheless, the payroll administrator may decide on certain detailed matters around the processing such as which software to use, how to distribute access within its own organisation etc. This does not alter its role as processor as long as the administrator does not"

The controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures for ensuring that, by default, only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed. Article 26 Joint controllers 1. Where two or more controllers jointly determine the purposes and means of processing, they shall be joint controllers. The representative shall be established in one of the Member States where the data subjects, whose personal data are processed in relation to the offering of goods or services to them, or whose behaviour is monitored, are. 4. The representative shall be mandated by the controller or processor to be addressed in addition to or instead of the controller or the processor by, in particular, supervisory authorities and data subjects, on all issues related to processing, for the purposes of ensuring compliance with this Regulation. 5. The designation of a representative by the controller or processor shall be without prejudice to legal actions which could be initiated against the controller or the processor themselves. Article 28 Processor 1. Where processing is to be carried out on behalf of a controller, the controller shall use only processors providing sufficient guarantees to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures in such a manner that processing will meet the requirements of this Regulation and ensure the protection of the rights of the data subject. 2. The processor shall not engage another processor without prior specific or general written authorisation of the controller. In the case of general written authorisation, the processor shall inform the controller of any intended changes concerning the addition or replacement of other processors, thereby giving the controller the opportunity to object to such changes. 3. Processing by a processor shall be governed by a contract or other legal act under Union or Member State law, that is binding on the processor with regard to the controller and that sets out the subject-matter and duration of the processing, the nature and purpose of the processing, the type of personal data and categories of data subjects and the obligations and rights of the controller. result.reason: The activity 'capture order' is a user task that collects customer order information. This inherently involves processing personal data such as customer names, addresses, contact details, and payment information to fulfill the order. The associated data object 'ArticelID Amount Date' suggests the order record includes transaction details linked to an individual customer.

The activity 'forward order' transmits the captured order details (which contain personal data like customer information and delivery address) internally from the Sales department to the Stock department for further processing. This constitutes transmission of personal data.

The activity 'make offer and sell' involves creating a commercial offer and finalizing a sale with a customer. This process uses the customer's personal data (like contact details and order history) to prepare the offer and likely generates a sales contract or invoice containing the customer's personal information.

The activity 'send to customer' involves dispatching the ordered goods to the customer. This requires processing the customer's delivery address (a personal identifier) and likely involves generating a shipping label or notification containing this personal data. The outgoing message flow indicates communication with an external party (e.g., a delivery service), which constitutes disclosure of personal data.

The activity 'analyze the customers' involves processing customer data to understand their behavior, preferences, or characteristics. This is a form of profiling or analytics that uses personal data (such as purchase history, contact details, or demographic information) to evaluate aspects of individuals.

The activity 'determine sales and inventory' analyzes data to make business decisions. It has an incoming data association from the 'Database' data store, which, based on the context of the process, stores order and customer information. Analyzing sales data inherently involves processing personal data linked to customer transactions.

The activity 'determine result of market research' consolidates findings from various analyses, including customer analysis. Since the customer analysis ('analyze the customers') processes personal data, the results determined here are based on or include insights derived from that personal data processing.

The activity 'prepare optimization report' creates a report based on market research results. As the market research involves analyzing customer data (personal data), the resulting report is likely to contain aggregated insights, summaries, or recommendations derived from that personal data processing.

The activity 'advice for buying new assortment' generates purchasing recommendations based on the optimization report. This advice is informed by the analysis of customer data and market trends, meaning the decision-making process uses insights derived from the processing of personal data.

The activity 'advice for selling stock ware with low price' creates sales strategy recommendations. This advice is derived from the market research and optimization report, which themselves process customer data. Therefore, this activity uses insights generated from personal data processing to make commercial decisions.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation between a Controller and a Data Protection Officer (DPO) is characterized by advisory support and assigned responsibility for data protection compliance, particularly under regulations such as the GDPR. The Controller is responsible for designating a DPO to help ensure adherence to these regulations. The DPO's role encompasses providing advice and information to the Controller on various data protection matters, including breach management, data protection methodologies, and audits. This includes actively participating in Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), which the Controller undertakes with the DPO's guidance. Controllers are mandated to seek the DPO's advice when conducting a DPIA, and they must ensure the DPO's timely involvement in all data protection issues, providing necessary resources and access to facilitate their tasks. Guidelines may be developed by the Controller to specify when the DPO must be consulted. While the DPO offers crucial guidance and assists in monitoring internal compliance with regulations, the ultimate responsibility for data protection compliance remains with the Controller. [person] Employee — An Employee is defined as an individual who is employed by an organization or person, belonging to the legal entity of a data controller or processor. These individuals are typically authorized to process personal data, acting under the authority of the controller. Their access to personal data should be restricted based on their specific duties and role within the company. Employees may interact with personal data in various ways, such as manually deleting personal data after its retention period in accordance with internal procedures. They can also be subjects whose personal data, such as their name, is processed by services (e.g., a taxi service in an illustrative example). Employee actions can also lead to incidents, such as when an employee of a controller makes a mistake resulting in a data breach, or when an employee of a service provider has their electronic notebook stolen, as depicted in CASE No. 11. While employees generally operate under established authority, there can be exceptional cases where they unlawfully exceed this authority. Furthermore, employees may face pressure concerning consent for data processing.
Employees are individuals within an organization who may have concerns or complaints.
An employee is a data subject who has a relevant and appropriate relationship with a controller, often forming the basis for legitimate interest in data processing within a group of undertakings.

A Business User is a party that requests access to data, including historic and real-time data, and is subject to monitoring by data protection supervisory authorities.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[concept] Processor — A Processor, as defined by Article 4(8) of the GDPR, is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that processes personal data on behalf of a controller. This entity's primary function is to handle personal data strictly according to the controller's documented instructions, without independently determining the purposes or means of the processing activity, and thus, processors do not pursue independent objectives for data processing. A website hosting company is an example of a Processor. Processors are responsible for protecting personal data and are involved in the processing of personal data, with specific legal obligations under the GDPR, including adherence to its principles, ensuring confidentiality, and implementing robust security measures. They must provide sufficient guarantees, such as compliance with codes of conduct or certification mechanisms, and are required to operate under a binding contract or legal act with the controller. This contract typically details their responsibilities, including assisting with Data Protection by Design and by Default (DPbDD), implementing technical and organizational measures, conducting data protection impact assessments (DPIA), and providing compliance information. The processor assists the controller in carrying out a DPIA, and its roles and responsibilities in a DPIA must be contractually defined. Processors are also obligated to notify the controller of any data breach without undue delay, inform the controller of any infringing instructions, and are subject to audits. Upon termination of processing activities, they must delete or return personal data. They have specific obligations regarding personal data breaches, as mentioned in Article 33 requirements, particularly Article 33(2). Processors can also act as exporters or importers of personal data, transferring data to third countries or international organizations under specific conditions, always on behalf of the controller and must implement appropriate safeguards for data transfers. While their name may not be explicitly included in consent forms, they are listed as recipients of data. They are held liable to the controller for the performance of their sub-processors' obligations, necessitating that sub-processors also provide sufficient guarantees. Processors' activities and processing operations are assessed for GDPR compliance, and they can be the direct cause of a data breach. They may be the subject of infringement claims, addressed by the final decision of a competent supervisory authority, and can be directly and individually concerned by an EDPB binding decision, against which they may bring an action for annulment. For Processors located in the EU, they must identify an applicable ground for transfer before responding to requests from third-country authorities, as stipulated under Article 48. The designation of a representative does not affect their liability under GDPR, and they may be subject to legal actions for damages if they infringe the regulation or act outside of controller instructions. A data subject can seek judicial remedies against a processor. A Processor may be required to designate a Data Protection Officer (DPO), especially if their core activities involve key operations to achieve their goals, or if their core activities require such a designation under GDPR. When a DPO is designated, the processor is required to publish and communicate the DPO's contact details according to Article 37(7) of the GDPR. The DPO advises the processor on GDPR obligations and assists in monitoring internal compliance with the GDPR. The processor may assign the task of maintaining records of processing operations to the DPO, and the processor supports and involves the Data Protection Officer. For the cooperation procedure to apply, a Processor involved in cross-border processing must have a main or single establishment in an EU Member State. This main establishment oversees such cross-border processing. The main establishment is where its central administration is located in the Union, or where its main processing activities take place if no central administration exists in the Union. Processors are subject to the authority of a Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) or Concerned Supervisory Authority (CSA), and LSAs may interact with Processors to gather relevant information, such as investigation findings, reports, and meeting records. Processors involved in cross-border processing are subject to procedures and potential enforcement action and may be directly targeted by decisions from the LSA. As parties targeted by a draft decision, their right to be heard must comply with national law, and their rights may be affected by changes in a revised draft decision. A Processor's actions can lead to complaints and prompt action by an LSA. Processors have obligations under Article 60(10), are informed of decisions by the LSA, and are obliged to notify the LSA of any measures adopted to comply with a decision entailing corrective measures. A processor can benefit from the one-stop-shop system if established in multiple Member States, and its establishment in multiple Member States can trigger the lead authority mechanism. Guidance can be provided on their implementation of appropriate measures and demonstration of compliance.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.
[concept] Period of Storage — The period of storage refers to how long personal data will be kept by the controller.

[concept] Exercise and Enjoyment of Rights and Benefits Related to Employment — The Exercise and Enjoyment of Rights and Benefits Related to Employment, on an individual or collective basis, is a purpose for processing employees' personal data.

[organization] Supervisory Authority — A Supervisory Authority (SA) is an independent public authority established by a European Union Member State, as mandated by Article 51 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Its core responsibility is to monitor and enforce the application of data protection law, primarily the GDPR, within its specific national jurisdiction. The overarching goal of an SA is to safeguard the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals regarding the processing of their personal data and to facilitate the free flow of personal data within the European Union. SAs act as competent national bodies under Articles 55 or 56 of the GDPR, endowed with a broad spectrum of powers, including investigation, corrective actions, authorization, and advisory functions. Their decisions, which carry legal effects, are subject to judicial remedies, and they are obligated to respect the right to be heard. Supervisory Authorities are responsible for handling complaints lodged by data subjects, especially when controllers fail to address their requests. They are also the competent national authority to which personal data breaches must be notified without undue delay, typically within 72 hours unless the breach is unlikely to pose a risk to individuals. For cross-border breaches, an SA can act as the lead authority, request further details, advise on informing individuals, and order controllers to do so. They also receive information about the Data Protection Officer's (DPO) name and contact details. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to determine the nature and gravity of infringements, ensure compliance, and order appropriate measures against data controllers or processors. This includes the ability to impose effective, proportionate, and dissuasive administrative fines for GDPR infringements, considering factors such as circumstances, economic viability, and proportionality. They may hold parent companies liable and impose fines for non-compliance with Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) requirements. Additionally, a supervisory authority must be consulted if a DPIA indicates a high residual risk that cannot be mitigated, and it possesses the power to prohibit such processing operations. They can also require documentation of a DPO designation analysis and request access to records of processing operations. Beyond enforcement, Supervisory Authorities play a crucial role in GDPR accreditation and certification mechanisms. This involves approving criteria, reviewing existing certifications, accrediting certification bodies, and potentially acting as a certification body themselves. They can establish additional accreditation requirements, sometimes in cooperation with a National Accreditation Body. SAs are authorized to oversee and approve administrative arrangements for data transfers under Article 46(3)(b) GDPR, adopt standard contractual clauses for data processing matters, approve safeguards, and apply consistency mechanisms. They are also responsible for publishing lists of processing operations subject to mandatory DPIAs and for conducting prior consultations if DPIA results indicate a high risk or if existing operations have been pre-checked. While typically one lead supervisory authority exists for cross-border processing, some Member States may have more than one SA, all of whom are bound by the content of a draft decision once consensus is reached. They are also responsible for verifying compliance with data protection regulations and may require a controller to communicate a personal data breach to the data subject.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data)" signifies that the Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This involves significant authority and responsibility over the entire lifecycle of personal data, encompassing decisions related to its processing, protection, management, and transference. The Controller is explicitly responsible for establishing the retention period for documentation containing personal data and makes choices regarding its deletion or return. A core obligation of the Controller is to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and to uphold data subject rights, including guaranteeing data accuracy and facilitating the exercise of those rights. The Controller is always required to have an appropriate lawful ground for the processing of personal data, and while explicit consent may be obtained, it is not always the sole lawful basis, especially when processing is essential for a contract. The Controller is also responsible for the overall protection and security of personal data, which includes managing and responding to any data breaches, and applying appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard it. This responsibility extends to implementing measures to minimize the processing of personal data. In addition to determining purposes and means, the Controller collects, processes, and stores personal data. The Controller may also determine its identification requirements and, in the EU, has the capability to make personal data accessible to a third-country authority, and may specifically process data indicating criminal acts when considered within their legitimate interest. Persons under the direct authority of the Controller are authorized to process personal data. The Controller is ultimately responsible and liable for any processing of personal data, including its transferring. Personal Data.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation `(Controller, Processing of Personal Data)` describes the multifaceted role and responsibilities of a controller concerning the processing of personal data. A controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This determination is made independently, and the specified purposes and means must explicitly relate to the processing of personal data. In this context, the controller is actively involved in and carries out the processing of personal data. A core responsibility of the controller is to ensure and demonstrate compliance with the principles governing personal data processing, particularly those outlined in the GDPR. This includes ensuring that all processing activities have an appropriate legal basis. Furthermore, controllers are expected to innovate to maintain compliance with evolving legal parameters. The controller's responsibilities also extend to respecting the rights of data subjects. Specifically, if a data subject objects to the processing of their personal data, the controller shall cease processing unless compelling legitimate grounds for the processing can be demonstrated. Under GDPR, Data Subject The relation "(Data Subject, Personal Data)" defines a fundamental connection where personal data belongs to, pertains to, or relates to a specific data subject. A data subject is understood as a natural person, an individual, to whom the personal data refers. This relationship is central to data processing, particularly in contexts like connected vehicles, and protects the privacy and data protection rights held by data subjects over their personal information. Personal data is any information that can identify or render identifiable a particular data subject. The data subject is the source of this data, which they may provide through their actions or technical means. When personal data is collected directly from a data subject, they must be informed about its processing. Similarly, the delisting of personal data also directly involves the data subject, who may have personal data in various contexts, such as within their bank account. Data subjects possess significant rights concerning their personal data, including the ability to receive, transmit, reuse, and control it. When personal data is transferred, the interests and fundamental rights of the data subject must be considered. While data subjects have rights over their data, they also bear responsibility for securing their personal data within their own systems. A data subject should not be surprised at the purpose of processing their personal data and it should not be disclosed without their consent. The processing of personal data involves protecting the interests and rights of the data subject.<SEP>Personal data is information that relates to an identified or identifiable natural person (the data subject).<SEP>Personal data relates to a data subject who is not or no longer identifiable after anonymization. For example, the data subject may request the deletion of their personal data when: the personal data are no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they were collected or otherwise processed;91 the controller has unduly relied upon Article 6(1)(f) GDPR to process the personal data;92 the data subject has successfully invoked its right to object against a processing based on Article 6(1)(f) GDPR, in accordance with the conditions laid down in Article 21 GDPR.93 As noted above, under the GDPR, data subjects enjoy a right to object, unless there are overriding compelling legitimate grounds which take precedence over the interests and rights and freedoms of that person, which it is for the controller to demonstrate. [interface] Dedicated Dashboard — An interface provided by gatekeepers to inform end users about specific recipients of their personal data, pursuant to Article 6(10) DMA.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[organization] Gatekeeper — A Gatekeeper is an entity designated under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically pursuant to Article 3(4) or Article 3(9), indicating its provision of Core Platform Services (CPSs). Prominent examples of such organizations include Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta. These Gatekeepers control access to specific digital services and are subject to extensive legal obligations under the DMA, and in many cases, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Their role is central to the regulatory framework designed to ensure fair and contestable digital markets. Gatekeepers process the personal data of end users, often acting as controllers or processors, and are responsible for ensuring that consent obtained for data processing, particularly for online advertising and data combination, complies with both GDPR and DMA requirements. This includes the meticulous recording of consent refusals or withdrawals. They are obligated to enable continuous and real-time access to data, prevent data accumulation, and ensure robust data security. Their responsibilities extend to providing data upon request by business users or authorized third parties, free of charge, and establishing appropriate authentication and authorization procedures for such access. They must also implement security measures for personal data, comply with portability requests under DMA Article 6(9), and provide comprehensive information to data subjects. Furthermore, Gatekeepers are tasked with selecting and implementing anonymization methods for end-user data shared under Article 6(11) DMA and must implement measures to maintain service integrity and security. They also have duties concerning interoperability, including exchanging message content and personal data with other providers while ensuring security for their end users. This includes protecting metadata, verifying communication authenticity, and ensuring compliance with geographical limitations and data protection regulations for Number-Independent Interpersonal Communication Services (NIICS). Gatekeepers must design online interfaces that do not undermine user autonomy, provide reminders, and ensure fair access to datasets by altering data to mitigate identification risks and imposing contractual measures on third-party undertakings for data access and compliance monitoring. Their conduct is subject to examination for compliance with both the DMA and GDPR, and they may have a "main establishment" under the GDPR. They are also separate controllers under GDPR for their own data processing and have obligations under Article 6(4) and Article 8(1) of the DMA.

[organization] Supervisory Authority — A Supervisory Authority (SA) is an independent public authority established by a European Union Member State, as mandated by Article 51 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Its core responsibility is to monitor and enforce the application of data protection law, primarily the GDPR, within its specific national jurisdiction. The overarching goal of an SA is to safeguard the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals regarding the processing of their personal data and to facilitate the free flow of personal data within the European Union. SAs act as competent national bodies under Articles 55 or 56 of the GDPR, endowed with a broad spectrum of powers, including investigation, corrective actions, authorization, and advisory functions. Their decisions, which carry legal effects, are subject to judicial remedies, and they are obligated to respect the right to be heard. Supervisory Authorities are responsible for handling complaints lodged by data subjects, especially when controllers fail to address their requests. They are also the competent national authority to which personal data breaches must be notified without undue delay, typically within 72 hours unless the breach is unlikely to pose a risk to individuals. For cross-border breaches, an SA can act as the lead authority, request further details, advise on informing individuals, and order controllers to do so. They also receive information about the Data Protection Officer's (DPO) name and contact details. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to determine the nature and gravity of infringements, ensure compliance, and order appropriate measures against data controllers or processors. This includes the ability to impose effective, proportionate, and dissuasive administrative fines for GDPR infringements, considering factors such as circumstances, economic viability, and proportionality. They may hold parent companies liable and impose fines for non-compliance with Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) requirements. Additionally, a supervisory authority must be consulted if a DPIA indicates a high residual risk that cannot be mitigated, and it possesses the power to prohibit such processing operations. They can also require documentation of a DPO designation analysis and request access to records of processing operations. Beyond enforcement, Supervisory Authorities play a crucial role in GDPR accreditation and certification mechanisms. This involves approving criteria, reviewing existing certifications, accrediting certification bodies, and potentially acting as a certification body themselves. They can establish additional accreditation requirements, sometimes in cooperation with a National Accreditation Body. SAs are authorized to oversee and approve administrative arrangements for data transfers under Article 46(3)(b) GDPR, adopt standard contractual clauses for data processing matters, approve safeguards, and apply consistency mechanisms. They are also responsible for publishing lists of processing operations subject to mandatory DPIAs and for conducting prior consultations if DPIA results indicate a high risk or if existing operations have been pre-checked. While typically one lead supervisory authority exists for cross-border processing, some Member States may have more than one SA, all of whom are bound by the content of a draft decision once consensus is reached. They are also responsible for verifying compliance with data protection regulations and may require a controller to communicate a personal data breach to the data subject.

[organization] Supervisory Authority — A Supervisory Authority (SA) is an independent public authority established by a European Union Member State, as mandated by Article 51 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Its core responsibility is to monitor and enforce the application of data protection law, primarily the GDPR, within its specific national jurisdiction. The overarching goal of an SA is to safeguard the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals regarding the processing of their personal data and to facilitate the free flow of personal data within the European Union. SAs act as competent national bodies under Articles 55 or 56 of the GDPR, endowed with a broad spectrum of powers, including investigation, corrective actions, authorization, and advisory functions. Their decisions, which carry legal effects, are subject to judicial remedies, and they are obligated to respect the right to be heard. Supervisory Authorities are responsible for handling complaints lodged by data subjects, especially when controllers fail to address their requests. They are also the competent national authority to which personal data breaches must be notified without undue delay, typically within 72 hours unless the breach is unlikely to pose a risk to individuals. For cross-border breaches, an SA can act as the lead authority, request further details, advise on informing individuals, and order controllers to do so. They also receive information about the Data Protection Officer's (DPO) name and contact details. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to determine the nature and gravity of infringements, ensure compliance, and order appropriate measures against data controllers or processors. This includes the ability to impose effective, proportionate, and dissuasive administrative fines for GDPR infringements, considering factors such as circumstances, economic viability, and proportionality. They may hold parent companies liable and impose fines for non-compliance with Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) requirements. Additionally, a supervisory authority must be consulted if a DPIA indicates a high residual risk that cannot be mitigated, and it possesses the power to prohibit such processing operations. They can also require documentation of a DPO designation analysis and request access to records of processing operations. Beyond enforcement, Supervisory Authorities play a crucial role in GDPR accreditation and certification mechanisms. This involves approving criteria, reviewing existing certifications, accrediting certification bodies, and potentially acting as a certification body themselves. They can establish additional accreditation requirements, sometimes in cooperation with a National Accreditation Body. SAs are authorized to oversee and approve administrative arrangements for data transfers under Article 46(3)(b) GDPR, adopt standard contractual clauses for data processing matters, approve safeguards, and apply consistency mechanisms. They are also responsible for publishing lists of processing operations subject to mandatory DPIAs and for conducting prior consultations if DPIA results indicate a high risk or if existing operations have been pre-checked. While typically one lead supervisory authority exists for cross-border processing, some Member States may have more than one SA, all of whom are bound by the content of a draft decision once consensus is reached. They are also responsible for verifying compliance with data protection regulations and may require a controller to communicate a personal data breach to the data subject.

[organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

On the other hand, it also means that individuals do not have to be actually 4 affected: the likelihood of a substantial effect is sufficient to bring the processing within the definition of ‘cross-border processing’. The fact that a data processing operation may involve the processing of a number – even a large number – of individuals’ personal data, in a number of Member States, does not necessarily mean that the processing has, or is likely to have, a substantial effect. Processing that does not have a substantial effect does not constitute cross-border processing for the purposes of the second part of the definition, regardless of how many individuals it affects. Supervisory Authorities will interpret ‘substantially affects’ on a case by case basis. We will take into account the context of the processing, the type of data, the purpose of the processing and factors such as whether the processing: o causes, or is likely to cause, damage, loss or distress to individuals; o has, or is likely to have, an actual effect in terms of limiting rights or denying an opportunity; o affects, or is likely to affect individuals’ health, well-being or peace of mind; o affects, or is likely to affect, individuals’ financial or economic status or circumstances; o leaves individuals open to discrimination or unfair treatment; o involves the analysis of the special categories of personal or other intrusive data, particularly the personal data of children; o causes, or is likely to cause individuals to change their behaviour in a significant way; o has unlikely, unanticipated or unwanted consequences for individuals; o creates embarrassment or other negative outcomes, including reputational damage; or o involves the processing of a wide range of personal data. Producers are key enablers for DPbDD, providing solutions to controllers that embed data protection.

A business user is a commercial entity or individual that utilizes gatekeeper products or services and may request access to end-user data.
An entity that requests access to end-user data from a gatekeeper under Article 6(10) DMA, with obligations under GDPR regarding data minimisation.
