Under GDPR, Electronic Means Electronic means are used with a standardised format for information exchange. Standardised Format.
Under GDPR, Continuous and Real-time Data Access Continuous and real-time data access addresses data accumulation by gatekeepers. Data Accumulation.

Under GDPR, Personal Data The relation "(Personal Data, Processor)" defines the role and responsibilities of a Processor in handling Personal Data. A Processor is an entity that processes personal data strictly on behalf of and under the instructions of a Controller, operating as an agent in managing, extracting, handling, and transferring this data. Key duties include the implementation of robust security measures to protect the personal data entrusted to them. Processors are authorized to perform operations involving personal data, and individuals working under the direct authority of the Processor are also permitted to process such data. Upon the termination of processing activities, the Processor is generally obligated to either delete or return the personal data to the Controller, unless a legal requirement necessitates its storage. Furthermore, a Processor may transfer personal data, and within the context of the EU, they might even make personal data accessible to a third-country authority. Processor.
Under GDPR, Other Providers Personal data is exchanged between gatekeepers and other providers to enable interoperability. Personal Data.

[method] Processing Operations — Processing Operations refer to any activities or a set of operations performed on data, particularly personal data, by institutions or data brokers. These operations encompass a vast array of actions, including the collection, storage, use, disclosure, further processing, the management of data subject rights, and the handling and manipulation of data. They can also involve linking data, forming different conducts, combining data, or cross-using data. Per Article 4(2) of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), these operations are defined as any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or on sets of personal data. These operations are composed of various components, such as data, systems, and processes, all of which should adhere to specific criteria. Activities often include the selection of targeting criteria and the display of advertisements to a specific target audience. Processing operations are a primary object of certification under the GDPR, potentially encompassing governance processes and leading to the creation of a product or service. Both data controllers and processors are obligated to demonstrate compliance when executing these operations. Actions performed on personal data should be limited to what is necessary, contributing to a defined processing purpose, and designed to process only the minimum amount of necessary data. Processing operations are actions carried out by a data controller using collected data, requiring specific information provisions and legal bases. They may also benefit from special regimes under GDPR. Examples include the collection, storage, use, or deletion of data. Some operations may involve the use of CCTV and are subject to the applicability of the household exemption. Records must be maintained for these data handling activities. Furthermore, processing operations that involve personal data may require a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) under GDPR if they pose a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. When a DPIA is required, these activities necessitate a systematic description, an assessment of necessity, proportionality, and risks, and the implementation of measures to address those risks.
Processing Operations refer to any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction.
Processing Operations involve any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, storage, etc.

[Source: edpb_guidelines_201904_dataprotection_by_design_and_by_default_v2.0_en] "Adopted 5 1 SCOPE 1. The Guidelines focus on controllers’ implementation of DPbDD based on the obligation in Article 25 of the GDPR.1 Other actors, such as processors and producers of products, services and applications (henceforth “producers”), who are not directly addressed in Article 25, may also find these Guidelines useful in creating GDPR compliant products and services that enable controllers to fulfil their data protection obligations.2 Recital 78 of the GDPR adds that DPbDD should be taken into consideration in the context of public tenders. Despite all controllers having the duty to integrate DPbDD into their processing activities, this provision fosters the adoption of the data protection principles, where public administrations should lead by example. The controller is responsible for the fulfilment of the DPbDD obligations for the processing carried out by their processors and sub-processors, they should therefore take this into account when contracting with these parties. 2. The requirement described in Article 25 is for controllers to have data protection designed into the processing of personal data and as a default setting and this applies throughout the processing lifecycle. DPbDD is also a requirement for processing systems pre-existing before the GDPR entered into force. Controllers must have the processing consistently updated in line with the GDPR. For more information on how to maintain an existing system in line with DPbDD, see subchapter 2.1.4 of these Guidelines. The core of the provision is to ensure appropriate and effective data protection both by design and by default, which means that controllers should be able to demonstrate that they have the appropriate measures and safeguards in the processing to ensure that the data protection principles and the rights and freedoms of data subjects are effective. 3. Chapter 2 of the Guidelines focuses on an interpretation of the requirements set forth by Article 25 and explores the legal obligations introduced by the provision. Examples on how to apply DPbDD in the context of specific data protection principles are provided in Chapter 3. 4. The Guidelines address the possibility to establish a certification mechanism to demonstrate compliance with Article 25 in Chapter 4, as well as how the Article may be enforced by supervisory authorities in Chapter 5. Finally, the Guidelines provide stakeholders with further recommendations on how to successfully implement DPbDD. The EDPB recognizes the challenges for small and medium enterprises (henceforth “SMEs”) to fully comply with the obligations of DPbDD, and provides additional recommendations specifically to SMEs in Chapter 6. 2 ANALYSIS OF ARTICLE 25(1) AND (2) DATA PROTECTION BY DESIGN AND BY DEFAULT 5. The aim of this Chapter is to explore and provide guidance on the requirements to data protection by design in Article 25(1) and to data protection by default in Article 25(2) respectively. Data protection 1 The interpretations provided herein equally apply to Article 20 of Directive (EU) 2016/680, and Article 27 of Regulation 2018/1725. 2 Recital 78 GDPR clearly states this need: “When developing, designing, selecting and using applications, services and products that are based on the processing of personal data or process personal data to fulfil their task, producers of the products, services and applications should be encouraged to take into account the right to data protection when developing and designing such products, services and applications and, with due regard to the “state of the art”, to make sure that controllers and processors are able to fulfil their data protection obligations”. Adopted 6 by design and data protection by default are complementary concepts, which mutually reinforce each other. Data subjects will benefit more from data protection by default if data protection by design is concurrently implemented – and vice versa. 6. DPbDD is a requirement for all controllers, including small businesses and multinational companies alike. That being the case, the complexity of implementing DPbDD may vary based on the individual processing operation. Regardless of the size however, in all cases, positive benefits for controller and data subject can be achieved by implementing DPbDD. 2.1 Article 25(1): Data protection by design 2.1.1 Controller’s obligation to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures and necessary safeguards into the processing 7. In line with Article 25(1) the controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures which are designed to implement the data protection principles and to integrate the necessary safeguards into the processing in order to meet the requirements and protect the rights and freedoms of data subjects. Both appropriate measures and necessary safeguards are meant to serve the same purpose of protecting the rights of data subjects and ensuring that the protection of their personal data is built into the processing. 8. Technical and organizational measures and necessary safeguards can be understood in a broad sense as any method or means that a controller may employ in the processing. Being appropriate means that the measures and necessary safeguards should be suited to achieve the intended purpose, i.e. they must implement the data protection principles effectively3. The requirement to appropriateness is thus closely related to the requirement of effectiveness. 9. A technical or organisational measure and safeguard can be anything from the use of advanced technical solutions to the basic training of personnel. Examples that may be suitable, depending on the context and risks associated with the processing in question, includes pseudonymization of personal data4; storing personal data available in a structured, commonly machine readable format; enabling data subjects to intervene in the processing; providing information about the storage of personal data; having malware detection systems; training employees about basic “cyber hygiene”;"

[Source: Guidelines_on_Personal_data_breach_notification_under_Regulation_2016679] "Article 34(3) states three conditions that, if met, do not require notification to individuals in the event of a breach. These are:  The controller has applied appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect personal data prior to the breach, in particular those measures that render personal data unintelligible to any person who is not authorised to access it. This could, for example, include protecting personal data with state-of-the-art encryption, or by tokenization.  Immediately following a breach, the controller has taken steps to ensure that the high risk posed to individuals’ rights and freedoms is no longer likely to materialise. For example, depending on the circumstances of the case, the controller may have immediately identified and taken action against the individual who has accessed personal data before they were able to do anything with it. Due regard still needs to be given to the possible consequences of any breach of confidentiality, again, depending on the nature of the data concerned.  It would involve disproportionate effort37 to contact individuals, perhaps where their contact details have been lost as a result of the breach or are not known in the first place. For example, the warehouse of a statistical office has flooded and the documents containing personal data were stored only in paper form. Instead, the controller must make a public communication or take a similar measure, whereby the individuals are informed in an equally effective manner. In the case of disproportionate effort, technical arrangements could also be envisaged to make information about the breach available on demand, which could prove useful to those individuals who may be affected by a breach, but the controller cannot otherwise contact. In accordance with the accountability principle controllers should be able to demonstrate to the supervisory authority that they meet one or more of these conditions 38. It should be borne in mind that while notification may initially not be required if there is no risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, this may change over time and the risk would have to be re-evaluated. If a controller decides not to communicate a breach to the individual, Article 34(4) explains that the supervisory authority can require it to do so, if it considers the breach is likely to result in a high risk to individuals. Alternatively, it may consider that the conditions in Article 34(3) have been met in which case notification to individuals is not required. If the supervisory authority determines that the decision not to notify data subjects is not well founded, it may consider employing its available powers and sanctions. IV. Assessing risk and high risk A. Risk as a trigger for notification 37 See WP29 Guidelines on transparency, which will consider the issue of disproportionate effort, available at http://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/just/document.cfm?doc_id=48850 38 See Article 5(2) 23 Although the GDPR introduces the obligation to notify a breach, it is not a requirement to do so in all circumstances:  Notification to the competent supervisory authority is required unless a breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals.  Communication of a breach to the individual is only triggered where it is likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms. This means that immediately upon becoming aware of a breach, it is vitally important that the controller should not only seek to contain the incident but it should also assess the risk that could result from it. There are two important reasons for this: firstly, knowing the likelihood and the potential severity of the impact on the individual will help the controller to take effective steps to contain and address the breach; secondly, it will help it to determine whether notification is required to the supervisory authority and, if necessary, to the individuals concerned. As explained above, notification of a breach is required unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, and the key trigger requiring communication of a breach to data subjects is where it is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. This risk exists when the breach may lead to physical, material or non-material damage for the individuals whose data have been breached. Examples of such damage are discrimination, identity theft or fraud, financial loss and damage to reputation. When the breach involves personal data that reveals racial or ethnic origin, political opinion, religion or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership, or includes genetic data, data concerning health or data concerning sex life, or criminal convictions and offences or related security measures, such damage should be considered likely to occur39. B. Factors to consider when assessing risk Recitals 75 and 76 of the GDPR suggest that generally when assessing risk, consideration should be given to both the likelihood and severity of the risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects. It further states that risk should be evaluated on the basis of an objective assessment. It should be noted that assessing the risk to people’s rights and freedoms as a result of a breach has a different focus to the risk considered in a DPIA)40. The DPIA considers both the risks of the data processing being carried out as planned, and the risks in case of a breach. When considering a potential breach, it looks in general terms at the likelihood of this occurring, and the damage to the data subject that might ensue; in other words, it is an assessment of a hypothetical event. [method] Processing Operations — Processing Operations refer to any activities or a set of operations performed on data, particularly personal data, by institutions or data brokers. They can also involve linking data, forming different conducts, combining data, or cross-using data. Activities often include the selection of targeting criteria and the display of advertisements to a specific target audience. [method] Processing Operations — Processing Operations refer to any activities or a set of operations performed on data, particularly personal data, by institutions or data brokers. These operations encompass a vast array of actions, including the collection, storage, use, disclosure, further processing, the management of data subject rights, and the handling and manipulation of data. They can also involve linking data, forming different conducts, combining data, or cross-using data. Per Article 4(2) of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), these operations are defined as any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or on sets of personal data. These operations are composed of various components, such as data, systems, and processes, all of which should adhere to specific criteria. Activities often include the selection of targeting criteria and the display of advertisements to a specific target audience. Processing operations are a primary object of certification under the GDPR, potentially encompassing governance processes and leading to the creation of a product or service. Both data controllers and processors are obligated to demonstrate compliance when executing these operations. Actions performed on personal data should be limited to what is necessary, contributing to a defined processing purpose, and designed to process only the minimum amount of necessary data. Processing operations are actions carried out by a data controller using collected data, requiring specific information provisions and legal bases. They may also benefit from special regimes under GDPR. Examples include the collection, storage, use, or deletion of data. Some operations may involve the use of CCTV and are subject to the applicability of the household exemption. Records must be maintained for these data handling activities. Furthermore, processing operations that involve personal data may require a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) under GDPR if they pose a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. [method] Data Protection Impact Assessment — A Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) is a fundamental and mandatory process, primarily introduced by Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR), designed to systematically identify, evaluate, and mitigate risks to individuals' rights and freedoms stemming from the processing of personal data. This assessment is particularly imperative for data processing activities that are likely to pose a high risk, especially when new technologies or high-risk operations are involved. The DPIA is a critical data protection requirement, evaluating the impact of processing activities on data protection and ensuring compliance by comprehensively understanding and ameliorating potential adverse effects on data subjects' rights and freedoms before any project or plan involving personal data processing is put into motion. Article 35 of the GDPR explicitly mandates the completion of a DPIA for systematic, large-scale monitoring of publicly accessible areas (e.g., video surveillance systems) and for other processing activities likely to result in a high risk to data subjects, such as contact tracing applications. Article 35(7) of the GDPR specifies the minimal content required for a DPIA, and Article 35(7)(d) notes its consideration when drafting certification criteria. The process involves systematically identifying, understanding, and mapping out personal data processing to determine potential high risks, including considerations for international data transfers. Controllers are required to perform a DPIA prior to implementation if high risks are identified in the context of personal data processing. The DPIA is an assessment carried out by the data controller prior to processing to assess the likelihood and severity of high risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects. It includes measures, safeguards, and mechanisms for mitigating risk and ensuring data protection. Data Protection Officers (DPOs) play a crucial role in the DPIA process, advising controllers or processors to carry one out, facilitating these accountability tools to help with compliance, and monitoring their performance. The DPIA also plays a role in informing initial breach risk assessments. While the process of conducting a DPIA is required, the summary itself must be carried out and made public to assess and mitigate privacy risks. It also serves as a process for evaluating the necessity and proportionality of processing operations, as per Article 35(4).

If the data used in an automated decision-making or profiling process is inaccurate, any resultant decision or profile will be flawed. Decisions may be made on the basis of outdated data or the incorrect interpretation of external data. Inaccuracies may lead to inappropriate predictions or statements about, for example, someone’s health, credit or insurance risk. Even if raw data is recorded accurately, the dataset may not be fully representative or the analytics may contain hidden bias. Controllers need to introduce robust measures to verify and ensure on an ongoing basis that data re- used or obtained indirectly is accurate and up to date. This reinforces the importance of providing clear information about the personal data being processed, so that the data subject can correct any inaccuracies and improve the quality of the data. 5. Article 5(1) (e) Storage limitation Machine-learning algorithms are designed to process large volumes of information and build correlations that allow organisations to build up very comprehensive, intimate profiles of individuals. Whilst there can be advantages to retaining data in the case of profiling, since there will be more data for the algorithm to learn from, controllers must comply with the data minimisation principle when they collect personal data and ensure that they retain those personal data for no longer than is necessary for and proportionate to the purposes for which the personal data are processed The controller’s retention policy should take into account the individuals’ rights and freedoms in line with the requirements of Article 5(1)(e). The controller should also make sure that the data remains updated throughout the retention period to reduce the risk of inaccuracies.11 B. result.reason: The task 'Check whether invoice amount has been received' involves verifying payment status linked to a specific customer. This requires accessing and processing the customer's financial transaction data (invoice, payment history), which is personal data.

The send task 'Notify legal department' transmits information about a customer's unpaid invoice to the legal department. This involves disclosing personal data (customer identity, financial details) to another internal department for further action.
The task 'Verification of the invoice amount' involves reviewing the customer's invoice and payment details received from After Sales. This constitutes processing of personal financial data.

The task 'SCHUFA check' involves querying a credit bureau (SCHUFA) to obtain a credit report or scoring information about an individual. This is a clear processing of personal data, specifically financial and creditworthiness data, which is highly sensitive.
The task 'Review of payment arrears' involves analyzing a customer's history of late or missing payments. This processes personal financial data and behavioral data related to the individual.

The task 'File police report' involves submitting a formal report to law enforcement authorities, which necessarily includes disclosing personal data about the alleged debtor (name, address, details of the alleged offence/fraud). This is a transmission of personal data for legal claims.

The task 'Issue summary proceedings' involves initiating legal proceedings against a customer. This requires processing and submitting personal data (identity, address, financial details) to a court, which is a disclosure for legal claims.

The task 'Close the case' involves finalizing a legal case concerning a specific individual. This decision and the associated record-keeping process personal data related to the customer and the dispute.

The task 'Create customer letter regarding blocking' involves generating a communication to a specific customer about account blocking or legal consequences. This uses the customer's personal data (name, address) to address the letter and discusses their personal financial situation.

The task 'Determination of further procedure' (in the customer pool) involves the customer making a decision based on personal information received from the Legal Department (e.g., a blocking notice). The customer processes this personal data concerning themselves to decide on next steps.

[content] Revised Draft Decision — A Revised Draft Decision is a formal, updated version of an initial draft decision, presented as a distinct legal instrument. The LSA (Legislation and Standards Authority) is obligated to submit a Revised Draft Decision if it intends to incorporate a relevant and reasoned objection, or if it has modified its initial decision based on informal exchanges or other considerations. This document is designed to reflect revisions made after considering objections and feedback, aiming to find consensus on previously disputed issues. This revised version is subject to a shorter assessment period compared to the initial draft. If no further objections are raised against it, the Revised Draft Decision can become legally binding. Under GDPR, 72-Hour Notification Deadline The controller is generally required to notify within 72 hours, but delays are permissible with reasons. Controller.

Under GDPR, Controller The controller wishes to market products and services through direct marketing.<SEP>Direct marketing purposes may be regarded as a legitimate interest of the controller. Direct Marketing.

Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Supervisory Authority is established primarily by data protection regulations, such as the GDPR, and focuses on compliance, breach management, and accountability. A central obligation of the Controller is to notify the Supervisory Authority of personal data breaches, typically within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach, especially if it poses a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, as per Article 33(1) and Article 27(5) GDPR. The Controller is responsible for determining if a breach is notifiable and must ensure the relevant Supervisory Authority is informed, potentially proactively notifying them of infringements or seeking advice. They must also inform the Supervisory Authority about data transfers, documenting assessments and safeguards. Controllers without an EU establishment are required to engage with local supervisory authorities in every Member State where they operate. Furthermore, the Controller must consult the Supervisory Authority if a high risk identified in a Data Protection Impact Assessment cannot be mitigated by reasonable means before processing. Controllers are also obligated to cooperate with and make records available to the Supervisory Authority upon request, demonstrating accountability and compliance. The Supervisory Authority plays a significant role in overseeing the Controller's data protection practices. It can advise Controllers on how to inform individuals about breaches and may even order them to do so, particularly for high-risk breaches. The Supervisory Authority verifies the Controller's compliance, handles complaints, and seeks amicable settlements regarding possible infringements. It possesses powers to require the Controller to provide information, carry out investigations, notify infringements, and obtain access to data and premises. The Supervisory Authority can issue warnings and reprimands, order compliance, and impose sanctions, including administrative fines under Article 83 GDPR, especially in cases of unjustified breaches. The level of the Controller's cooperation is considered by the Supervisory Authority when assessing mitigation efforts. The Supervisory Authority also promotes awareness among Controllers regarding their obligations under pertinent regulations and informs Controllers when a received complaint is dismissed or rejected. Supervisory Authority.
Under GDPR, Controller Codes of conduct recommend out-of-court proceedings for resolving disputes between controllers and data subjects. Out-Of-Court Proceedings.

Under GDPR, Controller The controller should differentiate between access privileges of authorized personnel and limit access to data for employees.<SEP>Employees are generally not considered controllers but act under the authority of the controller.<SEP>An employee under the direct authority of the controller can process personal data. Employee.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation between a Controller and a Data Protection Officer (DPO) is characterized by advisory support and assigned responsibility for data protection compliance, particularly under regulations such as the GDPR. The Controller is responsible for designating a DPO to help ensure adherence to these regulations. The DPO's role encompasses providing advice and information to the Controller on various data protection matters, including breach management, data protection methodologies, and audits. This includes actively participating in Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), which the Controller undertakes with the DPO's guidance. Controllers are mandated to seek the DPO's advice when conducting a DPIA, and they must ensure the DPO's timely involvement in all data protection issues, providing necessary resources and access to facilitate their tasks. Guidelines may be developed by the Controller to specify when the DPO must be consulted. While the DPO offers crucial guidance and assists in monitoring internal compliance with regulations, the ultimate responsibility for data protection compliance remains with the Controller. The DPO may be an employee of the Controller or an external party, but they must perform their duties independently. The Controller is obligated to record the name and contact details of the DPO, and these details must be included in the record of processing activities. Furthermore, in the event of a data breach, the Controller must communicate the DPO's name and contact details as a contact point for breach information as part of the notification process. Data Protection Officer.
Under GDPR, Complainant The complainant makes a claim against the controller, alleging an infringement.<SEP>The controller and complainant interact regarding the cross-border processing. Controller.

Under GDPR, Controller A controller determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.<SEP>The controller decides on the purposes and means of processing personal data.<SEP>A controller is involved in the same processing concerning data.<SEP>Any Controller involved in Processing shall be liable for damage caused by Processing which infringes this Regulation. Processing.

Under GDPR, Controller The processing of personal data to fulfill a legal obligation finds its legal basis in Article 6(1)(c) GDPR.<SEP>The controller is subject to legal obligations regarding personal data processing. Legal Obligation.
Under GDPR, Draft Decision The GDPR does not define the concept of the draft decision.<SEP>The GDPR states that a draft decision is to be submitted to CSAs for their opinion. GDPR.
Under GDPR, End User End users processing ported data for non-personal activities are bound by the GDPR.<SEP>End users' consent for data processing is required under GDPR. GDPR.
Under GDPR, End User Account Settings Gatekeepers prompt end users and record their preferences via signed-in end users’ account settings. Gatekeeper.
Under GDPR, Government Infringement Reports are transmitted to the Government. Infringement Reports.
Under GDPR, Controller or Processor The supervisory authority notifies its final decision to the controller or the processor. Supervisory Authority.
Under GDPR, Controller A plaintiff has the choice to bring an action against a Controller before courts where the Controller has an establishment or the Data Subject resides. National Court.

Under GDPR, Legal Person A legal person cannot challenge the validity of an EDPB binding decision in national courts if they failed to bring an action for annulment before the CJEU within the prescribed period.<SEP>A National Court may not refer a question on the validity of a Board decision at the request of a Legal Person if they had the opportunity to bring an action for annulment and did not. National Court.
Under GDPR, Judicial Authorities The Supervisory Authority can bring infringements to the attention of judicial authorities and commence legal proceedings. Supervisory Authority.
Under GDPR, Data Transfers Data transfers can be necessary in relation to a legal claim, including judicial, administrative, or out-of-court procedures. Legal Claim.
Under GDPR, Controller Controllers should verify the identity of a data subject requests access, particularly in context of online services. Online Services.
Under GDPR, Data Subject Personal data, though restricted, may be required by the data subject for legal claims. Legal Claims.

Under GDPR, Adequate Level of Protection The examination procedure should be used by the Commission for the adoption of implementing acts on the adequate level of protection afforded by a third country or international organisation.<SEP>The Commission decides whether an adequate level of protection is ensured. Commission.
Under GDPR, Commission's Initiative The EDPB replied to the Commission's Initiative for a voluntary business pledge. EDPB.

Under GDPR, GDPR The Supervisory Authority determines its approach to certification to pursue the intent of GDPR, considering its tasks and powers under GDPR articles, and monitors and enforces the application of the regulation.<SEP>The supervisory authority's accreditation function is a task pursuant to GDPR Articles 57(1)(q) and 58(3)(e).<SEP>The GDPR empowers the Supervisory Authority to perform accreditation and certification functions.<SEP>Supervisory Authorities are tasked with enforcing the GDPR.<SEP>The supervisory authority oversees the application of the GDPR and receives DPIA reports under specific conditions. Supervisory Authority.

Under GDPR, Controller The final decision of the competent supervisory authority will be addressed to the controller.<SEP>The controller has duties to ensure processing activities comply with the final decision, as per Article 60(10) GDPR.<SEP>The Controller shall take necessary measures to ensure compliance with the Final Decision. Final Decision.
Under GDPR, Controller The Controller ascertains the compatibility of Further Processing with the initial collection purpose. Further Processing.

Under GDPR, Controller A controller makes decisions on the purposes and means of processing activities.<SEP>The controller should maintain records of processing activities under its responsibility. Processing Activities.
Under GDPR, Delivery Service Identification details may be cross-used by a delivery service without consent, under Article 5(2), point (c) DMA. Personal Data.

Under GDPR, Data Protection Officer GDPR requires the designation of a data protection officer if processing involves regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects.<SEP>The GDPR specifies mandatory tasks for the Data Protection Officer.<SEP>The GDPR provides the legal framework in which Data Protection Officers operate and facilitates compliance.<SEP>The Data Protection Officer has duties defined by the GDPR, including monitoring compliance.<SEP>The DPO's role, resources, and independence are defined by the GDPR.<SEP>The Data Protection Officer's role is defined by the GDPR.<SEP>The DPO functions and requirements are governed by the GDPR. GDPR.
Under GDPR, Business User Business users authorizing third parties to process personal data must ensure compliance with GDPR, including contract requirements under Article 28 GDPR. GDPR.
Under GDPR, GDPR Processing activities must comply with the GDPR. Processing.

[person] Employee — An Employee is defined as an individual who is employed by an organization or person, belonging to the legal entity of a data controller or processor. These individuals are typically authorized to process personal data, acting under the authority of the controller. Their access to personal data should be restricted based on their specific duties and role within the company. Employees may interact with personal data in various ways, such as manually deleting personal data after its retention period in accordance with internal procedures. They can also be subjects whose personal data, such as their name, is processed by services (e.g., a taxi service in an illustrative example). Employee actions can also lead to incidents, such as when an employee of a controller makes a mistake resulting in a data breach, or when an employee of a service provider has their electronic notebook stolen, as depicted in CASE No. 11. While employees generally operate under established authority, there can be exceptional cases where they unlawfully exceed this authority. Furthermore, employees may face pressure concerning consent for data processing.
Employees are individuals within an organization who may have concerns or complaints.
An employee is a data subject who has a relevant and appropriate relationship with a controller, often forming the basis for legitimate interest in data processing within a group of undertakings.
[concept] Recruitment Purposes — Recruitment purposes involve processing personal data for hiring employees.
[artifact] Applications — Applications are products or services that process personal data.
[content] Judgment of the Court of Justice of 12 January 2023 — This refers to a legal judgment, specifically the case RW v Österreichische Post AG, C-154/21, ECLI:EU:C:2023:3, paragraph 46.

[method] Effectiveness Testing Process — An Effectiveness Testing Process involves regularly testing, assessing, and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organizational measures for ensuring security.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.
[data] Employees' Personal Data — Employees' personal data refers to information about employees that is subject to specific rules and safeguards regarding its processing in the employment context.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

[person] Data Subject — A Data Subject is defined as an identified or identifiable natural person to whom personal data relates and whose personal data undergoes processing, encompassing operations such as collection, holding, storing, or other manipulations, including biometric and location data. This individual can be identified, directly or indirectly, by reference to an identifier or specific factors of their identity. End users are often considered Data Subjects, and their vital interests may necessitate data processing. Even if a Data Subject's data has been anonymized such that they are no longer identifiable, they are still considered a Data Subject. Their behavior or identity may be monitored, and any personal data relating to them requires either consent or another legitimate basis for lawful processing. Data processing concerning Data Subjects is subject to regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly if goods or services are offered to them within the European Union. Under Article 6 of the GDPR, explicit consent is often required for processing, including profiling and automated decision-making. This consent must be demonstrably obtained through deliberate, informed action. Data Subjects possess fundamental rights to safeguard their human dignity and legitimate interests, including rights to access, rectification, erasure, objection to processing, and data portability. They also have the right to be informed about and challenge automated decision-making and, in some contexts, request delisting from search engines. They can monitor data processing, should be offered format choices for reusing their data, and can transmit their personal data from one controller to another, taking responsibility for securing it in their own system. Data controllers are obligated to provide Data Subjects with specific information, including the identity of their representative, and to communicate efficiently. Their views should be sought during a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) where appropriate. When biometric data is processed, an alternative solution must be offered, and Data Subjects should be consulted during the drafting of codes of conduct when feasible. A Data Subject is also an individual whose personal data may be affected by a data breach, putting their rights and freedoms at risk. In such an event, the controller must inform them, especially if there is a likely high risk of adverse effects or potential damage; communication of the breach is obligatory if their personal data has been compromised and depending on the severity of the consequences. Their vital interests, reasonable expectations (influenced by factors like age, public figure status, and professional position), and personal data require consistent protection, necessitating that their rights and freedoms be safeguarded. They may contact the Data Protection Officer, lodge complaints with supervisory authorities, and seek judicial remedy. A Data Subject has the right to compensation for material or non-material damage suffered due to an infringement of the regulation. Their identity may be scrutinized by a controller if doubts arise.

Where the processing for a purpose other than that for which the personal data have been collected is not based on the data subject's consent or on a Union or Member State law which constitutes a necessary and proportionate measure in a democratic society to safeguard the objectives referred to in Article 23(1), the controller shall, in order to ascertain whether processing for another purpose is compatible with the purpose for which the personal data are initially collected, take into account, inter alia: (a) any link between the purposes for which the personal data have been collected and the purposes of the intended further processing; (b) the context in which the personal data have been collected, in particular regarding the relationship between data subjects and the controller; (c) the nature of the personal data, in particular whether special categories of personal data are processed, pursuant to Article 9, or whether personal data related to criminal convictions and offences are processed, pursuant to Article 10; (d) the possible consequences of the intended further processing for data subjects; (e) the existence of appropriate safeguards, which may include encryption or pseudonymisation. Article 7 Conditions for consent 1. Where processing is based on consent, the controller shall be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented to processing of his or her personal data. 2. If the data subject's consent is given in the context of a written declaration which also concerns other matters, the request for consent shall be presented in a manner which is clearly distinguishable from the other matters, in an intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language. Any part of such a declaration which constitutes an infringement of this Regulation shall not be binding. 3. The data subject shall have the right to withdraw his or her consent at any time. The withdrawal of consent shall not affect the lawfulness of processing based on consent before its withdrawal. Prior to giving consent, the data subject shall be informed thereof. It shall be as easy to withdraw as to give consent. 4. When assessing whether consent is freely given, utmost account shall be taken of whether, inter alia, the performance of a contract, including the provision of a service, is conditional on consent to the processing of personal data that is not necessary for the performance of that contract. Article 8 Conditions applicable to child's consent in relation to information society services 1. Where point (a) of Article 6(1) applies, in relation to the offer of information society services directly to a child, the processing of the personal data of a child shall be lawful where the child is at least 16 years old. Where the child is below the age of 16 years, such processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility over the child. Member States may provide by law for a lower age for those purposes provided that such lower age is not below 13 years. 4.5.2016 L 119/37 Official Journal of the European Union EN 2. The controller shall make reasonable efforts to verify in such cases that consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility over the child, taking into consideration available technology. 3. Paragraph 1 shall not affect the general contract law of Member States such as the rules on the validity, formation or effect of a contract in relation to a child. [organization] Hospital — A Hospital is a healthcare institution responsible for collecting and managing significant quantities of sensitive patient data, often utilizing an electronic health record system. This organization has been noted for experiencing a personal data breach where staff members could view unauthorized patient health files due to issues with authorization monitoring, specifically concerning staff retaining access to patient files after transferring departments; an internal investigation was conducted to address this. The sensitive nature of the data processed means that data breaches at a Hospital are highly impactful, and the unavailability of critical medical data can pose a substantial risk to individuals' rights and freedoms. Furthermore, a Hospital can also be an organization involved in scientific research, as exemplified by "Project X," which necessitates the use of real patient dental records. The Hospital has also been identified as a victim of ransomware attacks (e.g., Case No. 03), where its information systems were compromised, leading to data encryption and subsequent delays in patient care. Consequently, a Hospital is an organization legally obliged to notify relevant authorities and affected individuals in cases of cyber-attacks impacting medical records.
A hospital's core activity is providing healthcare, which inextricably involves processing health data like patient health records.
An example of an organization whose core activities involve processing health data, thus requiring the designation of a DPO.
A hospital is an organization that processes patient data in the regular course of business.
An example context where unavailability of critical medical data can pose a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms.
A hospital is an organization that holds medical records and is obliged to notify in case of a data breach, especially if it poses a high risk to patients.
An institution that can be a source of data regarding a data subject's physiological or biomedical state.
[person] Health Professional — An individual, such as a physician, who provides information related to a data subject's physiological or biomedical state.

[data] Medical Records — Medical records are highly sensitive personal data.
Medical records contain sensitive patient information held by a hospital.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[concept] Preventive or Occupational Medicine — Medical practices related to preventing illness or managing health in the workplace, for which personal data processing may be necessary.
Medical practices related to preventing illness or managing health in the workplace, for which personal data processing may be necessary.

[person] Recipient — A "Recipient" refers to a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or any other body to whom personal data is disclosed. This definition is explicitly stated in GDPR Article 4(9) and is consistently applied across various contexts. The concept of a recipient encompasses entities to whom personal data is disclosed, irrespective of whether they are a third party or not. This includes processors, which controllers are obligated to list. The relationship of a recipient is defined in the Regulation, describing their connection to a controller or processor who facilitates the data disclosure. It is also suggested that the concept of a recipient should be defined in international agreements, highlighting its significance in global data protection frameworks.
An entity or individual who mistakenly receives personal data, such as a wrong department or supplier organization.
A recipient is a party that receives personal data, potentially in error, from a controller. They may be considered "trusted" depending on the controller's relationship and assurance level with them.
A natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body to which personal data are disclosed, as defined by Article 4.9 of the GDPR.
A recipient is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or another body to which personal data are disclosed.
A recipient is an entity to whom personal data has been disclosed.

[concept] Medical Diagnosis — The process of identifying a disease or condition, which often involves the processing of personal data.
The process of identifying a disease or condition, which often involves the processing of personal data.

[concept] Archiving Purposes — Archiving Purposes refers to the practice of collecting, preserving, and storing records and data, typically for long-term reference, historical preservation, or administrative reasons. This activity often serves the public interest, scientific research, or statistical research. Under various data protection frameworks, such as GDPR Article 17.3.d, Archiving Purposes can serve as a specific ground for processing personal data. This designation may allow for exceptions to certain individual rights, including the right to erasure (delisting) or exemptions from specific information provision obligations for data controllers. Such exceptions are generally foreseen under certain conditions and are often subject to appropriate safeguards to protect the rights and freedoms of data subjects.
Archiving purposes in the public interest can exempt controllers from certain information provision obligations or allow for data retention.
Archiving purposes is one of the reasons for processing personal data, often in the public interest, subject to safeguards.
The storage of records and data for historical preservation or long-term reference.

[concept] Processing — Processing, in the context of data management and privacy, encompasses any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or sets of personal data. These operations can be conducted through automated means or otherwise. This broad definition includes, but is not limited to, collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure, or destruction. The concept of processing extends to any act of handling or dealing with data, directly or indirectly, that has the potential to affect the interests and fundamental rights of data subjects. For operations involving personal data, it is crucial to determine specific purposes and means, often requiring consent from the data subject. A fundamental principle dictates that processing should be carried out in a fair and transparent manner. Processing activities can be performed by entities such as a controller or processor.
