It is, however, incumbent upon the supervisory authority to ensure that the same circumstances are not counted twice. In particular, supervisory authorities should not, under Chapter 7, repeat the increases or decreases relative to the turnover of the company, but rather revisit their evaluation of the appropriate starting amount. 65. For the reasons outlined above, the supervisory authority may consider adjusting the starting amount corresponding to the seriousness of the infringement in cases where this infringement is committed by an undertaking with an annual turnover not exceeding 2 million euros, an annual turnover not exceeding 10 million euros, or an annual turnover not exceeding 50 million euros30. - For undertakings with an annual turnover of ≤ €2m, supervisory authorities may consider to proceed calculations on the basis of a sum between 0.2% and 0.4% of the identified starting amount. - For undertakings with an annual turnover of €2m up until €10m, supervisory authorities may consider to proceed calculations on the basis of a sum between 0.3% and 2% of the identified starting amount. - For undertakings with an annual turnover of €10m up until €50m, supervisory authorities may consider to proceed calculations on the basis of a sum between 1.5% and 10% of the identified starting amount. 66. For the same reasons, the supervisory authority may consider adjusting the starting amount corresponding to the seriousness of the infringement in cases where this infringement is committed by an undertaking with an annual turnover not exceeding 100 million euros, an annual turnover not exceeding 250 million euros and an annual turnover not exceeding 500 million euros31. - For undertakings with an annual turnover of €50m up until €100m, supervisory authorities may consider to proceed calculations on the basis of a sum between 8% and 20% of the identified starting amount. 28 See also EDPB Binding Decision 1/2021, paragraphs 411 and 412: “[Insofar] the turnover of an undertaking is not exclusively relevant for the determination of the maximum fine amount in accordance with Article 83(4)-(6) GDPR, but it may also be considered [as one relevant element among others] for the calculation of the fine itself, where appropriate, to ensure the fine is effective, proportionate and dissuasive in accordance with Article 83(1) GDPR.” The turnover of the undertaking concerned is further elaborated on in Chapter 6.2 of these Guidelines. 29 This has been stated by the General Court in case T-25/06, Alliance One International, Inc. v European Commission, paragraph 211, referencing other case law for instance case T-9/99, HFB and Others v Commission, paragraphs 528 and 529 and case T-175/05, Akzo Nobel and Others v Commission, paragraph 114. 30 These turnover figures are inspired by the Commission Recommendation of 6 May 2003 concerning the definition of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. In determining the starting points, the EDPB relies on the annual turnover of the undertaking alone (see Chapter 6 below). 31 These figures are added to bridge the gap between the highest threshold of the previous paragraph and the turnover threshold identified in Article 83(4)–(6) GDPR. 25 Adopted - For undertakings with an annual turnover of €100m up until €250m, supervisory authorities may consider to proceed calculations on the basis of a sum between 15% and 50 % of the identified starting amount. - For undertakings with an annual turnover of €250m up until €500m,, supervisory authorities may consider to proceed calculations on the basis of a sum between 40% and 100% of the identified starting amount. - For undertakings with an annual turnover above €500m, supervisory authorities may consider to proceed without an adjustment of the identified starting amount. [method] Exchange of Information — The process by which controllers, processors, and supervisory authorities share relevant data for binding corporate rules.
[method] Fraud Monitoring and Prevention — Techniques and activities aimed at detecting and preventing fraudulent activities, which can be a basis for automated processing.

[concept] Binding Corporate Rules — Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) are a set of internal, legally binding provisions adopted by multinational corporations or a group of undertakings, and they serve as an appropriate safeguard and legal framework for the international transfer of personal data. These rules are applied to facilitate data transfers within the same corporate group, particularly when transferring personal data outside the European Economic Area (EEA) or the European Union (EU) to entities located in third countries. BCRs specify requirements for data transfer and processing within the group. They encompass provisions on crucial data protection principles, data subject rights, mechanisms for liability, and compliance, ensuring that adequate protection is maintained for the personal data. An important aspect of BCRs is that they require approval from a supervisory authority, and in specific contexts, they may also require Board approval as defined in Article 47. Additionally, BCRs are subject to specific formats and procedures for electronic information exchange between data controllers, processors, and supervisory authorities. They are also known to include requirements such as the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing, as referenced in Articles 47(1) and 47(2)(e) of relevant regulations. BCRs are recognized as a transfer tool for data, sometimes mentioned in relation to derogations from typical data transfer requirements.
[organization] Financial Market Authorities — Authorities responsible for the regulation and supervision of securities markets, to which personal data may be disclosed.
[organization] Group of Enterprises — A group of enterprises engaged in a joint economic activity, to which binding corporate rules may apply.
[method] Integrated Tools — Integrated tools are technical measures provided by gatekeepers for small volume business users to access data.

[data] Authorisation Proof — Proof of authorisation is documentation that gatekeepers should keep to demonstrate that third parties have obtained consent from end users, including the duration of such authorisation.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[method] Data Protection by Design — Data Protection by Design (DPbDD) is a fundamental principle and approach that mandates the integration of data protection safeguards and privacy considerations into the initial design and development stages of processing systems, products, and services. This means that data protection measures are not an afterthought but are built in from the outset, ensuring that they are considered from the earliest stages of system design. The principle dictates that data processing should be limited to the bare minimum, aligning with data protection considerations from the very beginning of a system's conceptualization. It involves embedding technical and organizational measures directly into a product or service to effectively implement data protection principles and integrate necessary safeguards, often with the aim of meeting regulatory requirements such as those outlined in GDPR. One description also mentions that Data Protection by Design is a concept that incorporates analysis into a data controller’s handbook for handling personal data breaches, suggesting its role extends to establishing protocols for breach management.

ragPromptContext: [concept] Legal Claim — A Legal Claim is a demand for legal or equitable relief, which may necessitate data transfers.
[method] Fraud Monitoring and Prevention — Techniques and activities aimed at detecting and preventing fraudulent activities, which can be a basis for automated processing.

[person] Employee — An Employee is defined as an individual who is employed by an organization or person, belonging to the legal entity of a data controller or processor. These individuals are typically authorized to process personal data, acting under the authority of the controller. Their access to personal data should be restricted based on their specific duties and role within the company. Employees may interact with personal data in various ways, such as manually deleting personal data after its retention period in accordance with internal procedures. They can also be subjects whose personal data, such as their name, is processed by services (e.g., a taxi service in an illustrative example). Employee actions can also lead to incidents, such as when an employee of a controller makes a mistake resulting in a data breach, or when an employee of a service provider has their electronic notebook stolen, as depicted in CASE No. 11. While employees generally operate under established authority, there can be exceptional cases where they unlawfully exceed this authority. Furthermore, employees may face pressure concerning consent for data processing.
Employees are individuals within an organization who may have concerns or complaints.
An employee is a data subject who has a relevant and appropriate relationship with a controller, often forming the basis for legitimate interest in data processing within a group of undertakings.

[concept] Legal Claims — Legal Claims refer to the establishment, exercise, or defense of legal rights in a legal context. These claims represent demands for legal or equitable relief made by one party against another, or a formal demand for legal action or compensation. In this capacity, they can justify the lawful retention of personal data and may necessitate the processing of such data. The concept of Legal Claims is pertinent to data protection regulations, specifically appearing as a basis for data processing under GDPR Article 17.3.e. This article allows for an exception to delisting requests, enabling the continued use of personal data when necessary for the establishment, exercise, or defense of legal claims, though this exemption is considered unlikely to be frequently invoked by search engine providers. Furthermore, Legal Claims serve as a basis for data transfers under Article 49 (1) (e), encompassing various procedures including judicial, administrative, and out-of-court settings. This implies that the transfer of personal data may be necessary for establishing, exercising, or defending rights through legal action. Additionally, the establishment, exercise, or defense of rights in a legal context, through Legal Claims, can be a reason for processing restricted personal data.
The establishment, exercise, or defence of legal claims can justify the lawful retention of personal data.
Claims made in a court of law that require personal data for establishment, exercise, or defence.
Legal Claims are formal demands for legal action or compensation, for which processing of personal data may be necessary.
Legal claims refer to the establishment, exercise, or defence of rights in a legal context, which can be a reason for processing restricted personal data.
Legal Claims refer to the establishment, exercise, or defense of rights through legal action, for which data transfer may be necessary.
[concept] Compensation — Compensation is the right for any person who has suffered damage due to an infringement of the Regulation to receive payment from the controller or processor.

[concept] Complaint — A Complaint is defined as a formal expression of grievance, grievance due to dissatisfaction, or dissatisfaction with an activity or service, such as the processing of personal data. These grievances are typically lodged with a supervisory authority, making it a Concerned Supervisory Authority (CSA) particularly involved in the case. A complaint serves as the basis for investigations, specifically regarding data subjects' rights and alleged GDPR infringements, and defines the scope of data processing under scrutiny for potential violations. Upon receiving a complaint, the supervisory authority can take various actions, including dismissing, rejecting, or acting upon it. The granting of a complaint can be full or partial, and any decision made regarding it by supervisory authorities is considered an envisaged action. Furthermore, a complaint is considered a piece of relevant information that CSAs are obligated to proactively disclose to the Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) and other CSAs. The lodging of a complaint necessitates that a draft decision be submitted, especially when it leads to an investigation.
A complaint is a formal grievance lodged by a data subject, which may be rejected in whole or in part by a supervisory authority.
A formal statement of grievance lodged with a supervisory authority concerning a possible infringement of the Regulation.
A Complaint is an official grievance lodged by a complainant with a supervisory authority, which leads to a decision of dismissal, rejection, or action.

[person] Data Subject — A Data Subject is defined as an identified or identifiable natural person to whom personal data relates and whose personal data undergoes processing, encompassing operations such as collection, holding, storing, or other manipulations, including biometric and location data. This individual can be identified, directly or indirectly, by reference to an identifier or specific factors of their identity. End users are often considered Data Subjects, and their vital interests may necessitate data processing. Even if a Data Subject's data has been anonymized such that they are no longer identifiable, they are still considered a Data Subject. Their behavior or identity may be monitored, and any personal data relating to them requires either consent or another legitimate basis for lawful processing. Data processing concerning Data Subjects is subject to regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly if goods or services are offered to them within the European Union. Under Article 6 of the GDPR, explicit consent is often required for processing, including profiling and automated decision-making. This consent must be demonstrably obtained through deliberate, informed action. Data Subjects possess fundamental rights to safeguard their human dignity and legitimate interests, including rights to access, rectification, erasure, objection to processing, and data portability. They also have the right to be informed about and challenge automated decision-making and, in some contexts, request delisting from search engines. They can monitor data processing, should be offered format choices for reusing their data, and can transmit their personal data from one controller to another, taking responsibility for securing it in their own system. Data controllers are obligated to provide Data Subjects with specific information, including the identity of their representative, and to communicate efficiently. Their views should be sought during a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) where appropriate. When biometric data is processed, an alternative solution must be offered, and Data Subjects should be consulted during the drafting of codes of conduct when feasible. A Data Subject is also an individual whose personal data may be affected by a data breach, putting their rights and freedoms at risk. In such an event, the controller must inform them, especially if there is a likely high risk of adverse effects or potential damage; communication of the breach is obligatory if their personal data has been compromised and depending on the severity of the consequences. Their vital interests, reasonable expectations (influenced by factors like age, public figure status, and professional position), and personal data require consistent protection, necessitating that their rights and freedoms be safeguarded. They may contact the Data Protection Officer, lodge complaints with supervisory authorities, and seek judicial remedy. A Data Subject has the right to compensation for material or non-material damage suffered due to an infringement of the regulation. Their identity may be scrutinized by a controller if doubts arise.

[organization] Gatekeeper — A Gatekeeper is an entity designated under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically pursuant to Article 3(4) or Article 3(9), indicating its provision of Core Platform Services (CPSs). Prominent examples of such organizations include Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta. These Gatekeepers control access to specific digital services and are subject to extensive legal obligations under the DMA, and in many cases, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Their role is central to the regulatory framework designed to ensure fair and contestable digital markets. Gatekeepers process the personal data of end users, often acting as controllers or processors, and are responsible for ensuring that consent obtained for data processing, particularly for online advertising and data combination, complies with both GDPR and DMA requirements. This includes the meticulous recording of consent refusals or withdrawals. They are obligated to enable continuous and real-time access to data, prevent data accumulation, and ensure robust data security. Their responsibilities extend to providing data upon request by business users or authorized third parties, free of charge, and establishing appropriate authentication and authorization procedures for such access. They must also implement security measures for personal data, comply with portability requests under DMA Article 6(9), and provide comprehensive information to data subjects. Furthermore, Gatekeepers are tasked with selecting and implementing anonymization methods for end-user data shared under Article 6(11) DMA and must implement measures to maintain service integrity and security. They also have duties concerning interoperability, including exchanging message content and personal data with other providers while ensuring security for their end users. This includes protecting metadata, verifying communication authenticity, and ensuring compliance with geographical limitations and data protection regulations for Number-Independent Interpersonal Communication Services (NIICS). Gatekeepers must design online interfaces that do not undermine user autonomy, provide reminders, and ensure fair access to datasets by altering data to mitigate identification risks and imposing contractual measures on third-party undertakings for data access and compliance monitoring. Their conduct is subject to examination for compliance with both the DMA and GDPR, and they may have a "main establishment" under the GDPR. They are also separate controllers under GDPR for their own data processing and have obligations under Article 6(4) and Article 8(1) of the DMA.
[concept] Expert Knowledge of Data Protection Law — Expert Knowledge of Data Protection Law refers to specialized understanding and proficiency in legal frameworks governing data protection.

[person] Employees — Employees are individuals who work for a company and are expected to comply with a code of conduct. Their personal data may be processed by employers, but consent for this processing is often not freely given due to an inherent imbalance of power between employer and employee. This group includes individuals authorized to process personal data, who require access to such data to perform their job tasks for which the processor was hired. Employees are considered a category of data subjects that can be affected by a data breach, a classification suggested by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB). This group also includes individuals from a U.S. company whose personal data is processed for human resources purposes during business trips. In some cases, employees are staff members whose actions might be monitored by employers, for example, through the use of company cars. Employees are also individuals who need training on recognizing and preventing IT attacks and reporting them, and they were among those affected by "The Breach."
Employees can be considered vulnerable data subjects due to a potential imbalance in the relationship with their employer.
Individuals who carry out processing and are advised by the DPO on their GDPR obligations.
Employees of a Controller or Processor who should be informed about existing breach procedures and how to react to breaches to ensure compliance with GDPR.
Employees are individuals whose salary details are obtained by a tax authority from their employers.
Individuals who carry out personal data processing and are to be informed and advised by the Data Protection Officer regarding their obligations.

Example 1 An insurance company wishes to use artificial intelligence (AI) to profile customers buying insurance as a basis for their decision making when calculating the insurance risk. When determining how their AI solutions should be developed, they are determining the means of processing and shall consider data protection by design when choosing an AI application from a vendor and when deciding on how to train the AI. When determining how to train the AI, the controller should have accurate data to achieve precise results. Therefore, the controller should ensure that the data used to train the AI is accurate. Granted that they have a valid legal basis to train the AI using personal data from a large subset of their existing customers, the controller chooses a pool of customers that is representative of the population to also avoid bias. The customer data is then collected from the respective data handling system, including data on the type of insurance, for example health insurance, home insurance, travel insurance, etc. as well as data from public registries they have lawful access to. All data are pseudonymized prior to transfer to the system dedicated to the training of the AI model. To ensure that the data used for AI training is as accurate as possible, the controller only collects data from data sources with correct and up-to date information. The insurance company tests whether the AI is reliable and provides non-discriminatory results both during its development and finally before the product is released. When the AI is fully trained and operative, the insurance company uses the results to support the insurance risk assessments, yet without solely relying on the AI to decide whether to grant insurance, unless the decision is made in accordance with the exceptions in Article 22 (2) GDPR. The insurance company will also regularly review the results from the AI, to maintain the reliability and when necessary adjust the algorithm. Example 2 The controller is a health institution looking to find methods to ensure the integrity and accuracy of personal data in their client registers. In situations where two persons arrive at the institution at the same time and receive the same treatment, there is a risk of mistaking them if the only parameter to distinguish them is by name. To ensure accuracy, the controller needs a unique identifier for each person, and therefore more information than just the name of the client. Adopted 25 The institution uses several systems containing personal information of clients, and needs to ensure that the information related to the client is correct, accurate and consistent in all the systems at any point in time. The institution has identified several risks that may arise if information is changed in one system but not in the others. The controller decides to mitigate the risk by using a hashing technique that can be used to ensure integrity of data in the treatment journal. Immutable cryptographic time stamps are created for treatment journal records and the client associated with them so that any changes can be recognized, correlated and traced if required. 3.7 Storage limitation 80. Measures and safeguards that implement the principle of storage limitation shall complement the rights and freedoms of the data subjects, specifically, the right to erasure and the right to object. 82. Under GDPR, Controller The relation between a Controller and a Data Protection Officer (DPO) is characterized by advisory support and assigned responsibility for data protection compliance, particularly under regulations such as the GDPR. The Controller is responsible for designating a DPO to help ensure adherence to these regulations. The DPO's role encompasses providing advice and information to the Controller on various data protection matters, including breach management, data protection methodologies, and audits. This includes actively participating in Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), which the Controller undertakes with the DPO's guidance. Controllers are mandated to seek the DPO's advice when conducting a DPIA, and they must ensure the DPO's timely involvement in all data protection issues, providing necessary resources and access to facilitate their tasks. Guidelines may be developed by the Controller to specify when the DPO must be consulted. While the DPO offers crucial guidance and assists in monitoring internal compliance with regulations, the ultimate responsibility for data protection compliance remains with the Controller. The DPO may be an employee of the Controller or an external party, but they must perform their duties independently. The Controller is obligated to record the name and contact details of the DPO, and these details must be included in the record of processing activities. Furthermore, in the event of a data breach, the Controller must communicate the DPO's name and contact details as a contact point for breach information as part of the notification process. [data] Employees' Personal Data — Employees' personal data refers to information about employees that is subject to specific rules and safeguards regarding its processing in the employment context.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.
[concept] Period of Storage — The period of storage refers to how long personal data will be kept by the controller.

[concept] Exercise and Enjoyment of Rights and Benefits Related to Employment — The Exercise and Enjoyment of Rights and Benefits Related to Employment, on an individual or collective basis, is a purpose for processing employees' personal data.

[organization] Supervisory Authority — A Supervisory Authority (SA) is an independent public authority established by a European Union Member State, as mandated by Article 51 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Its core responsibility is to monitor and enforce the application of data protection law, primarily the GDPR, within its specific national jurisdiction. The overarching goal of an SA is to safeguard the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals regarding the processing of their personal data and to facilitate the free flow of personal data within the European Union. SAs act as competent national bodies under Articles 55 or 56 of the GDPR, endowed with a broad spectrum of powers, including investigation, corrective actions, authorization, and advisory functions. Their decisions, which carry legal effects, are subject to judicial remedies, and they are obligated to respect the right to be heard. Supervisory Authorities are responsible for handling complaints lodged by data subjects, especially when controllers fail to address their requests. They are also the competent national authority to which personal data breaches must be notified without undue delay, typically within 72 hours unless the breach is unlikely to pose a risk to individuals. For cross-border breaches, an SA can act as the lead authority, request further details, advise on informing individuals, and order controllers to do so. They also receive information about the Data Protection Officer's (DPO) name and contact details. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to determine the nature and gravity of infringements, ensure compliance, and order appropriate measures against data controllers or processors. This includes the ability to impose effective, proportionate, and dissuasive administrative fines for GDPR infringements, considering factors such as circumstances, economic viability, and proportionality. They may hold parent companies liable and impose fines for non-compliance with Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) requirements. Additionally, a supervisory authority must be consulted if a DPIA indicates a high residual risk that cannot be mitigated, and it possesses the power to prohibit such processing operations. They can also require documentation of a DPO designation analysis and request access to records of processing operations. Beyond enforcement, Supervisory Authorities play a crucial role in GDPR accreditation and certification mechanisms. This involves approving criteria, reviewing existing certifications, accrediting certification bodies, and potentially acting as a certification body themselves. They can establish additional accreditation requirements, sometimes in cooperation with a National Accreditation Body. SAs are authorized to oversee and approve administrative arrangements for data transfers under Article 46(3)(b) GDPR, adopt standard contractual clauses for data processing matters, approve safeguards, and apply consistency mechanisms. They are also responsible for publishing lists of processing operations subject to mandatory DPIAs and for conducting prior consultations if DPIA results indicate a high risk or if existing operations have been pre-checked. While typically one lead supervisory authority exists for cross-border processing, some Member States may have more than one SA, all of whom are bound by the content of a draft decision once consensus is reached. They are also responsible for verifying compliance with data protection regulations and may require a controller to communicate a personal data breach to the data subject.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data)" signifies that the Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This involves significant authority and responsibility over the entire lifecycle of personal data, encompassing decisions related to its processing, protection, management, and transference. The Controller is explicitly responsible for establishing the retention period for documentation containing personal data and makes choices regarding its deletion or return. A core obligation of the Controller is to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and to uphold data subject rights, including guaranteeing data accuracy and facilitating the exercise of those rights. The Controller is always required to have an appropriate lawful ground for the processing of personal data, and while explicit consent may be obtained, it is not always the sole lawful basis, especially when processing is essential for a contract. The Controller is also responsible for the overall protection and security of personal data, which includes managing and responding to any data breaches, and applying appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard it. This responsibility extends to implementing measures to minimize the processing of personal data. In addition to determining purposes and means, the Controller collects, processes, and stores personal data. The Controller may also determine its identification requirements and, in the EU, has the capability to make personal data accessible to a third-country authority, and may specifically process data indicating criminal acts when considered within their legitimate interest. Persons under the direct authority of the Controller are authorized to process personal data. The Controller is ultimately responsible and liable for any processing of personal data, including its transferring. Personal Data.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation `(Controller, Processing of Personal Data)` describes the multifaceted role and responsibilities of a controller concerning the processing of personal data. A controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This determination is made independently, and the specified purposes and means must explicitly relate to the processing of personal data. In this context, the controller is actively involved in and carries out the processing of personal data. A core responsibility of the controller is to ensure and demonstrate compliance with the principles governing personal data processing, particularly those outlined in the GDPR. This includes ensuring that all processing activities have an appropriate legal basis. Furthermore, controllers are expected to innovate to maintain compliance with evolving legal parameters. The controller's responsibilities also extend to respecting the rights of data subjects. Specifically, if a data subject objects to the processing of their personal data, the controller shall cease processing unless compelling legitimate grounds for the processing can be demonstrated. Processing of Personal Data.

Under GDPR, Data Subject The relation "(Data Subject, Personal Data)" defines a fundamental connection where personal data belongs to, pertains to, or relates to a specific data subject. A data subject is understood as a natural person, an individual, to whom the personal data refers. This relationship is central to data processing, particularly in contexts like connected vehicles, and protects the privacy and data protection rights held by data subjects over their personal information. Personal data is any information that can identify or render identifiable a particular data subject. The data subject is the source of this data, which they may provide through their actions or technical means. When personal data is collected directly from a data subject, they must be informed about its processing. Similarly, the delisting of personal data also directly involves the data subject, who may have personal data in various contexts, such as within their bank account. Data subjects possess significant rights concerning their personal data, including the ability to receive, transmit, reuse, and control it. When personal data is transferred, the interests and fundamental rights of the data subject must be considered. While data subjects have rights over their data, they also bear responsibility for securing their personal data within their own systems. A data subject should not be surprised at the purpose of processing their personal data and it should not be disclosed without their consent. The processing of personal data involves protecting the interests and rights of the data subject.<SEP>Personal data is information that relates to an identified or identifiable natural person (the data subject).<SEP>Personal data relates to a data subject who is not or no longer identifiable after anonymization. [method] Profiling — Profiling is a sophisticated and automated form of processing personal data specifically designed to evaluate, analyze, or predict various personal aspects of a natural person. This includes their performance at work, economic situation, health, personal preferences or interests, reliability or behavior, location, or movements. It is considered a specific type of processing operation, with the definition often referencing Article 4(4) of the GDPR, and its implications necessitate particular attention in certification criteria due to potential serious consequences for individuals. This process distinguishes itself by continuously collecting, analyzing, building, and applying data to create a profile for an individual. It can even infer special categories of data from non-special category data when combined with other information, thereby generating derived or inferred data about individuals. Such created data is frequently invisible to the data subject and is utilized in decision-making processes. Consequently, profiling is subject to specific transparency requirements, especially when integrated into automated decision-making. Data controllers have clear transparency obligations, and data subjects possess a right to information regarding profiling activities. Profiling is widely employed across numerous sectors, notably in targeted advertising, where companies leverage these profiles to deliver personalized content, sometimes based on sensitive data. Social media platforms, for instance, extensively use profiling within their targeting mechanisms. While profiling can offer benefits like increased efficiencies and resource savings, it also presents significant risks to individuals' rights and freedoms, particularly concerning children. It can lead to the creation of consumer profiles that may be unfair or discriminatory. Furthermore, profiling carries potential risks if it falls under Article 22 of the GDPR and is subject to specific data protection rights and Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) requirements. Its applications are diverse, encompassing fraud prevention, marketing, and disease prediction.
The processing of personal data to evaluate certain personal aspects relating to a natural person, particularly for advertising based on special categories of data.
Profiling is defined as any automated processing of personal data used to evaluate certain personal aspects of a natural person, such as performance at work, economic situation, health, preferences, interests, reliability, behavior, location, or movements.

[concept] Core Platform Services (CPSs) — Core Platform Services are services to which the Digital Markets Act (DMA) applies, provided by undertakings designated as gatekeepers, and include categories such as online intermediation services, online search engines, and cloud computing services.
Core Platform Services (CPSs) are services provided by gatekeepers where vast amounts of personal data are collected.
Core Platform Services are relevant services for which data is provided or generated, falling under the data access obligation of gatekeepers.

[concept] Core Platform Services — Core Platform Services (CPSs) are defined as digital services utilized by end users. Gatekeepers are designated for these services under Article 3(9) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA), which also mandates that the right to data portability applies to them under DMA Article 6(9). Furthermore, gatekeepers providing Core Platform Services are required to implement user-friendly consent mechanisms and may apply consumer profiling techniques across these digital services.

[organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

[person] Business User — A business user is an individual or organization, natural or legal, operating in a commercial or professional capacity, identified as a beneficiary of the right to data access under Article 6(10) DMA.
A business user is a commercial entity or individual that utilizes gatekeeper products or services and may request access to end-user data.
An entity that requests access to end-user data from a gatekeeper under Article 6(10) DMA, with obligations under GDPR regarding data minimisation.
A Business User is a party that requests access to data, including historic and real-time data, and is subject to monitoring by data protection supervisory authorities.

Under GDPR, Administrative Costs The controller may charge a reasonable fee taking into account administrative costs for requests.<SEP>The Controller may charge a fee based on administrative costs for providing further copies. Controller.

Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Supervisory Authority is established primarily by data protection regulations, such as the GDPR, and focuses on compliance, breach management, and accountability. A central obligation of the Controller is to notify the Supervisory Authority of personal data breaches, typically within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach, especially if it poses a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, as per Article 33(1) and Article 27(5) GDPR. The Controller is responsible for determining if a breach is notifiable and must ensure the relevant Supervisory Authority is informed, potentially proactively notifying them of infringements or seeking advice. They must also inform the Supervisory Authority about data transfers, documenting assessments and safeguards. Controllers without an EU establishment are required to engage with local supervisory authorities in every Member State where they operate. Furthermore, the Controller must consult the Supervisory Authority if a high risk identified in a Data Protection Impact Assessment cannot be mitigated by reasonable means before processing. Controllers are also obligated to cooperate with and make records available to the Supervisory Authority upon request, demonstrating accountability and compliance. The Supervisory Authority plays a significant role in overseeing the Controller's data protection practices. It can advise Controllers on how to inform individuals about breaches and may even order them to do so, particularly for high-risk breaches. The Supervisory Authority verifies the Controller's compliance, handles complaints, and seeks amicable settlements regarding possible infringements. It possesses powers to require the Controller to provide information, carry out investigations, notify infringements, and obtain access to data and premises. The Supervisory Authority can issue warnings and reprimands, order compliance, and impose sanctions, including administrative fines under Article 83 GDPR, especially in cases of unjustified breaches. The level of the Controller's cooperation is considered by the Supervisory Authority when assessing mitigation efforts. The Supervisory Authority also promotes awareness among Controllers regarding their obligations under pertinent regulations and informs Controllers when a received complaint is dismissed or rejected. The activity 'Ausländischen Reiseverlauf anpassen' (Adjust foreign travel itinerary) involves modifying travel details for trips abroad, which includes personal data such as destinations, dates, and potentially border crossing information related to an identifiable traveler.

The activity 'Kürzungen angeben' (Specify deductions) involves entering or adjusting financial deduction information related to a business trip expense report. This is linked to a specific employee/traveler and constitutes processing of personal financial data.

The activity 'Fahrkosten anpassen' (Adjust travel costs) involves modifying expense data (e.g., ticket costs, mileage) that is directly associated with a specific traveler. This is processing of personal financial data.

The activity 'Finanzierungsdaten eingeben' (Enter financing data) involves inputting financial information (e.g., cost center, budget codes, project numbers) for a business trip. This data is linked to an employee and their activities, constituting processing of personal data related to economic or employment context.

The activity 'Daten zu Zahlungspartnern eingeben' (Enter data for payment partners) involves inputting information about entities involved in payment for the trip (e.g., external vendors, partners). This likely includes names or identifiers of individuals at those partners, or details necessary for financial transactions involving the traveler, and thus processes personal data.

The activity 'Notizen eingeben' (Enter notes) involves adding free-text notes to a business trip application. These notes can contain any information relating to the identifiable traveler, including personal observations, reasons for travel, or other details, and thus constitute processing of personal data.

The activity 'Dokumente hochladen' (Upload documents) involves adding files (e.g., receipts, tickets, invoices) to a trip application. These documents contain personal data such as the traveler's name, dates, locations, payment details, and potentially signatures. Uploading stores this personal data, which is processing.

The activity 'Antrag beenden und weiterleiten' (Complete and forward application) finalizes a business trip expense report containing extensive personal data (traveler identity, financial details, itineraries) and transmits (forwards) it to the next processor (e.g., approver, accounting). This involves 'disclosure by transmission' of personal data.

The activity 'Bankverbindung einsehen' (View bank details) involves consulting the bank account information (e.g., IBAN, account holder name) of the traveler for reimbursement purposes. This is retrieval and consultation of personal financial data, a special category of personal data due to its sensitivity.

The activity 'Änderungen zur Bankverbindung eingeben' (Enter changes to bank details) involves altering the bank account information (e.g., IBAN, account holder) of the traveler. This is 'adaptation or alteration' of sensitive personal financial data.

The activity 'Reiseverlauf anpassen' (Adjust travel itinerary) involves modifying the sequence of destinations, dates, and modes of transport for a business trip. This updates location data and travel patterns of an identifiable employee, constituting processing of personal data.

The activity 'Beförderungsmittel anpassen' (Adjust means of transport) involves changing the transportation method (e.g., flight, train, car) for a trip. This updates travel details linked to a specific traveler and is processing of personal data.

The activity 'Hotelrechnung anpassen' (Adjust hotel bill) involves modifying invoice details for hotel accommodation. This includes personal data such as the traveler's name, stay dates, room charges, and potentially payment information, constituting processing of personal and financial data.

The activity 'Übernachtung eingeben' (Enter overnight stay) involves inputting details about hotel or accommodation stays during a business trip. This includes personal data such as location, dates, and potentially the traveler's name on the booking, which is processing of personal data.

The activity 'Kürzungen angeben' (Specify deductions) involves entering or adjusting financial deduction information (similar to sid-1u4n). This is linked to a specific employee/traveler and constitutes processing of personal financial data.

The activity 'Nebenkosten eingeben' (Enter ancillary costs) involves inputting additional expense items (e.g., meals, taxi, conference fees) for a business trip. These costs are attributed to a specific traveler and form part of their financial reimbursement record, processing personal financial data.

The activity 'Wegstrecke angeben' (Specify route/distance) involves entering the distance traveled, typically for mileage reimbursement. This generates location and movement data (starting point, destination, kilometers) linked to an identifiable employee, which is personal data.

The activity 'PDF ausgeben' (Output PDF) generates a document containing the complete business trip application, which includes all the traveler's personal data (name, travel details, costs, bank information). Creating and outputting this document is 'dissemination or otherwise making available' of personal data.

Under GDPR, Controller In the context of the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), a Controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This role is fundamental to the GDPR framework, outlining significant obligations and responsibilities for any party involved in deciding how personal data is processed. Controllers are accountable for ensuring compliance with all GDPR provisions, particularly as detailed in Article 3. The Controller has legal obligations to ensure compliance with the GDPR and is responsible and liable under its provisions, with these obligations often referred to as "GDPR controller obligations." The responsibilities of a Controller include applying GDPR rules to data processing, adhering to foundational principles like lawfulness and fairness (Article 5(1)), and fulfilling transparency obligations. Specific duties extend to maintaining records of processing activities (Article 30), ensuring the security of processing (Article 32), conducting data protection impact assessments (Article 35), and engaging in prior consultation (Article 36) for managing risks. Controllers must also comply with regulations regarding data storage periods, implement appropriate technical and organizational measures, and adhere to specific legal bases, such as legitimate interest, for processing data. The GDPR places a significant burden of proof on the Controller, requiring them to demonstrate "compelling legitimate grounds for the processing" when applicable. They must ensure consent mechanisms meet GDPR standards and act upon withdrawal requests. Compliance with obligations related to accountability, engaging processors, and maintaining data security is paramount. Regarding data breaches, the GDPR mandates that controllers implement appropriate security measures, ensure compliance with processing principles, and adhere to relevant provisions for breach notification, as specified in Article 60(10). Unless a breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, the Controller is required to notify the competent supervisory authority and, in certain cases, the affected individuals. The GDPR further defines notification and communication requirements for Controllers regarding breaches, and they must retain documentation in accordance with Article 33(5) of the GDPR. The GDPR also places the burden of proof regarding objections on the Controller. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to take enforcement action, including imposing fines, for any infringement of GDPR provisions resulting from a Controller's actions. The ability for data controllers to obtain GDPR certifications further underscores their pivotal role and accountability within the regulatory framework, though some Controllers currently face broad and systemic issues in compliance with the GDPR. The GDPR recognizes that Controllers may not have all information immediately and allows for phased notification.<SEP>Controllers must comply with the provisions of the GDPR, including those related to information provision.<SEP>The controller must comply with GDPR requirements, including those related to transparency and notification.<SEP>A controller's responsibilities are defined under the GDPR. Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data)" signifies that the Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This involves significant authority and responsibility over the entire lifecycle of personal data, encompassing decisions related to its processing, protection, management, and transference. The Controller is explicitly responsible for establishing the retention period for documentation containing personal data and makes choices regarding its deletion or return. A core obligation of the Controller is to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and to uphold data subject rights, including guaranteeing data accuracy and facilitating the exercise of those rights. The Controller is always required to have an appropriate lawful ground for the processing of personal data, and while explicit consent may be obtained, it is not always the sole lawful basis, especially when processing is essential for a contract. The Controller is also responsible for the overall protection and security of personal data, which includes managing and responding to any data breaches, and applying appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard it. This responsibility extends to implementing measures to minimize the processing of personal data. In addition to determining purposes and means, the Controller collects, processes, and stores personal data. The Controller may also determine its identification requirements and, in the EU, has the capability to make personal data accessible to a third-country authority, and may specifically process data indicating criminal acts when considered within their legitimate interest. Persons under the direct authority of the Controller are authorized to process personal data. The Controller is ultimately responsible and liable for any processing of personal data, including its transferring. Personal Data.

[Source: edpb_guidelines_202006_psd2_afterpublicconsultation_en] "6(1)(b) of the GDPR (processing is necessary for the performance of a contract) Payment services are provided on a contractual basis between the payment services user and the payment services provider. The EDPB Guidelines 2/2019 on the processing of personal data under Article 6(1)(b) GDPR in the context of the provision of online services to data subjects make clear that controllers have to assess what processing of personal data is objectively necessary to perform the contract. The controller should be able to demonstrate how the main object of the specific contract with the data subject cannot, as a matter of fact, be performed if the specific processing of the personal data in question does not occur. Article 5 (1) (b) of the GDPR provides for the purpose limitation principle, which requires that personal data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes. Under GDPR, Controller The (Controller, Processor) relationship describes an arrangement, primarily defined by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), where a Processor handles personal data on behalf of a Controller. The Controller retains the primary and ultimate responsibility for ensuring overall compliance with data protection principles, including data protection by design and by default (DPbDD), and this accountability extends to any Processor and sub-processors involved. This relationship mandates that the Controller select Processors who offer sufficient guarantees regarding GDPR compliance. This relationship is formalized and governed by a legally binding contract or other legal act, often referred to as a processing agreement. This agreement details how GDPR requirements will be implemented, outlines specific obligations, and defines assistance duties. The Controller must provide documented instructions to the Processor on how to process personal data, and the Processor is obligated to comply. The Processor processes personal data only on these documented instructions. Even without a written agreement, the existence and definition of this relationship hold. The Processor has various duties, including assisting the Controller in fulfilling obligations related to data subject rights and Articles 32 to 36 of the GDPR, ensuring compliance with data protection obligations, and reporting to the Controller. This assistance includes deleting or returning personal data at the Controller's choice, providing compliance information, and cooperating with Controller-conducted audits. A critical obligation for the Processor is to notify the Controller "without undue delay" upon becoming aware of a personal data breach it is processing on behalf of the Controller, as mandated by Article 33(2) GDPR. Processors must also notify the Controller of any request from a third-country authority without undue delay and follow the Controller's instructions, unless prohibited by law. The Processor is liable to the Controller for fulfilling these obligations. The Controller can authorize the use of sub-processors, but the Processor must obtain prior written authorization from the Controller for engaging another processor. The Processor is liable to the Controller for the sub-processors' adherence to data protection obligations. In scenarios involving data transfers, such as a third-country company (Controller) engaging a non-EEA processor, the processor acts as a data exporter on behalf of the Controller. The Controller must provide a comprehensive list of all data recipients, including processors. The relationship demands good faith cooperation, involving contract negotiation and management of audit and instruction processes. Controllers also carry out Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) with the processors. In some cases, the lead supervisory authority of the Controller may also become the lead supervisory authority for the Processor. When an end user qualifies as a Controller, an authorized third party may act as a Processor. Processor.

Under GDPR, Controller In the context of the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), a Controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This role is fundamental to the GDPR framework, outlining significant obligations and responsibilities for any party involved in deciding how personal data is processed. Controllers are accountable for ensuring compliance with all GDPR provisions, particularly as detailed in Article 3. The Controller has legal obligations to ensure compliance with the GDPR and is responsible and liable under its provisions, with these obligations often referred to as "GDPR controller obligations." The responsibilities of a Controller include applying GDPR rules to data processing, adhering to foundational principles like lawfulness and fairness (Article 5(1)), and fulfilling transparency obligations. Specific duties extend to maintaining records of processing activities (Article 30), ensuring the security of processing (Article 32), conducting data protection impact assessments (Article 35), and engaging in prior consultation (Article 36) for managing risks. Controllers must also comply with regulations regarding data storage periods, implement appropriate technical and organizational measures, and adhere to specific legal bases, such as legitimate interest, for processing data. The GDPR places a significant burden of proof on the Controller, requiring them to demonstrate "compelling legitimate grounds for the processing" when applicable. They must ensure consent mechanisms meet GDPR standards and act upon withdrawal requests. Compliance with obligations related to accountability, engaging processors, and maintaining data security is paramount. Regarding data breaches, the GDPR mandates that controllers implement appropriate security measures, ensure compliance with processing principles, and adhere to relevant provisions for breach notification, as specified in Article 60(10). Unless a breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, the Controller is required to notify the competent supervisory authority and, in certain cases, the affected individuals. The GDPR further defines notification and communication requirements for Controllers regarding breaches, and they must retain documentation in accordance with Article 33(5) of the GDPR. The GDPR also places the burden of proof regarding objections on the Controller. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to take enforcement action, including imposing fines, for any infringement of GDPR provisions resulting from a Controller's actions. The ability for data controllers to obtain GDPR certifications further underscores their pivotal role and accountability within the regulatory framework, though some Controllers currently face broad and systemic issues in compliance with the GDPR. Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data)" signifies that the Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This involves significant authority and responsibility over the entire lifecycle of personal data, encompassing decisions related to its processing, protection, management, and transference. The Controller is explicitly responsible for establishing the retention period for documentation containing personal data and makes choices regarding its deletion or return. A core obligation of the Controller is to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and to uphold data subject rights, including guaranteeing data accuracy and facilitating the exercise of those rights. The Controller is always required to have an appropriate lawful ground for the processing of personal data, and while explicit consent may be obtained, it is not always the sole lawful basis, especially when processing is essential for a contract. The Controller is also responsible for the overall protection and security of personal data, which includes managing and responding to any data breaches, and applying appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard it. This responsibility extends to implementing measures to minimize the processing of personal data. In addition to determining purposes and means, the Controller collects, processes, and stores personal data. The Controller may also determine its identification requirements and, in the EU, has the capability to make personal data accessible to a third-country authority, and may specifically process data indicating criminal acts when considered within their legitimate interest. Persons under the direct authority of the Controller are authorized to process personal data. The Controller is ultimately responsible and liable for any processing of personal data, including its transferring. Personal Data.

Under GDPR, GDPR The relationship between GDPR and a Processor is characterized by specific obligations, responsibilities, and liabilities directly imposed upon the Processor by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). A processor is subject to the GDPR for any given processing operation, with its role and duties explicitly defined within the regulation. This subjection is set forth in Article 3 of the GDPR, which establishes its territorial scope and applicability, even extending to non-EEA processors when they are engaged by third-country companies. In such cases, these processors must also comply with Article 28 and Chapter V of the GDPR. The GDPR directly imposes various obligations on processors, detailing their responsibilities concerning personal data protection. Processors must ensure compliance with these requirements, particularly by adhering to the instructions provided by controllers. Key responsibilities include compliance with Article 30 (records of processing activities), Article 32 (security of processing), Article 35 (data protection impact assessment), and Article 36 (prior consultation with a supervisory authority) regarding risks. Processors are also subject to GDPR obligations relating to their liability for sub-processors, as outlined in Article 28(4). Furthermore, the GDPR requires processors to implement appropriate security measures and outlines their obligations regarding data breaches and notifications, including the requirement to notify any breach to their controller. Supervisory Authorities (SAs) have the power to take action against a processor for infringing GDPR provisions. The regulation categorizes various infringements that can lead to fines for processors. Certifications under the GDPR are also issued to data processors, further emphasizing their direct accountability and the regulatory oversight they are subject to.
