A case-by-case analysis of the processing at stake and the roles of the actors involved is necessary.12 Some examples of how personal data could be “made available” are by creating an account, granting access rights to an existing account, “confirming”/”accepting” an effective request for remote access, embedding a hard drive or submitting a password to a file. It should be kept in mind that remote access from a third country (even if it takes place only by means of displaying personal data on a screen, for example in support situations, troubleshooting or for administration purposes) and/or storage in a cloud situated outside the EEA offered by a service provider, is also considered to be a transfer, provided that the three criteria outlined in paragraph 9 above are met.13 Conversely, Chapter V does not apply to “internal processing”, i.e. where data is not disclosed by transmission or otherwise made available to another controller or processor, including where such processing takes place outside the EU.14 In this case, the controller or processor remains responsible for the processing, including to ensure compliance with all relevant provisions and safeguards of the GDPR which directly applies (see also Section 4 below), e.g. the EEA supervisory authorities can enforce the GDPR against these entities and data subjects can obtain redress in case of a violation of their rights. In addition, this second criterion cannot be considered as fulfilled when there is no controller or processor sending or making the data available (i.e. no “exporter”) to another controller or processor, such as when data are disclosed directly by the data subject15 to the recipient. 11 Idem, see page 22. 12 See page 9 of the EDPB Guidelines 07/2020 on the concepts of controller and processor in the GDPR. 13 See EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 on measures that supplement transfer tools to ensure compliance with the EU level of protection of personal data, page 11, paragraph 13 and footnote 28. 14 This is also reflected in the approach of Article 46 GDPR, which refers to contractual/bilateral transfer instruments concluded between different entities acting as controllers or processors. 15 The data subject cannot be considered a controller or processor. This follows from Article 4(10) GDPR which differentiates between controller/processor and data subject. Hence, a data subject disclosing his/her own personal data cannot be considered an “exporter”. This is without prejudice to the fact that a natural person can be a controller/processor in accordance with Article 4(7) and 4(8) GDPR (e.g. as a self-employed person). However, this does not limit the protection that natural persons acting as a controller/processor enjoy where their own personal data are concerned. In addition, it is important to recall that where the processing of personal data is carried out “by a natural person in the course of a purely personal or household activity”, such processing will, in accordance with Article 2(2)(c), fall outside the material scope of the GDPR. Finally, it should be noted Adopted 9 Example 1: Controller in a third country collects data directly from a data subject in the EU (under Article 3(2) GDPR) Maria, living in Italy, inserts her name, surname and postal address by filling in a form on an online clothing website in order to complete her order and receive the dress she bought online at her residence in Rome. The online clothing website is operated by a third country company that has no presence in the EU, but specifically targets the EU market. In this case, the data subject (Maria) passes her personal data to the third country company. This does not constitute a transfer of personal data since the data are not passed by an exporter (controller or processor), but directly collected from the data subject by the controller under Article 3(2) GDPR. Thus, Chapter V does not apply to this case. Nevertheless, the third country company will be required to apply the GDPR since its processing operations are subject to Article 3(2).16 Example 2: Controller in a third country collects data directly from a data subject in the EU (under Article 3(2) GDPR) and uses a processor outside the EU for some processing activities Maria, living in Italy, inserts her name, surname and postal address by filling in a form on an online clothing website in order to complete her order and receive the dress she bought online at her residence in Rome. The online clothing website is operated by a third country company that has no presence in the EU, but specifically targets the EU market. In order to process the orders received by means of the website, the third country company has engaged a non-EEA processor. In this case, the data subject (Maria) passes her personal data to the third country company and this does not constitute a transfer of personal data since the data are directly collected by the controller under Article 3(2) GDPR. Thus, the controller will have to apply the GDPR to the processing of this personal data. As far as it engages a non-EEA processor, such disclosure from the third country company to its non-EEA processor would amount to a transfer, and it will be required to apply Article 28 and Chapter V obligations so as to ensure that the level of protection afforded by the GDPR would not be undermined when data are processed on its behalf by the non-EEA-processor"

The 'Koordinierungsphase 2' (coordination phase 2) activity continues the coordination process for student admissions, involving further processing and potential sharing of applicant personal data between educational institutions.

The 'Clearingphase' (clearing phase) activity involves final coordination and clearing of student admissions, requiring processing of applicant personal data to resolve any remaining placement issues and finalize admission decisions across the university system.

[concept] Coordination — The process of interaction and collaboration between the European Commission and data protection supervisory authorities.

[organization] Host Supervisory Authority — A Host Supervisory Authority is the supervisory authority of a Member State in whose territory staff from other supervisory authorities operate during joint operations.

[method] Prior Consultation Procedure — A procedure referred to in Article 36(1) and (5) GDPR, where controllers can seek advice from SAs.
The Prior Consultation Procedure is a process where a Controller seeks advice from the Supervisory Authority on processing operations with high risks.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

Data processing operations can evolve quickly and new vulnerabilities can arise. Therefore, it should be noted that the revision of a DPIA is not only useful for continuous improvement, but also critical to maintain the level of data protection in a changing environment over time. A DPIA may also become necessary because the organisational or societal context for the processing activity has changed, for example because the effects of certain automated decisions have become more significant, or new categories of data subjects become vulnerable to discrimination. Each of these examples could be an element that leads to a change of the risk resulting from processing activity concerned. Conversely, certain changes could lower the risk as well. For example, a processing operation could evolve so that decisions are no longer automated or if a monitoring activity is no longer systematic. In that case, the review of the risk analysis made can show that the performance of a DPIA is no longer required. As a matter of good practice, a DPIA should be continuously reviewed and regularly re-assessed. Therefore, even if a DPIA is not required on 25 May 2018, it will be necessary, at the appropriate time, for the controller to conduct such a DPIA as part of its general accountability obligations. D. How to carry out a DPIA? a) At what moment should a DPIA be carried out? Prior to the processing. The DPIA should be carried out “prior to the processing” (Articles 35(1) and 35(10), recitals 90 and 93)23. This is consistent with data protection by design and by default principles (Article 25 and recital 78). The DPIA should be seen as a tool for helping decision-making concerning the processing. The DPIA should be started as early as is practicable in the design of the processing operation even if some of the processing operations are still unknown. Updating the DPIA throughout the lifecycle project will ensure that data protection and privacy are considered and will encourage the creation of solutions which promote compliance. It can also be necessary to repeat individual steps of the assessment as the development process progresses because the selection of certain technical or organizational measures may affect the severity or likelihood of the risks posed by the processing. The fact that the DPIA may need to be updated once the processing has actually started is not a valid reason for postponing or not carrying out a DPIA. The DPIA is an on-going process, especially where a processing operation is dynamic and subject to ongoing change. Carrying out a DPIA is a continual process, not a one-time exercise. b) Who is obliged to carry out the DPIA? The controller, with the DPO and processors. The controller is responsible for ensuring that the DPIA is carried out (Article 35(2)). Carrying out the DPIA may be done by someone else, inside or outside the organization, but the controller remains ultimately accountable for that task. 23 Except when it is an already existing processing that has been prior checked by the Supervisory Authority, in which case the DPIA should be carried out before undergoing significant changes. 15 The controller must also seek the advice of the Data Protection Officer (DPO), where designated (Article 35(2)) and this advice, and the decisions taken by the controller, should be documented within the DPIA. The DPO should also monitor the performance of the DPIA (Article 39(1)(c)). Further guidance is provided in the WP29 Guidelines on Data Protection Officer 16/EN WP 243. If the processing is wholly or partly performed by a data processor, the processor should assist the controller in carrying out the DPIA and provide any necessary information (in line with Article 28(3)(f)). The controller must “seek the views of data subjects or their representatives” (Article 35(9)), “where appropriate”. The WP29 considers that: - those views could be sought through a variety of means, depending on the context (e.g. a generic study related to the purpose and means of the processing operation, a question to the staff representatives, or usual surveys sent to the data controller’s future customers) ensuring that the controller has a lawful basis for processing any personal data involved in seeking such views. Although it should be noted that consent to processing is obviously not a way for seeking the views of the data subjects; - if the data controller’s final decision differs from the views of the data subjects, its reasons for going ahead or not should be documented; - the controller should also document its justification for not seeking the views of data subjects, if it decides that this is not appropriate, for example if doing so would compromise the confidentiality of companies’ business plans, or would be disproportionate or impracticable. [organization] Gatekeeper — A Gatekeeper is an entity designated under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically pursuant to Article 3(4) or Article 3(9), indicating its provision of Core Platform Services (CPSs). Prominent examples of such organizations include Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta. These Gatekeepers control access to specific digital services and are subject to extensive legal obligations under the DMA, and in many cases, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Their role is central to the regulatory framework designed to ensure fair and contestable digital markets. Gatekeepers process the personal data of end users, often acting as controllers or processors, and are responsible for ensuring that consent obtained for data processing, particularly for online advertising and data combination, complies with both GDPR and DMA requirements. This includes the meticulous recording of consent refusals or withdrawals. They are obligated to enable continuous and real-time access to data, prevent data accumulation, and ensure robust data security. Their responsibilities extend to providing data upon request by business users or authorized third parties, free of charge, and establishing appropriate authentication and authorization procedures for such access. They must also implement security measures for personal data, comply with portability requests under DMA Article 6(9), and provide comprehensive information to data subjects. Furthermore, Gatekeepers are tasked with selecting and implementing anonymization methods for end-user data shared under Article 6(11) DMA and must implement measures to maintain service integrity and security. They also have duties concerning interoperability, including exchanging message content and personal data with other providers while ensuring security for their end users. This includes protecting metadata, verifying communication authenticity, and ensuring compliance with geographical limitations and data protection regulations for Number-Independent Interpersonal Communication Services (NIICS). Gatekeepers must design online interfaces that do not undermine user autonomy, provide reminders, and ensure fair access to datasets by altering data to mitigate identification risks and imposing contractual measures on third-party undertakings for data access and compliance monitoring. Their conduct is subject to examination for compliance with both the DMA and GDPR, and they may have a "main establishment" under the GDPR. They are also separate controllers under GDPR for their own data processing and have obligations under Article 6(4) and Article 8(1) of the DMA.

Under GDPR, Consent Consent, in the context of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), is a fundamental concept for lawful processing of personal data. The GDPR defines consent and establishes it as one of the six lawful bases for processing personal data, explicitly listed in Article 6. It also sets forth specific conditions and requirements for valid consent, notably in Article 7, with Article 4(11) providing a crucial definitional baseline. The legal framework of the GDPR governs the validity of consent, playing a significant role in assessing whether consent is freely given, particularly as outlined in Article 7(4) and Recital 43. This framework includes stricter standards for how consent must be obtained and managed, requiring controllers to ensure their consent mechanisms are fully compliant with GDPR provisions. For specific types of sensitive data, such as biometric data, processing requires consent that adheres to the stricter requirements of Article 9(2)(a) GDPR. Furthermore, the notion of consent within the ePrivacy Directive is interpreted in light of the GDPR, aligning with the consent requirements provided by Articles 4(11) and 7 of the GDPR. This emphasizes that for data processing activities, particularly those involving cookies and similar technologies under the ePrivacy Directive, GDPR guidelines for consent must be followed to ensure legality and adherence to an internationally recognized privacy standard.<SEP>Consent is defined and regulated under the GDPR as one of the legal grounds for processing personal data.<SEP>The GDPR provides the legal definition of "consent" for data subjects.
